review:
From a gameplay perspective, this is a fantastic game with excellent sound design, music, and, I would say, atmosphere—though I can’t fully experience it. You’d expect a game set in what’s essentially an empty void with scattered islands to run well, but the reality is quite the opposite.

I encountered performance issues even with the demo. Granted, I run the game at 1440p, but even on the lowest settings, I could only manage an average of 40-50 FPS. Performance would frequently dip even lower when exploring or when more islands came into view. While the developers have made significant improvements since the demo, the performance is still far from acceptable. For a game that appears so lightweight, this level of optimization is, frankly, disappointing.

As much as I love the game’s concept and unique design, I sadly can’t give it a positive review in its current state. The only way I managed to achieve a stable 60-70 FPS was through AI frame generation—which is hardly a real fix. Without further optimizations, the performance remains a major drawback to an otherwise incredible experience.

review:
(This review could be changed in the future) When games are cocky enough to release themselves in early access, I'm cocky enough to leave an early review. This game is a very good concept and I honestly think that the actual gameplay is very fun. Here are my issues with the game:

1: THE ISLANDS ARE WAY TOO SMALL and there are not a whole lot of resources that you need on most of them. For example, when I was making my first island ship, I didn't have enough rope to build enough sails because I had already milked all the resources that i needed in order to make rope on all the other islands resulting in me having to create MULTIPLE new games just to get more myker fibre to make more rope and then bring it back to my original world, but in conclusion, for this problem is that if the islands were bigger, it would just be a lot more fun to explore and I feel like it would make the game FEEL a lot fuller and obviously the problem with finding resources could easily be fixed with having MORE islands to explore which leads me to my next issue.

2: THERE AREN'T NEARLY ENOUGH ISLANDS. In survival crafting games like these, you should be able to get an INFINTE amount of resources, but things tend to run out when you have a very limited amount of space in the world, which was what led me to have to create multiple new games to get the myker fibre on the corrupted islands to make more rope. I don't think this game is proceduraly generated. I know the starting islands aren't, but that could be something that they could think about doing later on.

3: IT IS VERY UNCLEAR ON HOW TO PROGRESS. When I glide around to other islands and learn a bunch of new crafting recipes, almost all of them require ingredients that I have never seen before and have no idea on how to get. With my experience playing this game, as of right now I have 3.5 hours of play time and I have probably spent 30 minutes on google searching how to find or make something in this game, because there is no clear guide in the game.

CONCLUSION: I know that this game is in early access, but they knew that harsh, but truthful reviews like this one would come out as soon as they released it. I will still continue to try and play the game for the time being, and hope that they make changes in the future, but sadly, most early access games never make any changes. Let's hope this one's different. That's why there needs to be more people like me to advise the developers as soon as the game releases on what they are doing wrong so they can't make too much money at first so that they can end up making a good game overall once it's out of early access. As right now though, as fun as I think this game is to actually play, I cannot recommend this game. I made this review so detailed because I want to believe in it and I think this game has a lot of potentiel. If I just flat out hated the game, I would've just left the review at "not recommend" and wouldn't have said anything. Please make me change my opinion in the future.

review:
So, this is a thumbs down review, but not because of gameplay reasons. Rather, it's targeted specifically for people who've had motion sickness in games and for those who intend to play solely in third-person. If motion sickness isn't an issue for you and you intend to play exclusively in first-person, feel free to ignore this review.

I, myself only occasionally experience motion sickness in first-person games, but this is the first time I've ever experienced it in third-person mode. Despite lowering camera sensitivity to 25% (below which it felt too slow to be playable), I still logged off feeling mildly ill and having a headache. I'm sure this isn't something everyone will have a problem with, but if you've ever experienced motion sickness in a game before, I'd go into this expecting a refund to be in your near future.  

Additionally, I found the third-person mode to have very poor animations and more challenging targeting. This does not feel like a game in which equal levels of attention and resources have been applied to both modes, it feels like a game developed primarily for first-person with third-person added later. Think Skyrim here; does third-person exist? Yes. Is it as playable and polished as first-person? No. That's something that could potentially be improved upon throughout early access, but it's not there as of the time I'm writing this.

review:
i'm gonna keep at this for a little longer, and this is a review from the early access version of the game, so I hope it doesn't age well, but I don't recommend it at the moment. The concept is incredibly novel, the game is beautiful, and the design is perfect for a cozy experience. The problem is, if you're going to make a survival building game, the survival and building need to be enjoyable, and at the moment, they aren't.

The gathering action is bad. It's not responsive enough, so it takes a half-second of staring at a thing before you pick it up. That sounds like not a long time, but there's a lot to gather here. There's a function in the game that occasionally highlights gatherable objects, but it's gone so fast, you'll see something out of the corner of your eye, but not find it, and there's no way to re-trigger that effect except to sit around and wait for it to happen again. All in, it feels clunky.

Tools are incredibly unfun. Basically, you click to swing, and then a timer pops up, and if you click again at the right time, you swing again, a little faster. Fine, in theory, but if you time it perfectly, swinging feels cumbersome and a little slow. If you time it wrong, it is positively glacial. Nothing about it is tactile, and, much like the gathering, if you're not pointed exactly where you need to be, you won't hit it.

Then there's combat. A game like this doesn't need a LOT of combat, but it should feel exciting, or at least interesting, when you do it. You swing your weapons exactly like you swing your tools, which means there's no way to attack quickly. The weapons injure enemies, but they don't react to being hit, so you'll hit them mid-swing, and they'll follow through and hit you. And when they hit YOU, you are thrown backward, and have to run back toward them to fight. It's not HARD to figure out how to fight them, but it's ponderous, slow, and again, there's nothing kinetic about it. Much like in material gathering, I don't feel like I'm HITTING anything.

This is early early access, so I'm hoping these things get resolved. But until they do, I just can't suggest playing the game.

review:
If you want a sandboxy, creative, flying island builder: this is a great game. If you're looking for more than that, you're going to want to wait for a bit more polish

I cannot reccomend it because of what it promises through it's tags (and it's description) as some are objectively false. This is not a survival game, you do not need to survive. Food water and sleep are not critical to staying alive, there is nothing, aside from combat that threatens your survival and even if you die in the slog that passes for combat, there is no punishment to dying, you just respawn. That's it, there's no stakes or tension.

The devs describe the game as a "feel-good, cozy survival" game but the feel-good part is being held back by a lack of focus. 
-Combat isn't engaging, the only thing that spices it up are the special attacks wich require stamina that takes too long to refresh. Because there's no death penalty, enemies are a hurdle rather than a threat
-The inventory management is tedious, and if you're hitting up an island with a bad ecosystem you'll be bringing a stupid amount of resources to account for every single thing that can be wrong
-you're constantly rifling through the 4 different inventory menus to move things on the hotbar because you have too many different tools that do different things clogging it up (remove dorkip and put its functionality into the pickaxe, same for the sickle and sword)
-the island-to-island resource gathering suffers from the late-game raft issue where very quickly you'll start going through the motions rather than exploring a new island.

If there is ever an update that updates the combat and adds more settings to world generation (survival mode, resource density, death penalties) hit me up and I'll adjust this comment and sing aloft's praises, but for now I cannot say it delivers what it promises.

review:
THE GOOD:
The exploration and expansion of resources is fun, along with the three different biomes. The building part of the game works well and there are a fair number of building pieces to choose from, allowing for creativity and enjoyable builds.

THE BAD:
The pace of the game is absolutely terrible.
Early game is okay. You will spend forever flying from one patch of islands to another, then going from one island in the group to another, picking up sometimes just one of a resource from an island, sometimes a few, never more. Chests' rewards for finding them is always "Meh". By mid-game you're going to be mostly looking for more recipes to build parts of buildings. This is when it starts to slow as you start to rush from one group of islands to another, check them all one by one for recipes, before moving the the next group. The mini game to revitalize the "sick" islands starts to feel like a nuisance that's just in your way. At some point you will have recipes to make things that you CAN'T make because you're missing other recipes to make the equipment to process the right resources. Best example is the sawmill. I had a recipe from early in the game that I could NOT use without boards, but I couldn't make boards without the sawmill. I searched forever for the thing, found broken ones everywhere, even from the start. The game became a real slog at that point and I was feeling frustrated. But since I had been having fun earlier in the game I stuck with it until I found the sawmill recipe on the other end of the map (which took FOREVER to fly my island to).

But it didn't end with the sawmill. Once I had it, I went back to building a bit, and exploring for more building recipes. The game became repeatitive at that point, and I started seeing lots of the same exact islands - copy/paste style. But then I found ALL the recipes and figured I'd make my way to the center of the map. Nope winds are too strong despite the highest tier sails. So... what to do? I've spent hours now flying back and forth across the map, just WAITING for the travel to happen, thinking I'm missing some final recipe needed to unlock the center. Thinking maybe I have to go in from a specific spot, maybe I have to reveal all the available tiles first, maybe I have to visit all the islands marked by an atlas stone. Nope none of those things. The game does not help guide in this.

I have finally decided to throw in the towel and move on from this game, leaving unfulfilled, never to return. In the end I wish I had stuck with other building games that have more content, better visuals, frequent updates, and a SUSPICIOUSLY similar glider system for movement...

review:
Eh... where do I begin....

I guess, first what I'll say is that I realize it is in Early Access. 

Then I'll state the positives. The concept is very unique and neat and the base building aspect is enjoyable - though a bit wonky sometimes). The visuals of the sky are pretty as well for what it is.

But, after playing for quite some time, I realize that the game is a skeleton of one. An empty adventure.

It seems that the devs were so set on making a large map, that they completely overlooked the core of what the player enjoying an adventure game gets excited about - and its simply this - finding cool loot.

You spend hours searching countless islands, find caves, get excited, search cave, empty. Repeat this 50+ times and its really frustrating. This also applies to buildings that are massive, chests you loot that contain wood and stone, and various other things. The work you put into the game exploring, gives you NOTHING.

The devs might argue that you'll find these knowledge stones that teach you various things - but some of these stones require you to 'restore the islands ecosystem' by adding bugs, planting trees, repairing birdhouses - its a hassle. The last 2 islands I just did, it took me a while, and my reward? A trellis recipe on one island, and the same trellis recipe (but a different shape) for the other. Thats like slapping me in the face through the screen for searching for something worthwhile loot wise that gets me excited to continue.

The combat is very childish and not challenging (even though the enemies do quite a bit of damage) - it just feels like a childrens game.

I'm just mainly bummed that I love adventure games with base building - but the entire idea of finding cool loot that get you excited in exchange for the time you took exploring/fighting/ect is missing entirely.

Oh yeah, I forgot to mention that it is optimized poorly. My PC runs it fine,but my GPU gets really hot when my island is parked. When I'm 'driving' around - temps go down. I see much lower temps on demanding games.

review:
-----------------------
Disclaimer:

I believe in a game being GOOD or NOT GOOD.

Not "It's good for the money" or "buy it if it's on sale" or "It has the POTENTIAL to be a good game" or "It's EA so it might be good eventually"

No.

IS IT A GOOD GAME at the time that you invested your time and energy into it, was it GOOD compared to OTHER good games?

That's what I go by.

If a developer posts shovelware, but it's only $.50... it's still shovelware.
--------------------------
What they do good, they do great.

The ambience, visuals and graphics are amazing.

Beyond that, it all kind of falls flat.

It has a pointless building mechanic that apparently doesn't matter even slightly since you can build workbenches outside, sleep outside (even in the rain), put your storages outside, etc.

The whole "Look, Wendy I can fly!" thing is fun for about 5 minutes, then it becomes realistically the ONLY way to get around since all the islands are tiny and spread apart (the 5 or 6 that exist so far anyway)

The whole ONE monster you can fight is only on specific islands that are "corrupted" and you have to kill a tree with two roots so you can basically ad-nauseum loot the island.  Just like you did on the last 5 islands.

The only real difference in the islands appears to be the rare nodes where you can "learn" something you can craft that really has no impact whatsoever.  You can literally fly from start to finish across ALL islands at the very start.  Collect all the learning nodes and ignore everything else. That's.... pretty much it.  Then you go back to YOUR island and "build" things that have relatively no impact beyond being just something to build.

That's it.

That's the game.  it's basically a cozy builder with an opt-in fight if you happen to need/want to go to an island that's corrupted. 

Beyond that, there isn't much to do.  Will it get better?  maybe, but as it stands NOW is it a good game?  It's a building simulator and a lukewarm one at that.  Not the "survival" game it's billed out to be.  Not eating does nothing, not drinking does nothing, falling does nothing, if you die... you get a message saying "I should go home" and get respawned a few yards away with half health.  It's anything but a survival game.

So if you like cozy games, this one is for you.

review:
The pros :

The updates are adding more gameplay, more structure, more exploring. That's a very important piece of gameplay. 

They have included more challenges, more glider types, more character customization. 

I like the upgraded tools, and the ship building mechanics. 

The recent updates to how restoring an ecosystems works is very peaceful, and satisfying.

The cons : 
There's no instruction on the fact that you have to go to every island. I assumed the game worked how previous iterations worked, where you could skip some islands and still be fine, you just wouldn't have all of the building options available to you since they'd be locked. You'd be down on some rare resources. This was not the case, and I got locked out of advancement for skipping one island chain near the start of the game, and had to spend 40 minutes backtracking. 

The base-building options are ugly. You don't have the amount of freedom I wish you did, so even if 90% of the block you're placing is out of the ground it won't let you place it. This creates a jagged edge, and overall just limits style choices. The blocks themselves are also unpleasing to the eye, an example being that you can't fit all the stairs together in a neat fashion. Why are the endgame hardwood stairs not stackable? The final stair in a set is longer, and it creates an awkward plateau. The trellises also don't fit inside all of the window/frame options, and the window options themselves have rendering issues, meaning any building you attempt to add a window to looks weird. 

In order to plant seeds, you need to place down a dirt mound, and then place a single seed. That would be all great and good and all, but why does it only spawn a single, tiny plant after you do that? The game used to have lush forests available, and now it doesn't. The trees also seem to drop less saplings than before. 

Possibly the worst part is that the wildlife doesn't feel real anymore. The birds/bugs/frogs don't wander about the island repopulating as they used to. They stay where I dropped them from my inventory for 2+ hours and just look strange. 

I hate to see updates in an early access game push the game backwards. Unfortunately, that is how this game seems to be leaning.

review:
"Crying Over Competition"
★☆☆☆☆

Remember when Drug Dealer Simulator was the only game of its kind, barely hanging on with janky mechanics, stiff animations but over all a pretty fun experience and decent game to play? Good times. Well, fast forward to now when a game called Schedule 1 comes along a game that absolutely smokes DDS1 and 2  in every way, funny interactions, better drugs, better gameplay, actual depth… like, they made a really really good game.

And how does DDS respond? By suing them.
SUING. THEM.

Not improving their own game, not innovating, not taking the L with some grace and working harder, nope... They went full copyright copium. It’s giving salty. It’s giving insecure. It’s giving “we peaked with patch 1.2 and didn’t know what to do next vibes.”
Instead of just improving, adding more content? hell even dropping a good DLC or 2 to get players back into DDS, the studio behind DDS is now trying to drag others down because someone did their job better (alot better mind you) Imagine if Rockstar sued CD Projekt because Cyberpunk had cars. That’s how ridiculous this is.
At this point, Drug Dealer Simulator isn’t a game, it’s a cautionary tale. A story of what happens when you stop trying and start whining. If I wanted to watch a washed-up has-been throw tantrums over competition, I’d scroll FaceBook.

Save your money. Play Schedule 1. Support an actual dev who cares.

review: Saw it advertised.  Figured I would give it a try since it was only $9.99 and had a positive rating.  Two hours later, I can say it was cute but not for me.  A noir detective send up, The Duck Detective allowed for little actual mystery solving as the majority of the work is done through a mad-libs style interface where you fill in the major happenings in the story.  It is a simple little detective story with forgettable characters, tropes galore, and plenty of frustrating moments of trying to get all of your clue phrases from people so that you can solve the story.  While it did have some cute moments of animal humor, the vast majority of the game was repetitive and unrewarding.  I found myself committing to the slog so that I could just get it over with.  There were no real moments where I was glad I played the game aside from the first five minutes when I found out that you could make titular Duck Detective quack, he had an addiction to bread, and had a deep voice that made me chuckle at first.  If you are really bored, this might be fun for you but if you are looking for a really great detective romp, look elsewhere.  The best part of the game was the Paper Mario style art design that allowed for a whimsical take on a gritty noir mystery.  While it wasn't for me, it might be something that others enjoy.

review:
It's cute, but very short. Voice acting, character designs are pretty well done, but there's no substance. Despite being called Duck Detective, and being the main character, the game gives you nearly nothing about him and you get 1 case to solve, that's it. Would make a cute short kids game, but that doesn't seem to be the target audience given the deduction logic has some major stretches tl;dr not worth the full price. 

They did a lot of framework it just needs more content than it currently has, 10 or so deduction puzzles and 5 rooms. Pretty standard gameplay, find an item or dialogue, receive a clue word to use to make a deduction. ad-lib your way to solve the specific puzzle. You can solve the puzzle without finding all clue words as long as you've found the right ones. 

I felt a number of the puzzles were a bit of a stretch. Non-spoiler: Some of the dialogue is not repeated so although you can meta-game the answer (no consequence for guessing!) it's not ever explicitly stated. I'd be fine with that given it's a deductive reasoning type of game, but it really didn't vibe well when 99% of a puzzle is straightforward with 1 dangling piece that's a complete guess (and you can actually just brute force it) which happened three times for me because the sole clue seemed to be the proximity of a character to an object regarding the action taking place. 

For the spoiler: [spoiler] Kidnapping vs murder, zero context other than Sophie is gone. The bus as the place she's been placed. There's literally nowhere else I guess? I guessed that because the character I thought responsible was standing in that area. That's a hard stretch imo. The blackmail subplot, the puzzle that starts it pretty blank. So it's also a stretch because why would it even factor in? I thought that puzzle would be about the accomplices at first. Also severely disappointed I couldn't hand out consequences to the blackmailer. That's a crime too. [/spoiler]

Overall, I liked the concept as I love this genre and I'm happy to see where this developer goes, but I can't really recommend it for most unless it's either more fleshed out or on sale.

I really don't want to come off saying that Duck Detective is a bad game. The art style and visuals are great, the audio and voice acting are solid, and the mechanics behind the mystery gameplay are engaging.  And the low price point certainly lines up with the short play time.  But seeing that this is currently rated as Overwhelmingly Positive, I can't really bring myself to say that I recommend it.

The title character, Duck Detective, is woefully underutilized.  On paper, it is such a great character concept, with a catchy name and a striking visual design.  But there is very little relevance to the Duck part of the character.  I can only name three things: There is a dedicated Quack button, a core detective mechanic is a pun in which you make DeDUCKtions, and the character has a drug-like addiction to bread.  All of these are experienced within the first few minutes of the game.  For the rest of the game, nothing about being a duck is relevant, not mechanically, not narratively, not even for comic relief.  This game could have been Dog Detective or even Human Detective, and it would have been a nearly identical experience.  None of the other animal characters have any relevant animal quirks either.  For a game that screams "You are a DUCK!", they really don't seem to embrace that detail.

While the core mystery solving mechanics are enjoyable, a lot of the execution doesn't really come together.  There were a number of moments throughout the game where I felt like I had all of the information available to me, but I still didn't understand what DeDUCKtion the game wanted me to come to.  Because there's no penalty for getting it wrong, and you are just immediately informed when it is correct, there's incentive to just keep guessing until you stumble into the right answer.  Even after seeing what some of the DeDUCKtions were meant to be, I still didn't understand how you were supposed to come to that conclusion.  The game clearly marks everything you can investigate, so I feel confident that I didn't just miss something.  It would have been much more satisfying and enjoyable if the details of the case had come together more cohesively, instead of just arbitrarily coming up with conclusions that seemed entirely out of left field.

Those two major elements left me unsatisfied with the Duck Detective experience.  If $10 is no object and you want to see the game with the cute duck, by all means, go for it.  But if you were hoping for a genuinely great duck-centric mystery solving game, then maybe just keep your fingers crossed for the sequel.

review:
I give it credit for its art style and voice acting, but this is not a game that I would give a glowing review for.

The story is just very confused and muddled, and the goofy, nonsensical tone of the game doesn't help matters either. While I usually get on most other mystery game's cases for holding my hand too much, this one I found did the exact opposite. The clues are typically vague, and the suspects hardly ever give you any useful information. I STILL don't understand some of the conclusions that the detective came to, even after revisiting every piece of dialogue multiple times, and yet the game will act like it's all connected even though a player would still be very understandably confused like I was. Not even the hint system would give me a push in the right direction if I happened to be stumped; it constantly gives you the same generic advice of "I should make sure to talk with everyone" or "I should make sure to inspect everything." I sincerely don't understand why that was implemented if it's not going to provide anything substantial to the player.

Even the paltry fill-in-the-blank style gameplay just feels sorely flawed, and often feels like trial and error; I didn't feel like I was solving the mystery because I was connecting everything together, I was solving the mystery because the game was telling me that my word fields were wrong. Instead of it becoming a goal, it just became an inevitability because of the game allowing the player to brute force each deduction, which is a HUGE problem.

It's cute at best, but this is a mystery game worth skipping.

review:
Art style and voice acting are great. While I did enjoy going around picking up clues and such (although this might be tedious for some; as all I did was run around and made sure I did every single interaction possible; the map helped with this), the "solving the mystery" or "deduc(k)tions" aspect of the game is done through your little notebook / journal and you... kind of just fill in the blanks.

There were some majors details I noticed in the beginning, and so I immediately guessed on my own who the culprit was. But apparently instead of inputting the name of my primary suspect in the "deduc(k)tion", I had to key in "the Salami Bandit" because... I guess I wasn't supposed to have it figured out right from the get go? Even though it was kind of obvious who it was?

Other reviews have described the mechanic of the "deduc(k)tions" as something you can brute force by trial and error as long as you have all of the information. And I kind of agree with that. As I progressed through the story, my initial suspicions were backed up by the little clues I found here and there, but instead of feeling rewarded for guessing correctly from the start, I had to deal with collecting enough info to fill in enough blanks. And even though I knew where the game was taking me, I spent too much time mixing and matching the information just to see which combination or string of words would even fit.

Maybe others found it fun, but it's not my fave mechanic.

Game was cute. It has potential. But I guess I just had different expectations.

review:

I played with a partner, we had a few laughs, but mostly we didn't feel like we were investigating anything remotely rational, which means we ended up doing a lot of guesswork, and it worked, and then when the game validated our guesses, we didn't have any more clues as to why/how that was the correct guess. In the beginning you're just like "ah well it'll make sense soon" and by the end of the game you're either putting in the very obvious bits of information you gather or you do guesswork for the rest and it just feels random. I get the fact that the game wants to be humorous, and it does that a few times, but it seems like in this case it hinders the gameplay of actual puzzle deduction. For a spoiler, I'm not the only person here mentioning the [spoiler]kidnapping of Sophie and her current location[/spoiler] being information that is just guessed out of thin air.

In case you'd rather play something more serious about deduction, I would recommend Golden Idol instead.

review:
I wanted to like this a lot more than I did. I was in the mood for a point-and-click mystery and while this is cute and the characters and voice acting are fun, the mystery leaves a lot to be desired. I really liked the mechanics of how the investigations are done and conclusions are reached, but the vast majority of clues are spoon fed to you. Literally, there are screens where you can't move on to something else until you find all the clues. That makes the few times that there's a subtle clue so easy to overlook, not because it's hard but because it doesn't have a neon sign flashing "CLUE HERE!" in your face. But, if you do miss them, it also doesn't matter because you can just keep guessing at solutions until you get it right (and some of the solutions more or less force this approach since the wording doesn't always make it obvious what you're supposed to be concluding). When I finished, I actually checked to see if I'd accidentally turned on easy/story mode, but it was still off, which makes me wonder how much easier it can be.

Hoping this studio follows up with a better mystery and maybe a harder mode. I don't want it to be impossible, but I also don't want to feel like an eight-year-old.

review:
This game has enjoyable aspects but ultimately feels like a demo for a more full game. The visuals and voice acting are lovely and there is some fun parts to the writing but the mechanics have a lack of feedback and satisfaction that some tweaks could really add to - as it stands, the mystery solving is sadly far more unsatisfying than I would hope for a game in this genre. The short playtime doesn't give us enough time for the characters to feel properly memorable and frankly it also just doesn't quite feel worth the asking price. My biggest issue overall is probably the ending. 

If you are interested here is my explanation: 
[spoiler]Toward the end of this short game, two characters are revealed to be embezzling money from the company. You uncover this with evidence and they even admit to this crime as well as blackmailing openly in multiple endings. However, despite the game giving the player the option to arrest three characters in the end (including one who was unaware any wrongdoing was occurring) there is no option to arrest the embezzlers or resolve this in any way at all. With how unlikable much of the cast is and how many of them are implicated in the finale, I think an ending where you can arrest even more characters would only add to the comedy - you, a washed up duck effectively wiping this bus company branch off the map is a ridiculous snowball effect of being hired to investigate a stolen lunch. [/spoiler]

I hadn't intended for this review to sound so negative. The passion poured into this game is apparent. It is just frustrating that with a range of positives this game exemplifies, these fundamentals aren't quite there for me. I am very excited to see what these artists and devs make next and hope this in no way gives discouragement - I just wanted to be honest with my experience.

The main gripe that I had about this game was that a lot of the deductions that you need to make are just tenuous guesswork. The clues towards the end of the game don't really point you in any direction, so instead of being a puzzle to solve, it ends up at times being a case of just brute forcing your way through suspect names.

For a game that's as short as it is (around 2 hours), I would expect the story and the puzzles to be airtight. Sadly Duck Detective appears to have forgone logic and puzzle design in favour of (admittedly adorable) art.

Other instances required logical jumps that made no sense, even with the answer in front of me.

Too much frustration, not enough clarity of logic and clues.

So disappointing. It's two hours long and I didn't even want to finish it.

On the positive side, it looks nice - the Paper Mario style works really well, the UI is clean and the main character's voice acting is great (although some other characters sound like they're doing a bad impression of an accent - the janitor has the worst English accent since Al Pacino in The Local Stigmatic).

But it just doesn't hold up as a detective game. The story itself is boring and the "collecting clues to make deduc(k)tions" mechanic falls apart quickly. Half of the game is trying to guess what the game is thinking as it hasn't given you enough information to form a proper conclusion, and the other half is the game propelling itself forward by inventing things out of thin air. The most effective way to play is to brute force answers by picking the words which look like they'd fit the sentence most closely.

The process of collecting clues is also tedious. Examining characters to find out more about them is mildly interesting (although it's nothing more than pointing to a feature and the game using it to leap to a conclusion on your behalf) but traversing the small environment is slow and the map, which tells you which characters or items you need to interact with at that point, is inconsistent - it shows a coffee machine and a work bag as apparently important items, but you can't interact with either at any point.

Not for me unfortunately.

name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
This is a cute idea and a short game with a cute premise, fun writing, great animation, and great voice acting.

Unfortunately, it feels more like ad libs the game rather than actually solving a mystery. I spent more time just arbitrarily moving around words to see what stuck rather than actually questioning people or looking at evidence. There are clues and it does encourage you to think through things. But it's more annoying than actually exciting to solve anything, and some stuff I truly don't understand the reasoning for. After figuring out who was who, I got an, "Yay, that's over" feeling whenever I "solved" a section. I'm not sure if it's meant to be pointed that the detective reaches random conclusions about all the information he comes across, much of which is useless or contradictory, rather than leading straight to the solution.

I'm also not sure why looking at someone's public Blue Sky page, seeing a book promo, and checking out the book, is considered stalking. I know the protagonist is meant to be a parody of a hardboiled (lol bird puns /end sarcasm) detective, and thus hyper paranoid and also an asshole, but this particular rehash of "Facebook stalking" where people browse publicly and easily accessible information is very stupid.

I appreciate the idea of smaller point and click-style games rather than, say, the much longer Monkey Island or Grim Fandango-style ones, because those just take a while to go through (worth it for the journey, but longer games can be difficult investments). And I appreciate that, rather than having to visit everywhere again or write everything down, your inventory keeps images of all the clues you can easily browse back through. This is far more accessible than any other similar point-and-click game I've played. And I applaud that.

But I won't be playing the next one. I wish these developers the best, though!

review:
I wanted to LOVE this game so much. I love detective/mystery/puzzle games. And I love cutesy/cozy games. This feels like it's right up my alley. It made me a bit sad. :( 

It simultaneously felt too easy and too difficult. I felt like I could have done more if I had been given more options, more freedom. The focus of the game for me ended up being trying to find out what exact, specific words they were looking for that didn't always make sense. I wanted to focus on the clues and putting them together. The fill-in-the-blanks didn't always make sense to me, like I said, so that made the game difficult and frustrating. I ended up needing hints which was super annoying for such a short game. 

Finding the clues was super fun, but I wasn't able to deduct things from the clues. It was as if I was finding clues just to find them. Because the focus was...the fill-in-the-blank stuff. Ugh. That probably made intuitive sense to some people's brains, and they probably loved this. It's just not what I expected. 

The vibes are so fun, goofy, and engaging. The voice work, story, and animation are stellar. I wish it had a replay value, because I would have loved to have experienced all of that again. I really, REALLY enjoyed that part of it. I wish I could give it a "maybe." But, ultimately, I don't recommend it, unless maybe it's really on sale.

review:
(I hate the rating system on Steam. I don't think this game is bad, I just wouldn't recommend it)
This is a very close recommendation from me, but it's just not there.
The art is nice, the voice acting is great, the humor is cute, dumb and silly.
I do like the actual story - it's very silly, but rides that silliness all the way. And for the most part, I liked trying to piece together the story.

But, man, I've played quite a bit of detective games now, and some of these puzzles were just... whack. Too often I just looked at a "quest" and thought "Why is that relevant for the case?" or "I have literally no information on that". But most egregiously, I was able to easily brute force solutions (which I hate even being able to do, because I want to SOLVE it), because there are so few combination of inputs, that you can just kinda deduce from that instead of from engaging with the story/gameplay. There's still a handful of them that I don't know how you were even supposed to deduce.

The puzzle I disliked the most was [spoiler]cracking the safe code[/spoiler]. It just made no sense narratively to me. Why would Duck Detective (and the player for that matter) ever think that [spoiler]there being two desks[/spoiler] was significant in any way?? [spoiler]They're just randomly highlighted numbers[/spoiler]! Or the fact that you had to piece together that [spoiler]Margaret was planning a surprise party.[/spoiler] Why was that important to progress? And how was I actually supposed to figure it out? I have a bad feeling, that some crucial information is given ONCE in a cutscene, and if so, that is ridiculous.

After the [spoiler]safe[/spoiler] puzzle, I just kinda hit a point of annoyance I couldn't bounce back from, and I had a hard time enjoying the rest of the game. Which is a shame, because there's a lot to love!

review:
TLDR: currently not worth the price because of lack of content imo

Not worth 35 bucks/40 euros right now at this state, No Early Access badge, but feels like one with amount of content it has. 5 missions, 3 levels of access each, 2 missions later this year. I think it is around 6 hours of missions in total since I've completed half of them in my release time... Weapons do not feel good, because there is not so good feedback from shots, completely different feel compared to it's trailers. First game from Remedy that managed to feel like half-baked. No bugs encountered tho, but has an extreme lack of content on full release. I've played the playtest for a couple of hours and loved the concept, waited for the full release to add extra content. However, the only difference are 3 new missions that are shorter than those on playtest. While I like variety in how tasks look and feel, but they are either "go to first point, then next" or "bring item X to place Y", just with different objects and explanation behind them. There is no difficulty progression in missions (level 1 of first mission and last one take the same time to complete), because difficulty is chosen by party host before starting the mission, there is no incentive to play new levels other than to change scenery, because you were tired of previous one.

Don't get me wrong, game is fun to play sometimes, but I won't force myself to justify paying 40 euros on release for so little content. If they will update the game and add at least comparable to L4D content amount on it's release, then I could re-evaluate my opinion, but not now in this state of the game. If you want, play it, it is on Game Pass, I will pass...

review:
Unfortunately, FBC: Firebeak- despite being my most anticipated release of this whole year- Falls completely short of being a good game. 

First, when playing there is barely any guidance on what to do during a mission, just a short dialogue from the radio-guy and you're set off to run around and figure it out yourself.

Second, most of the cool utility mechanics that you see in the trailer are NOT accessible on hour 0 of your playthrough. They must be unlocked with in-game tokens similar to the medals of Helldivers 2. But now imagine locking behind core gameplay features of a kit behind a warbond page, how ridiculous is that? Artificial content-locking I say.

Third, acquiring these ingame tokens are very one dimensional. Aka, just kill an enemy with a screen-wide healthbar and pick up their dead drops. Very engaging, I know.

Fourth, Mission lengths. The point of Co-Ops is to play through a whole mission with your team and complete it as a team, that's what makes it fun. Here? You drop in for 5 minutes running around aimlessly randomly shooting hiss that spawn with no real reason nor choreographed waves until you accidentally complete an objective and press a button to extract in less than a minute. That doesn't feel rewarding or stressful or fun in any way shape or form. By the way, notice how I said an OBJECTIVE, SINGULAR.

You drop in to do ONE THING AND THEN LEAVE. 

In a cramped map that IS ALWAYS THE SAME.

With a kit you MUST SPEND TOKENS TO HAVE FUN WITH.

With guns that BARELY KILL ANYTHING.

Trying to do missions that are BORING.

This is the type of torture people infected by The Hiss go through, this is probably what they have to play in their heads whilst floating in the air, where I get to play as an actual cool character with cool mechanics in Control.

Heed this warning, Remedy. Go back to making Alan Wake 3, lest you figure out this type of game isn't a loop, but a spiral for this studio.

review:
[b]I love Remedy games with all my heart, but this one is straight up dogshit.

Gameplay feels very boring and repetitive. Movement is very slow and stiff. All weapons feel the same and unresponsive, you just hold one button and shoot crazy zombies. To heal you need to run to the very beginning of location and stand in shower for about 5 seconds. To refill your ammo you need to run to the beginning of the location again, stand infront of some thing and press Q and E, or go look for some bunker. There are like 3 enemy types: zombie, spongy guy and zombie in flying chair. There are about 5 different missions, each takes place in different location, but all missions feel the same. You are sent to a revamped location from Control, you fix some shit by pressing Q and E and kill zombies. There are also some “bosses” that are actually just same zombies with a lot of hp. All missions are finished in 5-10 minutes.

No voice or text chat in coop game that they think worth 40$. That is honestly unbelievable. 

I chose a mission and waited for someone to join my squad, but for some reason no one ever joined me. I was only able to play with other players if I play quick game. New weapons are unlocked through something like battle pass. In general, the progression here is not interesting.

FBC Firebreak looks like a game that was made by an indie team of 10-15 people and released in early access, the only difference is that FBC has "AAA" graphics. It seems that in mid development they did not know what to do with this game but still decided to release it hoping for a miracle.

Do not even think about buying this game even with a discount. If you have Xbox Game Pass and you are thinking of trying this game, trust me this shit is not worth an hour of your time.

I think fate of this game is obvious - in a month it will be at 50% discount, they will release content they promised, and gonna abandon this disgrace.[/b]

review:
Personal experience and opinion from playing at launch

The game has quite a nice foundation and I see the vision, I want to like it, but in practice is not fun moment to moment, so will refund for now and wait to see if in a month or a few it gets better

In general my biggest complaint is how sluggish and unresponsive the entire game feels, not in a technical aspect as it runs fine for me, but in that it always feels like you don't get a good feedback of what you're doing, click a button in the UI? have to wait a second before the game notices it, characters feel slow, base weapons feel like toys (and the melee is laughable), it's hard to tell if you're even damaging enemies as it seems their health bars take a second to update after you hit them, animations feel slow, the "press Q and E" QTE is just kinda annoying and repetitive, and so on and so on

It's understandable wanting to make the player feel like they're struggling, but making the game feel like walking trough mud, shooting nerf darts, and hitting with a pillow is not the fun kind of struggling. (And don't come to me with "the game gets better later", a game should feel good from the start! Even if you feel underpowered the game should feel engaging and like your actions are meaningful)

This is more situational probably because it's launch day, but I honestly could barely play online, as I was constantly being disconnected in the middle of the missions, out of the dozen or so I tried playing, could only get trough 2 in their totality, every other I got a connection error or got kicked for seemingly no reason

And what didn't help that is how few missions there are, I got to play "shoot the stickies in the office" quite a few times more than anything... (why is there no way to select which mission you want to play in quick play?)

Not a 'bad' game, but certainly not engaging when you have options that are better in many aspects from the start

review:
It's another fun first-person 4-player PvE co-op game. You know the type: L4D2, Vermintide, Darktide, Deep Rock Galactic, etc. 

- FBC's early progression system means you won't have access to much at the very beginning, but your options will open up a lot the more you play. There are a lot of unlockables to work towards, which you can see in your Research menu and Requisition menu. 
- Game objectives are varied like games like Outlast Trials and The Blackout Club, while also having plenty of combat like Left 4 Dead 2, Deep Rock Galactic, and GTFO. 
- Game session length (called Clearance) is customizable just like the mission difficulty at the mission lobby. Missions can be very short or much lengthier, and the short ones are surprisingly short, reminding me of Warframe's mobile defense missions. This will definitely be convenient for people wanting to squeeze a little game time into busier days.

BAD:
- Menu keybinds are weird/bad and too varied in a lot of specific instances. Usually, this is a hallmark that a game was made for controller/gamepad. Also, the Requisition page is nigh identical to the battle pass-esque catalogs in Outlast Trials, and unlike the catalogs, you can't use the mousewheel to scroll through Requisition pages.
- You may often lose connection with the host, sending you back to the main menu. This is the worst part of the experience.

Honestly, I love Remedy. I love Max Payne, Control, and I love their universes. This feels like a hollowed out shell of a game that still needs many months to bring to market. The fact that there's a deluxe DLC selling a bundle of cosmetics makes me feel like this is almost a timeshift attempt at revenue to either offload or continue working on this.

I wouldn't buy this right now unless you've got a friend stack and are truly, truly dedicated to playing something set in the Control universe. It's also on gamepass, which I think gives this a MUCH better avenue for experimentation and deciding if you value this. To charge $40 for this feels insane. I'd maybe comfortable paying $9.99.

review:
I've been really excited about visiting FBC Firebreak so I hope to provide some helpful feedback to others while benefiting the game overall <3 This review is day one with about ninety minutes of play. I do not intend to refund the game right now, and hope to change my recommendation. I've seen reviews say you need to spend more time with it, and I hope that's true, but this is how I feel right now, as a simple excited gamer.

I love a lot of Remedy, especially Control, and was drawn into Firebreak almost exclusively for this reason. This world and the FBC are very intriguing and it's a fun universe to fit this type of game into. The big and bold FBC level intros and their fonts put me right back into The Building, the voice acting has been welcoming more than distracting, the soundtrack fits; I am okay with the premise of this game in the universe and was never wholly torn away from immersion. Big plus!

I love shooting stuff, especially when it feels good. I'm not a competitive FPS player, barely even a casual in the genre. Shooting stuff feels pretty good to me here so far. The starting weapons have a good punch to them, and I think the feel fits in with the aesthetic. Does the feeling compare to picking up and shooting the Director's pistol in Control? No, but it doesn't seem to be going for that exact vibe, and it does have that Remedy charm and production quality.

BUT, for someone looking at Firebreak right now who doesn't have a shared love of Control or friends to play with: I'm not sure there's enough here gameplay wise right now to justify the purchase. 
I don't know really know what's going on from the moment I boot up the game. The tutorial didn't really help me understand the aspects of the game I would want the tutorial to explain to me. 
I have mostly shot stuff, and won. There have been a couple mechanics, like running over a bunch of sticky notes and cleaning them off in the shower (which I though would culminate in the big sticky note boss from the trailer, but I guess that's at a higher level), 
but otherwise I have shot stuff, got on an elevator, and have either moved on to another 10ish minute round with the same party or been forced back to the menu to queue again; positively both of which were quick and seamless options. Adding another plus here, I have had zero connectivity or performance issues in my time with the game.

This is a somewhat unique blend of an established single-player franchise and multiplayer genre, and as long as they can pull off somewhat captivating gameplay, the strength of the franchise and production budget can carry a lot of weight. However, Elden Ring Nightreign just came out, and it's hard not to make some comparisons, especially at the same price point. For a three-player romp through an established franchise in Q2 2025, this game is outclassed.

My main takeaway is that I feel good about casually shooting stuff and getting some easy wins, especially in a universe I'm happy to explore more of, but this feels a tad like an early access release without a hook in a sea of similar games it may drown in.

review:
When reviewing this game, I had to think to myself what it is that really makes this one miss the mark. What makes games like Deep Rock Galactic, Earth Defense Force, and Risk of Rain 2 succeed where this one fails.

Let's start at the gunplay. It's bad. Each class can use any of the weapons, but none of them feel good fundamentally to use. They are unbalanced for a horde shooter and lack punch when you use them.

The music is bad. The exit music that happens every time you exit a level is just horrible, and when horde waves come through, there is no audio indicator that this is happening to really amp you up for things getting serious. That being said, the boom box  gadget has a song I found really pleasant to listen to.

The classes and gadgets, while varied, don't do enough to make them that impactful. Your classes do unlock more gadgets to help that, but with the game length being less than 4 hours to complete. Unless you grind previous levels, you may not even play with unlockable gadgets.

The level designs are simple and small and don't change at all between runs. You must do the levels in 3 intervals: the first section - then extract, the first and second - then extract, then all three sections together. That leads to playing the same levels over... and over again. With a singular level having a boss battle out of 5.

All this to say, the game is just boring after the first time you do the game loop. You have seen it all. The same 4 enemy types, the same levels, the same bad gameplay loop. What a miss this was, I was very excited for this one. This is just an unfinished, early access title sold for full price. I'm definitely  looking at Remedy Entertainment a bit differently now.

If you're going to have a perk system, why not encourage it add more replay variety through it than just get a different weapon? Why have different weapons when barely any of them change anything about each kit? (jumper is basically the only one) All these issues and more so make this feel mundane and boring to play through, even with friend. This is basically an early access game, which wouldn't be a problem if this wasn't retail and released as it is. Get the game when its on sale, not for the price it is now and don't expect much replay value/ want to finish through the entire game

review:
It's cool, but definitely not fully fleshed out and realized. The game could have really benefited from random level generation to increase replayability. The missions are always the same set pieces, which means players will get very familiar with the levels in time. Although I admit at this point I'm not sure how randomized objective locations are within these set pieces. So far they seem very much the same, with maybe some elements being placed differently, but not varied enough. But there are some fun ideas here, just wish the level structure was more varied each time.

Now the enemies in the game. There just isn't enough variety here either. Pretty lacking. I feel like only one mission has a unique enemy in it. But you'll be combating the same handful of enemies every mission, and they also just aren't interesting to fight really.

And unfortunately weapon variety here is yet again, lacking. What's here is alright, but I feel it needs more, and weapon cuztomization. The gadgets you unlock access to as you progress are fun, but again, I feel like there should be more choices here. Each class just has their 3 unique gadgets. Which are useful and fun, but give me some more alternatives for each class. All in all, I want more loadout options with more guns and gadgets/tools.

Also, no text chat or even voice chat. Just a ping system. Kinda hard to communicate with your fellow players. As of right now everyone is new and a lot of people are very clueless as what needs to be done during a mission, as it isn't very obvious in some cases.

There will be two major updates later this year, one in the fall and in winter. Both of which are to include a new mission and new enemies. And also new gameplay systems, not really sure what that means. And of course some new unlockables. Hopefully those are weapons and gadgets.

Still, I am enjoying it and I want to continue unlocking everything and play all the classes and see how it feels when I get even more familiar with the game.

Update -
I have to say, once you start playing harder missions with corruption and have competent team mates, the game becomes quite a bit more fun. Abusing the elemental damage types and combining them together just melts enemies. A splash kit user and a jump kit user working together to just shock hordes of enemies is very satisfying.

review:
Bad game that can eventually be good, and i will change my review if they manage to fix the problems this game has.
I wont repeat what is already here but i will say my 2 cents.

The game wants you to stick together via the shield system which is good, however the game does not want you to team with friends as the party system is convoluted, and the game is designed around having 3 people in the game at once. In fact the game encourages quick play with randoms. This game NEEDS a communication system. You cannot communicate with your team in literally any way other than your characters auto callouts which tell you literally nothing. 
Are you on fire and dying? Character says "Damn!"
Are you being encased in sticky notes or goo? Character says "Damn!"
You cant say "I need water" if you are going to burn out, you just need to trust the random guy to do their job well or you suffer and die slowly. The only way to get someones attention is to friendly fire them, intentionally frustrating design for no reason.
Also the Jumper kit "Ultimate Ability" the gnome, is a buggy mess that sometimes works, and other times just sits on my kit and i can't use it at all until it suddenly comes out while Im shooting a different gun and it kills me. 
The missions themselves are fantastic too, but only at the higher levels of difficulty. There's no reason why the lower level missions only difference is the amount of rooms you get to go. Thats why everyone is saying the game has no content. A level 3 mission takes on average 30 or so minutes, its action packed! 
Remove the requirement to Unlock Levels 2 and 3 and or do away with the system entirely and make every mission max length and the only change is the difficulty. The corruption system is fine the way it is and honestly had me coming back.

review: Wanted to love this game as a Remedy fan, but as it stands, the sauce is just not there. Barebones, poorly optimized, and missing that extra spark that makes these role-based co-op shooters work. There is fun to be had, but it demands an outrageous amount of your time considering how minimal the content offering is. Modifiers don't make up for the meager 5 missions, and frankly, it needs at least twice that many to avoid feeling repetitive and stale. For the ludicrous $55 CAD asking price, Firebreak just cannot compete with the other games it's clearly drawing so much from, and it's disappointing to see Remedy completely avoid all the things that make their other games great - characters, story, interesting and varied settings, and great gameplay hooks. This feels like the suits took Sam Lake aside after spending 10 years on Alan Wake 2 and told him to make some money by year's end.

There is very limited enemy variety aswell, aside of your regular mooks, melee and with guns there is like 2 special mobs along with 2 elites.

Lastly the game is way too easy, at one point we just picked the highest difficulty and rushed through each mission with ease despite being rather unorganized.

The maps have no random element to it, they are always the same, they could have utlized changing layouts since the FBC building has a thing going for it of its changing layout and mostly non-sensical layouts which has not been utilized here at all.

There is some good however. The Kits you can choose from are pretty neat, the tools you are given are mostly pretty useful espicially the Splash kit. The controls handle well aside of minor gripes in the movement i have.

TL:DR: I was kinda hyped for this but despite the long dev cycle the game has not much to show for with alot of problems needing immediate adressing. It gave me the weird feeling anything coming out on Gamepass on release day might be a red flag.

review:
there is a lot here to like, but there's some major hiccups when it comes to player onboarding, progression, and matchmaking.
like, things i feel are fundamental to gameplay are never explained. equal to if helldivers 2 never explained that you can blow up bug holes with grenades. but instead you go crazy during a match with people you can't chat with, trying to piece together why bullets aren't working on the flying tambourine the game keeps telling you to neutralize. it turns out a limited use weapon you can pick up  is the only thing that can damage it and that can easily be used up on regular enemies by an unknowing teammate. (it looks like there's a mod that can add the "neutralizing" effect that sometimes works to your gun but that's not unlocked until level 19)
and that's just one of many, constant, frustrating moments of "figure it out yourself" 
and even when you do learn this you can't communicate to future teammates because there seems to be no in game chat. 
progression is also pretty ambiguous, turns out most class features are locked behind a helldivers style unlock shop, and not from leveling up the class itself. that class leveling is for mod install slots only for some reason. and so many fundamental class features and weapon upgrades are locked in the shop and not from a class or weapon progression.
and the matchmaking runs pretty poorly. But I can't tell if its because of matchmaking issues or in game bugs 
 and glitches. there's big stutters, enemies skipping around, interactions not registering, objectives being touch and go. and it acts as a compounding issue on the "figure it out yourself" gameplay, because you can't tell if you're doing something wrong... or the game just isn't working like it should.
i hate to say it because there's a lot of fun to have currently. but if you buy and play it now you're gonna be a beta tester. if you're not up for that, wait until the wrinkles are ironed out. 
If they are.

review:
I'll be frank. I saw this and thought "L4D in the Control universe? Hell yea!" Control is easily my favorite store-based game in the last decade.

This game... Does not play like L4D, nor Control. It plays a little more like Visceral Cleanup Detail with poor direction. I spent 40 minutes filling barrels and doing furnace maintenance. I spent another 30 with a broom sweeping up post-it notes. And then another 30 trying to get rid of some pests in the basement. Even when I was shooting and being shot at, it felt tedium, until a horde of 40+ enemies spawned and then I felt helpless, until I realized I could cheese it with the water gun.

The interact and fix-it mechanics are cool. I like the ideas for the classes (though the water one seems to be leagues above the others). I just... Can't help but feel that whatever it is they were going for here, they missed the mark. I played for 2 hours and felt like I was doing chores but getting nothing done. I quite two zones into the third mission.

____________________________________________________
EDIT: Alright.... I've put another 6 hours into this game. I've had a few realizations:

First off, it's more fun once you realize what it's asking of you. The new player introduction is harsh, there's goals and objectives given but how you make those happen is sorta missing. Once you've played through a mission once, it's a lot more fun. The first time is the worst. 

This, however, highlights the bigger issue: *There is no content.* I did 2 and a half missions at Clearance 3, thinking that this was the lowest tier. It was not, it was the longest tier. So.... I have now done all 5 missions (total!) avaialbe in-game. I have done them at the longest setting, and done them on the Hard difficulty. I have most all of the equipment unlocked. I am only 8 hours into the game total.

My review still has to say "Do not recommend". The game needs at least 2x the number of separate missions, and then each of these missions has to be like twice as long before I can recommend this.  Again, great concept, great setting... But the execution is still lacking.

ALSO: There's no chat of any type. No text, no voice. I've watched so many people run past the water foundations, their health bar so low it doesn't render, and I can't tell them what to do with the stupid water fountain, the ping doesn't highlight it... The new player experience is made worse by lack of ANY type of communication in game.

All respect to Remedy as they've got a good team behind the art, but it really seems like nailing gameplay is just completely out of their reach with their current team, it feels as if they haven't made a game with tight gameplay since Max Payne 2.

review:
[h1]I really wish I could recommend this game but at it's current state I just can't.[/h1]
I want to preface this by saying these are just my personal bad experiences and gripes with the game, I hope to come back to this review and edit it down the road and hopefully be able to recommend it! 

[h3]Starting with the negatives[/h3]
Me and my friends were so excited for firebreak we immediately purchased it as it came out. At first the content seemed plenty for a new live service game and we could look passed the bugs as they weren't game breakingly bad and more of a challenge if anything. 
Now 3 months from launch the bugs seem to have gotten a little out of hand and are frustrating us more than giving us joy. One day we can play and have the best of fun and then the next we can't even complete 2 jobs because the game refuses to let us revive, making us restart the game only for then the status effects to not be showing on your screen or healthbar and so you just die out of nowhere. Another one of my gripes has been the lack of content in 3 months, for a live service game this just feels too slow and i really hope to possibly see a build up to new content in the future. In game events would be really cool or even just new cosmetics for the inbetween periods like now, and id really love to see maybe a 'lore' tab with some of the files we collect in the oldest house the loading screens move way too fast to be able to read anything on them.

[h3]Now for the positives[/h3]
I really really love the witty voice lines between characters. Hank and jerry are so interesting to me and its been fun just puzzling their stories together from the few lines we get in the lobby menu. The game play loops are fun and challenging and I really love the different area's we get to revisit from control in a different way. Trying to come up with new perk sets for our individual play styles and strategise with different weapons feels really good. There's a lot of goofy funny things that can happen especially playing with the right group of friends when the game works it can be a lot of fun!

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
[b]Safe to say that firebreak sadly can't compete with other live service games at it's current state. However, I still won't give up hope and am looking forward to future updates! Please don't give up on this game it still holds so much potential it just needs that polish to make it shine.[/b]

review:
I’m going to be completely honest: this game can be great—amazing, even—but certain decisions and the lack of important bug fixes made the original release frustrating at times.

The core gameplay had potential. I loved the original five missions: they were fun, thrilling, and exciting. But they got old quickly, especially since the content pool felt thin. On top of that, the bugs made things worse and discouraged long-term play.

I waited until this most recent update to give my thoughts, and unfortunately, what I’ve seen so far is even more disappointing. The new mission cycling system feels like a miss. Sure, it’s a twist, but not one the game really needed. The update also changed the corrupted items—arguably the original mechanic that made the game stand out. Instead of being a consistent part of the experience, they’re now locked to randomized missions. While I understand the intent (to encourage players to try different missions for rewards), the scattered placement makes progression unreliable. Players can’t be sure whether they’ll get the resources they need to level up.

This game still has massive potential, and I don’t want to give up on it yet. But the direction it’s heading is worrying. The lack of content, frequent bugs and crashes, and questionable update decisions make it harder and harder for players to stick with it. If the developers don’t address these issues soon, they risk burying the game before it ever gets the chance to shine.

I genuinely hope they can turn things around, because there is still so much here worth building on.

For now It's not recommended, but I really hope to change this in the future if the devs turn things around.
