review:
I liked the idea behind this game; however, just after 6 hours of game play, I've come to notice the small things that could run a little better. With that in mind, I do see they are planning a relatively large update as of June of 2025, so I look forward to that for sure. Some of the updates I hope to see in the new version:

Weather:  It rains and thunders/lightening far too much and gets annoying after awhile so you can't play for too long at a time.

Shelving:  It can be time consuming and frustrating to attempt to place boxes on storage shelving as it sometimes just refuses to let you put two boxes on one shelf.

Boxes: Allowing naming on outside of box so you can see what you are looking for. Currently you can hover over the box and see the name, but it would be better with the picture.

Cart:  It would be nice to have a cart to haul multiple boxes into the store at one time rather than running around like a loose chicken back and forth.

More decorations/better lighting: I see decorations and furniture updates are coming in June.

I am also hoping the game will run less Janky once updated and I look forward to the update. 

For now, I recommended players to not buy the game in its current state. Once the update comes out in June, I will update my review.

review:
In the nineteen hours I've played Sengoku Dynasty back in it's earlier betas It was really enjoyable. Yes, some glitching was present. Load times are long, and the game needed work but you can tell it had potential from its former Medieval Dynasty Brethren. This game recently just had a massive update bringing QoL changes and man they look great, but also broke certain parts of the game in the process. I have had more NPCs with broken animations, Load times are still horribly long despite the update log saying they are reduced, Player Character animations break more then I've seen since I started a new save and in general this major update just brought minor aspects to the game that it needed prior. Nothing stunning. We now have farming, Player character now has needs, and you get more buildings for town, also a ton of bugfixes. 

While this is great progress I would save your money, buy or keep playing Medieval Dynasty and advise Toplitz Productions, who I believe are the publishers of these Dynasty titles to focus on one or two game titles and Quality control before pumping out another Dynasty game as they have 4-5 Dynasty titles now including this one and Medieval Dynasty. review:
I've played for nine hours and really want to be able to recommend this game but it is absolute garbage in its current state. Toplitz is making bank off of the 'Dynasty' title when Medieval Dynasty is the only good game in the franchise. 

The performance is awful and you can read the horror stories in other reviews but honestly there really isn't anything promising about the game at all aside from the general concept of a Sengoku period 'Dynasty' title ON PAPER. The dialogue is so amateurish that it's immersion breaking at times reading text that almost sounds like modern day teenagers talking. There are a handful of good musical tracks but the animations are the worst and the "water-color" style just come off as cheap. The music is also inconsistent and doesn't align with the weird cut-scenes. The model work and textures seem fine but there's nothing that really makes the game stand out at the moment. The character animations are terrible and sluggish most of the time and the amount of heads disappearing from characters randomly is comical. 

You have the option to play in either Third-Person or FPS but they haven't seemed to figure out how to make that work with the movement, building and combat. In FPS your character will frequently engage in a strange climbing animation that will cause your head to detach from your body and spin around so that you watch your torso and limbs "climb" up rocks and obstacles behind you though it makes zero sense because you can't "climb" over anything more than maybe 2 ft tall. In Third Person mode you have the issue of not being able to target properly. For some reason switching between modes seems to affect hitboxes for items and enemies. It's a strange problem that I don't even know how to better describe. It's most noticeable when it comes to building placement which is one of the biggest problems I have with the game.

The building placement is absolutely the worst aspect of the game after performance. The restrictions on where you can build and what can and can't obstruct placement is arbitrary at best. You can have a giant completely vacant lot with no foliage or objects in sight but for some reason you can only place a tiny building at a specific angle. This is SOMEHOW affected by your camera view as well! Sometimes you can't even place a building unless you switch to Third Person and vice versa. To top all that off sometimes when you initially place the building it will rotate it 90 degrees and now you have a door facing the wall of another building and the only way to fix it is to start over again which can take a LOT of time when trying to line things up in this HORRENDOUS system. There is no reason why there can't be some sort of means by which to align buildings in this game. Either that or they need to be FAR more forgiving with clipping. This especially rings true considering how difficult it is to even place an item. Half the time the 'placeholder' that you set down when you decide to build something doesn't even visually match what it turns into when you construct it leading to stairs and doors being in unwanted places. Did I mention you don't get your resources back once you've placed the flooring down which has to be completed BEFORE the game reveals to you that your building has been rotated? It also wastes hammer durability building and re-building. It wouldn't be that big of an issue if you could freely move doors and windows which you sometimes can and sometimes can't!

With all that out of the way I think the biggest problem with the game to me personally is that it doesn't feel Japanese at all. The icon for the game is just fake Kanji and it really symbolizes the crux of the issues with the aesthetics: this is a game that is trying to LOOK like it takes place in Sengoku era Japan. What the game is desperately missing and I suspect won't ever be fixed is that the game doesn't FEEL like it takes place in Japan at all. It feels like a cheap asset pack using the Medieval Dynasty engine with some lite nods to Japanese culture thrown in to pander to a western audience. It's so off-putting at times that I can't help but wonder who exactly involved in the development of this game is the one in charge of adapting Japanese culture because I find it hard to believe it's anyone with anything more than a superficial knowledge of Japan and access to Wikipedia.

It will take a LOT of work to fix the problems with this game. I know Toplitz games are notorious for poor optimization because I was barely able to run Medieval Dynasty when it launched but I'm fairly sure the gameplay mechanics can be fixed at least when it comes to building placement since it's a pivotal part of the game. The one thing that I will remain skeptical of until I see otherwise is the general vibe and aesthetic of the game. 

The most recent Kintsugi Update released with a trailer that is almost comically unaware of itself. Kintsugi is the art of repairing broken pottery with golden lacquer yet you have to carry 5 axes on you at all times because they're constantly breaking and you have to build new ones rather than repair the one you have. An update based on the theme of repairing broken items in a game that won't let you repair broken items. They also state that they chose the Sengoku setting because it was a time in Japanese history when anyone could become a daimyo. This is an absolutely ridiculous justification for placing a game in this era and is clearly just using the words Sengoku and daimyo because of their popularity in Japanese media and subsequent export to other countries. They make it sound like it was a period of upward mobility and social advancement when in reality it was a consolidation of power between multiple warring factions that bathed the land in blood. This game could take place at any point in feudal Japan with the premise of just being a refugee of war starting a village in the middle of nowhere yet they went with a false pretense. The decision-making at Toplitz is baffling.

review:
Shows promise – but clearly still has a long way to go. 
The landscape, day – night cycle, weather and changing seasons are visually impressive and immersive. 
Sadly, the same cannot be told for the people. There is no player customization, not even gender wise. The look changes somewhat depending on the clothes being worn, but these can’t be customized or dyed and there is a clear progression, that makes lower tier clothing obsolete. NPC villagers all look the same, although there are males and females. While you can produce clothing, you can’t make your villagers wear it. Or if you can, I didn’t find out how. 
Finding out how to do things is what I spent a lot of time doing. There was very little guidance inside the game. As can be expected, the game is also pretty grindy. I don’t mind resource gathering, but after having cut down enough trees to build the Spanish Armada, chasing logs tumbling downhill becomes repetitive. I feel on normal difficulty it would be reasonable to expect villagers to be able to provide for themselves, but there is always something missing, forcing you to stop doing whatever it is you were doing and running back to the village to stuff their mouths or wipe their …
Progression felt weird. There are a lot of different resources. Sadly, not all can be found around your starting village. Eventually, as you discover more of the area, you will come across other resources, but some of them are in constant demand, so you need to do resource runs. And there is always something missing. Not only quantity wise (your axe will soon be your best friend), but also quality wise. And then it is a matter of the hen and the egg. At one point, I was asked to produce steel tools. Naturally, the NPCs would not allow me to use their forge, so I had to go home and build one. But to build one, you need to be a certain “dynasty” level, which is mostly done by recruiting (otherwise mostly useless) villagers. And then you need other resources, and tools, which require new resources and buildings to make… the list is endless. Which would not be problematic, if there was some sort of natural progression. 
Combat felt like a transplant, something pushed into the game to make it less dull. After having bum-rushed by wolves for the third time, the charm wore off quickly though. For some reason, boars, wolves and especially bears are much harder than the NPC bandits. And unlike bandits, they don’t have a visible health bar, for some reason. I can understand the immersion factor in not knowing their health, but on the other hand, humans have a health bar, and so do your tools.
There is some sort of quest system in place, but it is very basic and honestly not much fun. It also decidedly needs more information on how to accomplish certain goals. 
Talking about basic: there is no voice over at all after the intro. Granted the conversations with the NPCs aren’t especially exciting anyway. 
For how basic the game is, it is surprisingly hardware-demanding. I had to tune down some of the recommended settings because my computer started to make worrying levels of noise. There really is no reason why such a quaint game should be more resource demanding than say Cyberpunk 2077. Clearly, optimization is possible (and badly needed).

Verdict: Would not buy again.
Recommendation: Wait a year and then buy for 20 $ or less.

review: This game is great and I was very captivated at launch.  Put the game down for a while and decided to give it another go a couple days ago to check out the new updates.  Still think it's a fun game, but is ruined by janky gamepad controls.  If you use keyboard and mouse, you probably won't run into as many issues, but many of the gamepad controls are completely broken.  The layout is fine, but many of them don't work as intended.  It's as though the different controls that are implemented for different interactions are fighting with each other.  For example, Y button crouches, Y button also interacts with merchants, but still activates crouch.  Right trigger should rotate structures while placing them, but instead cancels structure placement.  Also a problem I encountered for both gamepad and mouse is that when you hold the button to draw an arrow from bow, you release the button and sometimes the arrow doesn't shoot and the arrow remains drawn as though you were still holding the button down.  Spamming the shoot button doesn't shoot the arrow either when this happens.  Animal you were hunting escapes or attacking bandit kills you.  Very infuriating.  I love using gyro aiming and when I can, I use gyro as mouse because mouse is more responsive.  Few games allow gamepad and mouse functionality and this game is one of them, which is awesome, but when I activate gyro to mouse, a mouse cursor shows up on the screen while aiming.  Doesn't happen when using only mouse and keyboard though, so I couldn't begin to guess why it would in this specific scenario, but it's very distracting.  There were many other problems with the controls that I encountered but didn't really write them down and can't remember them all.  I hope they fix these issues, because it really is a gem of a gaming experience.  Even with these frustrations, I put up with them for over 70 hrs of play.  Done now though.

review:
Dont bother.
This is a total piece of rubbish.
Every single system is badly programmed, unfinished, and likely to be a 'worst in class'.
The inventory is terrible. The ability to switch items in your hotbar is terrible.
The combat is buggy. You will get stuck on the interface and the game will refuse to fire your arrows.
The deep water is instant death. You drown quicker than a hollywood movie.

Basically, they have a great setting, some very nice graphics - and then they punish you every moment you play.

I played it for a bit, but I ended up frustrated every few minutes with something that the designers should either have fixed, never started with, done the same way as every other quality game, or just spent three seconds thinking about before they created a crappy solution to an already solved problem.

Absolutely the worst implementation I have ever had the misfortune to play.

[EDIT]
Played again after they fixed a few things. So I knew what I was getting into the second time.
I hear that the devs call this a 'village simulator' rather than an RPG. I'm not thrilled by that idea, but let's take it on board and examine.
Is it a village simulator? No. You build things, sure. But your villagers are not simulated. They are just a set of numbers for production and consumption. And if that is the case, then surely there are systems to help you manage production and consumption. Again, sadly, no. Everything is hidden behind some 'interesting' design and interface choices. Or to be more honest, some worst-in-class screens and layouts. Nothing here is simple, nothing is made clear to you, and there are no consolidated stats as you might expect. And even if there were, it would just be a spreadsheet focused on the least interesting part of the game IMO.

The best part of the game is the world, and expanding your knowledge of places and what you can build and grow. This will occupy your actual brain time. Not the village, or at least only in steps as you add a new refugee, tell them what to do, and then forget them forever.
If that is the case, the devs have indeed created an RPG. And it is actually quite good at this. But without quests and personalities, you are stuck with gated adventuring and combat situations that lead towards new areas.

Combat though, just sucks. Absolutely sucks. I'm not overstating that it is without doubt the most bug ridden useless piece of junk ever released. In theory, the one to one combat has nuance and flair. But the ranged attacks are god awful, the enemy pathing is abysmal, and I'm running out of bad words to use. Truly terrible. Never should have been released, and I would be ashamed as a dev to say that it is in a 'release 1.0 state' at all.

So where does it go from here? I could imagine new expansion lands, new items to build, new crops to grow (and god help us because seasons for your crops is an exercise in self-abuse for the player). This would all be pointless because it wouldn't address the real challenges.

Can they fix combat? Sure. Everybody else has. Lets assume they can too.
Can they make the village management better? The screen redesign would be in theory very simple and helpful and add some overall statistics. 
But. 
Yes, that's a standalone statement. I'm just feeling that the devs are in love with their own interface and had it developed by separate sub-teams who just didn't talk or share with each other. So I'm betting the answer here is actually a hard 'no'.
Can they introduce personalities and quests? What would be the point in this and how would it work with the other things so sadly lacking. Not clear how this would make it better, or fit thematically.

And now for the good bit(s). The game is absolutely beautiful. The visuals are at least an eight out of ten. Building your buildings is fun for a while and rewarding in a repeated-clicking manner. But after a time, its just make-work. If you have a whole bunch of cool stuff available, make it have an impact. Make your village impossible to build without paying attention to detail. But then illuminate those details to the player. That would be extremely cool, and in keeping with the style. To make this a great village simulator, with complex systems, they need to be intelligible without a spreadsheet. Help us envision that. Force us to make beautiful and functional homes, and to husband those scarce resources to best effect. Give me easy ways to create repeat buildings, and let me focus on the new stuff and making everything individualised (with game impact driven by it).

And for god sake, take away the stamina bar. Sure, in combat would be fine. But everywhere else, just ditch it. Hosing your own game is never smart.

Would I buy it again? On special, yes, absolutely. But it is a one-and-done game. And there was a lot of swearing, and an awfully large amount of 'why the hell did they do it that way' discussion. Not in a positive light, to be clear. The pretty graphics made it liveable, but I would not recommend it with the flaws. They are too deep, and too obvious. If they were going to be fixed, they would already be fixed. So this one is on a pathway downwards unless there is a change at the helm.

To obtain two to three villagers per season, you must traverse the entire map. Which is the speed of the sail. Because of this, my population cap is constantly higher than the actual population count. It's just artificial bull crap limitation.  

Other than village count cap and constant lack of villagers, you have to unlock regions. And boi its mess on whole other level. You need to build notable buildings to unlock regions. You need to assign villagers to build notable buildings. The severe shortage of villagers forced me to reassign villagers from food production. This doesn't count as village automation in my mind if I have to change jobs every season.

And if you do unlock a region with higher quality resources, pay attention because a building that can process these resources is unlocked in a different region at the other end of the map.

There are too many mechanics that limit your advancement and none that reward you for trying to actually play the game.

review:
For a 1.0 release, it's pretty buggy. I'm into the mid/late game and the cracks are really showing. I dealt with the very clunky combat up to the iron stage and it really feels bad the further you go. Enemies with knives are starting to bug out and spam attacks endlessly and are unaffected by parries entirely. The combat has boiled down to trading hits with knife enemies since their poise is seemingly infinite. 

Parry timing is hit or miss on most enemies. Sometimes it works and sometimes you just get a block or just take damage even though you timed the parry perfectly. I had to really tune down the damage enemies could deal since the game likes to throw 3 enemies at a time at you, but the mechanics aren't built for it. Katana enemies will 2 shot you even though you are wearing heavy armor. The game is horribly balanced. 

Since production doesn't finish until the end of the day, the game does a horrendous synchronous update that causes the game to freeze for 10 seconds when the day ends. This is pretty trivial, but then the game drops frames into the sub 30's while the game is trying to catch back up. I'm only at Dynasty level 15 with 58 villagers and it's chugging this bad already. No amount of DLSS 3.5 can keep the frames up. My PC is no slouch either. 

Villagers are starting to unreliably complete their tasks each day now too. My smithy is only producing iron hammers in spite of having pickaxes, knives, Axes, etc. selected. I have checked and rechecked all materials are available and made sure all proper storage is available in the smithy, yet it won't produce anything else but hammers. 

This game is probably going to need some more time in the oven before it's ready. $30 is a little steep given the state this game is in. Honestly, given this team was willing to slap a 1.0 on this game in this state, I wouldn't expect the above complaints to improve much.

review:
1.0 has been pretty underwhelming.    I really loved the EA and was very much excited for this game, but the latest release feels very rushed, and that's disappoint because it's ALMOST a really great game.  However, the new update does NOT mesh with previous updates and they really need to take it back to development to fix it up.

I'll caveat I've gotten three villages and "control" most of the map, so I'm not sure but consider myself approaching end-game (e.g. about to unlock the last set of buildings).

For details: I'll compare it to Medieval Dynasty, as it's in the same genre.

The Good:

- Some improvements over Village Management in Medival Dynasty.
  - Luxury, Spiritual and Safety needs are interesting
  - Filling needs with *jobs* and services, vs. items is good addition
- Interesting combat system.
  - Very different animations across weapons
  - Enemy camp "dungeons" with bosses to take down
- Region Control mechanic.  Requires "building" key control points to gain access to advanced resources.

The Bad

- Pacing. They added quests in EA and for this release they just changed them all with Region Control so that the quest and story just doesn't make sense anymore.  E.g. there's a quest to learn ironworking that requires you to advance much past where the quest is to acheive the quest.  Additionally the quest is still worded as if it unlocked ironworking (like in EA), when in fact it does nothing of the sort.  Lots of instances where mid-game "better recipes" is locked behind quests, but you can rush towards later game recipes instead with better outcomes.
- Clunky. There's a LOT of missing quality of life features.  E.g. a notice that workers are doing something not valid in the current season, a notice that workers don't have enough source material for the % you have them allocated to a task.  Or even just the ability to *sort* in any menu, ever.
- Economy. The one BIG missing feature from Medieval Dynasty is having sales people sell your stuff.  I usually have my villagers make massive amounts of one item and I craft/derive the needs from there.  However, at some point I wound up with a ridiculous number of logs and it was VERY hard to craft all of them or even sell them, due to how the interfaces work.  This is after I had moved to oil for heat, but had forgotten to tone down the deforestation.


The Ugly

- Base/Town Building.  They have TONS of great decoration, but simple things like getting walls to line up or controlling the roof-style of *some* buildings is buggy or not working.  There's no great way to control the terrain around your base, and some buildings you expect to line up (like mansions/monastery) just may never line up if you didn't pick flat enough ground.
- Depth. Crafting is fun. Combat is fun. Managing the Village is fun.  But you can easily get to a point where you're either doing something you've already done a thousand times.  Additionally, leveling "monk"/"spiritual" just never made sense to me and I could barely get anything out of it.  I wish there was more quests or content around this aspect of the game.  Or that having a family actually DID something, not just "hey great, we sent your kid somewhere else to live".


Don't get me wrong, I do like the game, I just think once you get past the early game it just leaves you hanging with what looks like deep, rich content, but isn't.

review:
The building selection UI is horrible and still black&white while the rest of the game looks great. There were a lot of times I was really confused in which section what building or whatever structure is. It needs a rework into something either standard or more intuitive.

The game does not provide guidance on progression. It is true that the game is survival type, yet survival is the easiest thing to do - in fact, after 1h of gameplay you will forget this fact. The game is all about unlocking building and items, then managing your villages and population. So I thought, why not just kick everyone out and just keep building stuff to upgrade myself and just razing the map. Well on normal and  difficulty(probably also higher) you also have to build special project that require villagers which tend to leave you if they are not happy. Bummer. The big problem is that in order to balance something you will be recruiting people and assign them jobs, but the more you recruit the more stuff you unlock and with that more problems/villager needs. It was really hard to make every box green. In fact I only managed to do it while on 50 population and still the spiritual/luxury needs were in red(last unlockable needs) - never really enjoyed the gameplay because of it. It was a constant struggle to figure out what to do with the village.

You can build only 4 villages(and probably 100 villagers) in total but you can not demolish the previous. The map has regions and regions have resources, your villagers can harvest. The problem is that once you unlock iron, you won't need bronze, so if i made a mistake by settling in starter area like everyone else who did not read forums/wiki, then you are f-ed because you will need such things like ice and later more resources. This shows that you will not be able to automate everything by using villagers. So why struggle with base management to begin with?

The resource management UI is also bad. It does not allow to pick the amount i would like to store for Winter or, as another example, "get and keep 20 bronze in storage, after that amount continue on consuming it on whatever".

Why can't I assign the same person to work on different things during different season without manual intervention?(or to do the same with building resources) This made every production like even more annoying to manage. For example, during winter almost nothing grows, so you either stock up(which you should) or choose different things to grow like wasabi or enoki mushrooms or hunt for meat, get more fish.

The game does not guide you towards the usefulness of the items much. This is either because of the UI or lack of guidance. Want better heat? Get charcoal kiln. How? F you. Want to know which food gives you more village needs right from the menu? Lol, go to the traders and look for that food. I would really appreciate an in game "help" section where i can look for every recipe or mechanic instead of checking said wiki and forums.

The whole game is pretty much like this. Go build special projects and kill boss in the region if it has one. There is really nothing else to do. There are quests, but those are really silly and irrelevant except the one that gives you the bell to establish another village.

The combat approach is weird but it works. Essentially you are a 1 man army against the map. Can't use villagers for anything related to combat.

Probably the biggest goal of the game is to get as rich as possible and as fast as possible. Without money you can't unlock anything and have only other choice of scavenging - not for the game progression, but for base management - it doesn't make sense.

I strongly believe this game is made to play on the creative mode an not on any other difficulty otherwise it's just not worth the time. It has good graphics, theme, music but most mechanics are simply bad and not enjoyable by the balancing the game gives you. I do understand that it could be more efficient to play as 4 people multiplayer, but at that point, the game is not worth its price. I'd recommend just skipping this game as it does not deliver equal or more worth than something standard like DayZ or Subnautica.

The UI is buggy and ugly with lots of typos, and performance is pretty bad. This game doesn't look good if you're not using 4K upscaling, and this still runs poorly.

review:
Sengoku Dynasty – When "Dynasty" Means Downgrade

If you ever wondered what Medieval Dynasty would be like if it lost a bet and had to wear its cousin's hand-me-downs, welcome to Sengoku Dynasty! It takes everything its older sibling did… and does it slightly worse. Every. Single. Thing.

Let’s break it down:

Graphics? Imagine Medieval Dynasty but after eating some bad sushi. The textures feel like they took a vow of simplicity, and the lighting makes me wonder if feudal Japan was just permanently overcast.

Mechanics? Think Medieval Dynasty, but with all the screws a little loose. Movement feels off, combat is about as smooth as a rice field in a drought, and every action seems like it needs an extra step—because, why not?

Building? I hope you enjoy watching your character struggle to place structures in the most unintuitive way possible! In Medieval Dynasty, building was a pleasure. Here, it’s more of a meditation exercise in patience.

Combat? If you’ve ever wanted to fight enemies with the intensity of two drunk samurais trying to swat a fly, this is your game. The AI attacks with the coordination of a toddler wielding a broom.

Story? There is one…  But like a missing katana in the mud, it’s hard to find and even harder to care about.

Despite all of this, the game could be fun if you enjoy open-world survival and have a high tolerance for jank. Maybe one day with enough patches, Sengoku Dynasty will be worthy of the “Dynasty” name. But for now, it feels like the "bargain-bin" edition of its predecessor.

Final Verdict: 5/10 – Needs more honor and polish.

You start with stone tools, get copper, bronze, iron, steel...I'm on iron now, and nothing feels different. They're no faster, they don't gather more, they don't last longer. But I have them, and some things require I have them. Box checked.

You have a food meter, and you have food. The food meter has a numerical representation, and food items say "X Food". Except...that variable is completely fucking worthless because it never restores as much as it says. I eat a 60 food item with 50 food missing and MY FOOD ISN'T FULL! Box checked though!

You have weapons and armor.
There are enemies to fight.
Hahahahaha holy freaking poop IT SUCKS! Box checked though.

One of the most egregious boxes though? There is gravity. Gravity means fall damage. Except fall damage is...negated by armor...'cause plummeting six stories naked kills you, but that same fall in steel armor? Barely a sprained ankle. Box. Fucking. Checked.

Now, a lot of this could be because I'm not host in a multiplayer game, and that CLEARLY comes with problems. A lot of perks I unlock clearly don't do fudge all unless I reconnect, and even then...only if it feels like it.

This game EXISTS. It is - technically - functional in that you can launch it and play it. Is it GOOD though? No. No it isn't. Don't spend full price, and only play with people to laugh at the jank as your friend scream "BUT WHY THOUGH?!"

review:
I find it hilarious that the main menu image depicts a pretty cool game with attractive looking characters, and then when you actually get into the game, you have a bunch of grandpa/granny faces with the most limited and basic character customization ever. 

That's what Sengoku Dynasty feels like, an advertisement of a hamburger. It looks all juicy, plump, and rich looking. But when you buy the actual burger, its flat, squashed, sauce all over the place, buns aren't aligned, and they forgot the cheese.

Not only does all the characters look ugly with a ultra simple and limited character customization, you have-

A really bad combat system where enemies can't be read through animations at all. Whether they are stunned, or knocked on their arse, the animation is janky and has no in-between moments. So a guy flat on his ass will shoot back up and start attacking you. Enemies you think are 'stun locked' will just start swinging at you without a moments notice.

Badly dumbed down version of Medieval Dynasty. Only 1 worker can be assigned to a building, you cant upgrade it. All you can do is build another huge work table inside the already-small building to assign more workers. What do you get with a brainded AI npc? They either just teleport or get stuck in/on table walking forever in place. Actually the work doesn't even need the AI's to actually be at the table, so you can just make a building filled to the brim with tables if you don't mind seeing jank AI everywhere.

Villages is really bad. You have to satisfy not only food and water, but maintenance, security, medicine, etc etc. How do you satisfy them? By getting your villagers to work in specific buildings. But they need tools to do work, how do you get them? By putting npcs in buildings to produce them. But you need resources to make tools, what now? Put npcs into buildings to get resources. But the farming seed bags can't be produced until way later in the game, how can we farm? By grinding for it through other means. The village mechanic is not only tedious, but very annoying to manage due to the clunky management UI. When assigning jobs, you can't even see what's listed for the very bottom people because another UI hud is blocking it.

You have jittering tree and log physics... Trees you cut down are so jank, they fall at 15 fps.

Swimming kills you, literally. If you plunge into deep waters it actually just takes a chunk of your health, not stamina.

I could go on but I don't see the point. The only thing this had going for me is the fact that it's set in Feudal Japan. Other than that, Medival Dynasty is by far better designed and polished than this is. Even if you level the playing field, and go back a couple updates on Medieval to match with Sengoku, Medieval takes the win. The only reason I'm bringing up Medieval is because they both have the same publisher. Actually, Toplitz Productions seems to green light a lot of these Base Building games. So do your research, and beware when buying from them. Some are good, some are bad like this one.

review:
Sniper elite is that kind of game, that's a fun 7/10 game where you know what you're getting for a lower price.
The problem is... from SE3 to Resistance, it feels the same, almost looks the same and never goes beyond that. 

The Xrays... it was a fun gimmick in SE2, but every future game they say "it's the best its ever been" but after 10 kills, you seen it all. There's no nuance, no custom camera or replay speed you can control. The Xray camera focusses on the organ you hit so you don't really have an idea of the damage the bullet did during from entry to exit with detail. "See bullets ricochet off bones" Never seen it. I barely even seen soldiers with grenades on their belts. In SE2, when you did a multi kill, you had a camera for each enemy you hit, it followed the bullet from enemy to enemy. That's gone! I honestly removed Xrays after the 2nd mission.

Now for the biggest biittching i have to do, the missions. SE1 and SE2 had cool tailored missions, with scripted events that kept the campaign rolling. Ever since Africa, it's just boring open ended maps after boring open ended maps.
This wouldn't be a problem, if there was some actual good sniping to do. You know, Sniper maps.
If there was more snipers to hunt, more hidden/staged enemies or shooting angles made for long ranges, it would make the game way better, but instead, you get villages and towns, with enemies all within hearing range. And worst of all, a lot of them have you fighting underground or inside... There was one good map, during the night, with rain, it was nice and moody, but the rest is just boring. There's barely any sound mask events that are native to the map and unique. You get one in the first mission (The dam) and first thing you do, is have to break the pipes and cut the sound. There's one in mission 7... but the rest is trucks and generators you have to break. I'd prefer if the game was a shooting gallery type game made like Hitman Sniper Mission, where they could focus on improving the sniping/gunplay, making the xray stuff fancier, and making tailored scenes, instead of getting a wannabe Saboteur (Pandemic Games) game with some sniping where people just walk in patrols like idiots and forget about the sniper threat after 2 minutes.

In the end, i am done with the franchise. Until they announce a rework of the franchise/engine, with a change in era like Vietnam/Cold War, never buying it again. Especially not for 100$ CAD for a 2 day access. If i paid 40$, i'd be pleased.

It's a shame, i want Rebellion to keep making games, they're one of the last good ones that make games like they want instead of doing live crap like most publishers do... but sadly other games evolve with time, and Sniper Elite, did not.

review:
It's a Sniper Elite 5 level pack.

The features are the same, the look's the same, the problems are the same. I'm not sure how this took almost 3 years to make.

The main problem remains:
For a game called Sniper Elite, the game sure loves overwhelmingly throwing you into CQB scenarios that require your typical stealth shenanigans. Throw a bottle to distract someone, sneak up behind them, knock them out. Guns are a no-go even with silencers, so the old bottle tactic reigns supreme.

Same old, seen it a million times in a million games that play just like this.


Except, here you also get to deal with hyperaware enemies tuned to spot you at distances you'll almost never get to engage them at, janky AI and player movement. AI will get stuck on stairs. AI will spot you trying to sneak up stairs.

AI won't spot you walking straight past you when you hide by a doorway. AI won't spot your head visibly peaking out over a wall.
An enemy kill target will happily take over truck duty from someone else and drive straight off the map. An enemy group will happily investigate your position because a mine detonated halfway across the map.


If you want to make a game about sniping, make a game about sniping. Not a standard ubisoft stealth game that's somehow even more jank than those titles.

review:
1. **Poor Objective Design & Uninspired Gameplay**  
   - The mission objectives are vague and frustratingly difficult to follow. Unlike modern game design, which provides clear guidance, this game simply marks a broad area, forcing players to waste time searching for objectives manually.  
   - The level design heavily relies on cramped indoor environments, making movement and combat frustrating. The inability to adjust the camera further adds to the discomfort.  
   - Many aspects feel like a direct copy of *Sniper Elite 5*, but with less polish and minimal innovation.  

2. **Severe Bugs & Technical Issues**  
   - The game is riddled with long-standing bugs that have persisted across multiple installments.  
   - Character collisions are poorly implemented, leading to enemies getting stuck in walls and becoming invincible.  
   - Enemy death animations are glitchy, often resulting in unnatural and distorted positions.  
   - A critical bug involving placing explosives on a safe—if the player defuses it by unlocking the safe manually, the explosive is sometimes refunded, but may still explode randomly. Worse, if this happens before an auto-save, reloading the save leads to instant death upon spawn.  

3. **Performance & Gameplay Flow Issues**  
   - The game performs poorly, with stuttering and optimization problems that make it run terribly on decent hardware.  
   - Maps are smaller than expected, reducing the variety and strategic sniping opportunities.  
   - The game lacks innovation, offering minimal new weapons and features. Some special takedown challenges in later missions are outright broken due to bugs, making them impossible to complete.  

4. **Unbalanced Gameplay & Lack of Sniping Focus**  
   - Despite being a "sniper" game, the level design often forces close-quarters combat, making pistols or melee combat a more viable option than actual sniping.  
   - Enemies are often hard to spot due to poor lighting design, making the difficulty feel artificial rather than skill-based.  
   - Key mechanics, such as finding enemies with keys, are inconsistent. Sometimes enemies automatically get marked, while other times, they do not, forcing tedious trial and error by reloading saves.  

Overall, this game does not meet my expectations for a full-priced title. It feels rushed, unpolished, and not worth the cost.

review:
Sniper Elite:Resistance, was not super hyped for it but was interested as I really enjoyed the previous games. I am no professional reviewer so I will keep it simple.

For starters I have completed the main campaign and got all the collectables for those missions, however personally for me I did not find the campaign very compelling or intriguing and it did not grip my attention, the only thing that kept me going was the sniping and stealth gameplay.

Also personally for £70 for the deluxe was not worth the price even £45 for the base game, if you are interested wait until it is on sale or you get it for a decent price because the Cons just out way the Pros, the bugs can be fixed but I very much doubt they will go out of their way to actually fix the terrain and it just really ruins your experience seeing mass floating objects and AI stuck on bits of rubble or stairs.

While I enjoyed sniping and being a stealthy Soldier, it unfortunately has a few downsides.

Pros:

- Same Sniping glory from the other games
- Stealth is exactly the same so not a hard transition

Cons:

- Bugs, had to restart a few times on a certain mission due to a missing prompt (not saying what due to spoilers), there has also been some really bad FPS drop which I have fixed by turning of keyboard lights in accessibility.
- Graphics seem to have degraded since the last game
- AI is buggy and gets stuck in loops or just take a while to figure out what to do
- Terrain especially in the later levels is rushed and appalling the amount of floating objects I witnessed its like they just pushed it out without checking or play testing, another thing with terrain your player and the AI like to get stuck on areas especially stairs or wooden bridges or bits of rubble.


I hope this helps anyone who was interested in this game.

Overall Rating - 2.5/5

I regret giving this game too much of a chance.  Not because I can't get my money back (although that would be nice) but because I spent the better part of a week pushing through and hoping it would get better.

It's Sniper Elite - gotta be good right?  When a good studio asks us to put out top dollar for a game, it's not unfair or unreasonable for us to expect a good game in return.  This is why I have bought every single Sniper Elite as far back as I can recall.

Clipping sprites, soldiers being launched through the ceiling from a bullet impact, terrain that won't let you traverse for no good reason.  Poor level design with shots longer than a few meters being made very few and far between.  A kill mission that sets a condition to have a VIP die in a fall that places the map edge at the drop so you actually can't throw him off.  All things that should have been weeded out during testing.

What all of this adds up to is another beloved title that spent too much time and money on the newest, brightest physics engine and not enough doing what we actually pay for.  Making a game that's fun to play.

 Instead, we get a title with too many mistakes, poor design decisions and straight up corners cut.  In a word - inexcusable.

review:
[h3]Where am I supposed to go?[/h3]

Let me offer a perspective about the game's design that I'm not seeing a lot of reviews about- the lack of mega structures or "super weapons". In previous Sniper Elite titles, a player starting a map for the first time will be able to look out in the distance and observe a clearly defined point of interest. Things like giant radio towers, large bunkers, massive artillery cannons on bridges. This game suffers from only having 1 or 2 memorable, large-scale POI's to investigate. 

The game's plot revolves around (Spoiler:) [spoiler]a superweapon so secret, that only a select portion of [strike]Nazi[/strike] intelligence are aware of it. Not even the dictator himself. Turns out this "superweapon" is just a chemical nerve agent, and can easily be hidden underground.[/spoiler] And oh boy, do the game devs like hiding everything underground. Instead of feeling like a sniper game, this game leans heavily into the close quarters stealth aspect. Sniping isn't as intuitive, and is too loud when you're constantly inside of buildings, meticulously picking off enemies just a few meters away from you. The few maps that do offer some decent long-range sniping, the enemies you instinctively want to shoot, are very often in the line of sight of another enemy you can't see. Instead, all you can do is take out enemy snipers that can die unseen in their lookout positions, which gives you more freedom to try and [i]sneak[/i] through open fields, just so you can get within stabbing distance of your next enemy. 

Bring back the skyline dominating mega structures. Stop putting everything underground. Give me something to Snipe, not something to stab.

review:
It's ok, but the premium price for game quality is unacceptable. This game should be about $20-$30 dollars max.  I regret buying it significantly. Battlefield 1 and even the ancient game Saboteur are far better games. As others have said, it feels like DLC and blatant rehashing of the same assets and mechanics (I played Sniper Elite 3 but not 4 or 5). The story is generic and superficially executed. The characters are flat and empty as is the voice acting. The phony French and German accents are especially irritating. 

The map and level design is mediocre.  The physicality of collisions with character controller movement is terrible; sometimes you can vault over sandbags, sometimes you can't; sometimes you can drop off a ledge or over a railing, sometimes you can't. None of the maps feel like real sites, but instead game-world levels. The lighting and illumination feels like it's from the mid 2000's, and is especially poor compared to something like Battlefield 1, the Last of Us or most high-priced modern games. The navigable areas feel highly restrictive (most likely to ensure that AI can move and access the areas) but are still confusingly janky and poorly designed. You will encounter many invisible walls in areas that look walkable (even in the middle of the map) or wide gaps that look like you can walk between something like a truck and a wall but no, you can't walk there. I had one of my grenades stick to an invisible wall 3 feet in front of me.  Harry Hawker might be posing on a roof ready to snipe in the cover image, but you will never be on a roof like that.  This game feels like it should be a sandbox of creativity for getting kills and accomplishing missions, but it always feels the same.  None of your decisions will actually mean anything or do anything to change any outcome.  

If the game designers want to take Sniper Elite to the next level, they might need to look to other stories and media for inspiration. Imagine if they took inspiration from Inglorious Basterds, The Pianist, a Soldier of Orange, Operation Valkyrie or Saving Private Ryan. There are no stakes in this game, there are no people, just cartoons. There's no reason to care and thus no meaning. Once you've done 10 headshots and grenade or mine kills, you've done them all.

The remaining 10% are performed by the new protagonist, and that one does not come even close to the stoic Karl Fairburne who is rightfully beloved by the Sniper Elite player community. The "new guy" annoys me because of, in my opinion, badly written and overly chatty dialogue. The British accent is fine in my book, but an accent alone does not infuse personality or likability into a one-dimensional, scraggly-bearded guy that I find not much reason to care about. Also, he talks so much that I wish being able to mute his voice altogether.

I waited a long time for a Steam sale to purchase the standard edition of Sniper Elite Resistance, and yet I still feel ripped off by Rebellion. Frankly, if I was not an avid fan of the SE franchise from the very beginning and enjoyed how installments of the series kept improving more and more, I would be even more annoyed. I close my eyes and try to think happy thoughts, but SER is too brief and too expensive to warrant my recommendation.

review:
Played Sniper Elite 5 a lot, and did a lot of survival with friends. Lots of good times.

This game will just disappoint your if you are coming from a Similar background.


Campaign

The campaign missions are significantly worse. Most of the new maps are significantly smaller than SE5, and every single map has a massive underground bunker. Massive Underground bunker is a fun trope for 1 mission or something, but every single one is just too much. Especially considering this game is supposed to be about sniping, there is just way too much close quarters. Close quarters and stealth wouldn't be a big issue, but I personally find the combat controls to be very clunky. Kind of a personal gripe, but i feel like if the devs want the speed of intensity of a first person shooter, they can't have that in a third person shooter. This was also true to some degree for SE5, but not nearly as noticeable. 


Survival

Coop Survival was why i bought this game, as my friends and I loved that in SE5. Nobody wanted to buy this game because it seemed like a lot for the same game we were already playing. I decided to be the guinea pig and buy the game on sale with all the dlcs. All the dlcs except the k98 and the 1911 because i'm not going to debase myself that far to buy those. The new guns and maps for survival were why i was interested in this game, far more than anything else it offered. The new survival maps are bad. Very bad. Of the three new maps, two of them (I can't be bothered to remember their stupid names) have absolutely no elevation, which just feels odd for a sniping game. The map with the windmill is nice, but feels like a massive missed opportunity. It's very small, and every operation plays out the same way. I don't know why the tunnels are blocked off, they would have been nice. I don't know why the map is so small, they could have easily expanded the map across the river like the dlc mission it was based on. The map could have been much more diverse than either sit in windmill or sit in barn. The new town map makes my soul very angry, because it seems to have been made out of spite more than anything else. A town map, with 0 enterable buildins. A town map with spires and steeples, that are completely sealed off. Most of the outposts are out in the open, and will be lost if you don't mine the whole map to obilivion. Forgive my uncouth expectations, but i would prefer sniping in my sniping game instead of mine laying. And this map also suffers from being very small, inexplicably. The last new map is a massive flat open area with a sligtly raised path in the middle. Can you fight in the massive hotel like in the campaign? No that's out of bounds silly.  Can you get up in the massive railway tower thing and snipe from up high? No that's all sealed off you silly willy. The devs want you to sit in a concrete parking lot, and that is all you will do. Thankfully the devs have added 3 survival maps from se5, and these three maps are all much better than any of the new ones. Please just add the rest of the se5 survival maps, and we can collectively ignore the new ones. 

Guns

I'm a massive history swine so cool old guns will get me to buy any game or dlc eventually. Hearing about the new guns in this game got me really excited. Some of the new guns are nice, some of them are missed opportunities and some are just bad. I think all three of these ideas kind of are true in equal parts, so i don't feel any of them should be a tagline for the whole topic. The Ruby, model 1935 and the berthier are nice, good job on those. The nagant revolver, and the svt 40 are nice, but not my personal cup of tea so often forget they are even there. The lebel is a swing and a miss. Its close to good, but why does it do less damage than the berthier despite firing the same cartridge from a longer barrel? I could overlook that, but they did not add any french scopes. There absolutely were scoped lebel rifles, but you can't have an accurate one in the game. As a strange aside, most scoped weapons can use a japanese scope, despite japanese weapons being nowhere in the game. They were in se5 but their scoped somhow carried over to resistance. The lebel is close to good, just use iron sights and wonder why it magically does less damage than the berthier. The mas has one of the most iconic, weird looking bolt handles of any ww2 rifle. This was completely ignored and just has a straight bold handle in the game for some reason. None of the french rifles have access to their iconic spike bayonets either. the M1 garand is nice to have, and i like using it. Im just confused that there is a flash hider upgrade in the game, but its not available for the m1. Scoped m1s are possibly the only guns in the game that had flash hiders on their real world counterparts, but almost every gun in the game except the m1 can use a flash hider. Just seems like a strange oversight. The Udm 42 was a nice addition, it would have been cool to have the real stacked mags, even if they weren't functional. Still nice either way. The BAR was a nice addition, especially that it is the ww1 version, its very unique just for that. Its annoying that it does so little damage, despite firing a full size rifle cartridge but thats a common annoyance i have with many games so whatever at this point. The bad guns are very bad. The Mas submachinegun is impossible to configure like its real world counterpart, there is no way to take the goofy foregrip off, and most upgrades give it an aircooled shroud from an m1919 for some reason. Looks stupid, for no reason. The browning hi power is one of my all time favourite guns so i was excited to see it in the game. It actually had a stock option in real life that is not available in the game, but you can get some random stock options from other guns instead. And the magazine round count is off for some reason, it holds 10 when it should hold 13. A lot of guns have wrong round counts, but this one is irritating because it was one of the hallmarks of the hi power. In ww2 when most sidearms held 7 to 8 rounds, the hi power having 13 was a massive distinction. The johnson rifle is also one of my favourite guns of all time. The real life version has a big goofy stupid looking front sight, that is one of the most recognizeable and distinctive parts of the gun. This is inexplicably removed in the game, and it makes me very sad. The fg42 can be used used as a found weapon, so I don't place as much gravitas on its issues as its not a regularly usable gun but still. For some reason the devs turned it into a weird rare submachinegun. The mag holds 30 instead of 20, and it does an absolutely pitiful amount of damage. Same as the BAR, why does a gun firing a full size rifle cartridge do so little damage. But this leads into one of the strangest changes for resistance from SE5, you can't use any german guns. you can pick them up as found weapons, but you can't use them in your loadouts. I don't know why this change was made, but it makes me sad. The guns are already in the game, you just can't use them. 


TLDR
Campaign Sucks
Survival Sucks
New guns Kinda Suck, Kinda good

Devs TLDR
Please add the rest of the survival maps from SE5
Please add the rest of the guns that were available in SE5
Just have resistance be the defacto complete version of the game for Coop survival

review:
Tom, get rid of the profanity.  

I've had the good fortune of playing several betas.  I gave feedback on this in every one, and that was after seeing only a fraction of the profanity.  I had no idea there would be this much of it in the final game.  I tried appealing to your pride in your product for making this game a future classic.  I am done trying to make that appeal.  It is so unnecessary, so unpleasant, so unwelcoming.  I'm sick and tired of feeling embarrassed every time I read a scene to my stream audience.  

I've been looking forward to this game for over five years.  I've been so keen on sitting down and getting through it.  Yet every play session sends me away with unfond memories.  I'm sick of it.  I adore (nearly) everything else about this game.  I don't regret my purchase at all.  But I can't stand it anymore.  It's like biting into a pristine apple and coming away with a worm between my teeth on the very first bite.  It ruins the whole experience.  It is such a lazy crutch in the otherwise savantly humorous writing.  You don't need it.  The script doesn't need it.  Just get rid of it.  

I have been playing it every day since it came out.  And every day I've tried thinking of a polite way of framing a review to convince you to do the right thing.  I've been [b]actually losing sleep[/b] trying to think of polite things to say.  I'm done being polite.  I tried making the appeal that no self-respecting parent of impressionable minds could be recommended, purchase, or play this game.  Kids are moot by now.  I'm a grown man with a colorful RL backstory of my own and even I can't stand the profanity in here.  

I don't care how good every other aspect of this phenomenally well-crafted game may be.  This review will absolutely stay red until you give us some means of filtering/blanking out every single word of profanity in the entire game.  PLEASE stop force-feeding me that unnecessary garbage.  I'm begging you, please.  It demeans the entire game.  I won't ask for a refund but, good gravy, just stop making me dread sitting down to play this beautiful game.  Do better.  

.
.
.
Edit: I see several hours after I've posted this that I've received a bunch of "funny" votes and Jester awards.  I want to clarify I am 100% serious with this feedback.  Feel free to retract your Jesters at your leisure.  I know profanity is part of every day life.  My time in the military was no walk in the park; I got a lot of grief for my intolerance, and I did, over time, relent partially.  But TBW is a game.  It's a source of FUN that I play on MY time in MY home.  I don't need scene after scene after scene of obscenities thrust in my face by a lazy crutch-leaning writer who wants his game to be taken "seriously" by a "mature" audience. review:
A decent yet generic tactical squad game brought low by embarrassing attempts at witty dialogue in the vain of Rick and Morty, blatant self-insert characters (for example, a furry who has the power to transform into a dog and is the most bad-ass assassin in the world), and low-effort political lecturing which is so incoherent in it's message that, at first, it's hard to even tell which political philosophy the game is attempting to attack, only that the author believes that the IRL followers of said philosophy deserve death. 

Later it becomes clear that the "bad guys" are supposed to be American Republicans who are portrayed as raving super-villains who hold secret Illuminati-style meetings at which they openly admit to being evil racists who want world domination. While there is nothing wrong with having a politically-focused plot, at no point in the entire game is there any attempt at a deep philosophical investigation of the politics at hand. Unfortunately, the game believes that simply writing scenes where republicans admit to being evil somehow qualifies as political dialogue, which makes the story utterly substance-less, tiring, and irrelevant for anyone who does not live in the United States (like myself). Even propaganda would have more effort put into it that this game's story does, as it would actually have the goal of changing peoples minds, rather than the authors clear goal of writing a self-serving fantasy where all of his politics are proven right. Even this would be forgivable if it didn't completely consume the game's plot, which unfortunately it does, with all other story elements effectively being put on hold for 95% of the games runtime whilst we are told about how bad the orange man is, then suddenly coming back to the forefront at the very final level in an an unsatisfying conclusion which serves only to reach the technical requirement of concluding the mystery which at first was portrayed as the driving force behind the narrative. In fact, the evil republicans you spend much of the game fighting are an entirely separate faction to the one which the main nemesis is a member of, making it even more irrelevant to the overarching story, while the main nemesis's faction is also run by an evil sociopathic billionaire hell-bent of world domination, meaning the game somehow manages to have two separate analogies for the evil orange man at the same time. Additionally, this plot swerve into anti-republican slogan chanting suspiciously begins almost immediately after the 2-hour-mark, which conveniently makes it impossible to refund the game once it becomes clear that the games promise of having a "story-driven campaign" will not be met.

TLDR;

The game's story effectively ceases to exist almost exactly two hours into the game. Buy it if you think the pricetag is acceptable for a typical tactical puzzle game. Swerve if you expected a compelling narrative.

I'd love to rate this game positively. Once again, Suspicious Developments knocks it out of the park with great gameplay and character design. The music isn't particularly memorable, but it all works for the game's purposes and doesn't ever distract you from what you're doing. So really, it all comes down to the writing.
I loved Gunpoint. I think their style of writing is still alive and well with TBW. Unfortunately, when half the lines are quippy snark where characters are building off each other, and the plot is relatively basic, it doesn't take much to break immersion and investment in the story with modern politics. There are other problems, narratively - one of the characters can revive everyone else, so it never feels like there are any stakes, even with the opponent having some crazy god powers. If you can overlook a few calls to modern politics, you'll enjoy the game. Personally, I'm downright exhausted about it, so when halfway through the game, it slapped me upside the head, it was very disappointing. If SD makes another game, I'll probably still buy it. I just hope they stick to what they're good at - fun writing - and leave parallels to the real world off the table.

review:
TL;DR - The games about a 7/10, with the core game play mechanic being the only real selling point. I'm not recommending because I can't in good conscious do so when so many other reviews are just raving about it without talking about it's flaws.

If you're wanting a closer experience to XCOM: Chimera Squad that's still fun and quirky, go play Rogue Waters. It does the same style of gameplay better, is more fun overall, and the black humour is genuinely funny through and through.

Gameplay:
It's hard to not recommend, it IS a good game, but tentatively, that's kind of the problem. The game follows your small team of "Wizards" as they encounter tactical breach situations, which on the surface sounds like you'll be facing some high octane battles as your team ventures into the sprawling compounds you infiltrate. You do not. 

Every mission is basically a short lived puzzle game, with bonus clothing being the reward for finding more stylish or complex methods of defenestration. This wouldn't be so egregious if the boss battles weren't treated the same; most of the bosses simply being a higher hit point chump with the same weakness to windows as every other enemy in the game. Now, to be fair, the actually significant threats you face DO require some tactical gameplay to work over, which makes those particular missions an absolute JOY to play. If those missions had been the operational standard, instead of being the odd battle you see over 2/3 of the way trough the game, I would have whole-heartedly recommended this game to anyone and absolutely raved about it.

As to the writing:
A lot of emphasis is placed on the writing, and honestly, it's kind of canned. The story itself is ok and there's basically two ways to look at it. From a setting POV, the story is cool. It's a clever mix of Magical fantasy elements and Modern aesthetics, complete with some viable technology emerging from the two. If I were to run a modern-fantasy TTRPG, this setting would make an awesome world to play in. Special call out to the DRUID MAFIA. That concept alone sounded so outlandish and is very cool to contemplate.  The story board itself is.. well.. ok. It's not bad, it just isn't good either. It has an extremely copy/pasta feel, like it was ripped right out of a Marvel/DC movie. Each story beat feels more like an excuse to rapidly transit to a new country and beat up people there, with all semblance of planning being treated as a joke. On a tactical level, your wizards have some sound grasp of tactics. On the strategic level, each and every one of them is constantly flailing about and getting lucky about how they proceed to the next area. It's funny the first time, but by the fourth it's lost all the charm and appeal. Seriously, the story makes it feel like the bad guys lost because they're unlucky, not because of YOUR intervention. Zan (the guy on the game's cover) is the biggest casualty in this department, as despite ostensibly having over 25 years of special operations experience (not even counting prior life experiences or general military experience) he's generally portrayed as a semi-competent dotard with half-baked plans rather than the veteran of  of MANY battles (in game lore!!) that he is, with countless portrayals of how those battles play out since he has the ability to ALWAYS SEE HOW HIS AND HIS TEAM'S ACTIONS WILL IMMEDIATELY AFFECT HIS AND OTHER'S FUTURES. Your other characters are generally portrayed in a positive light, with some time dedicated to showing their flaws, but Zan's just doesn't add-up after awhile. The other negative stand out is Dall, your Riot Priest. On the one hand, on a meta level she's hella cool. Home-made power armor made out of a cop car, BIG MFIN' SHIELD SLAPS, tactical teleports! Hands down, awesome kit. Then you look at her aesthetic, and it's just.. too on the nose for our world instead of the game's world. She's a black woman who's class is called the Riot Priest, who wears power armor made out of cop car (I hate making this seem like a negative), wields a flail made out of magically held together spray cans, and the arch-villain of her arc is a rich man leading an ultranationalist and zealous religious police state. If it weren't treated 100% serious in game, I would've thought it a parody, or a look into how it appears from the outside. At one point, you find your enemies as your allies, given a position of trust over your squad, and their numbers feature a POLICE OFFICER. But it's your team who's treated as the expendable, untrustworthy asset.

This brings us to the "Humorous Dialogue":
Honestly, it's good. At first anyways. It starts with some genuinely amusing quips and the odd bit of office rivalry humor, but by the time you've illegally entered your 2nd country, it's gotten stale. It's the same style of joke, the same self-depreciation, the same devaluation of Zan. There's a brief light of hope when Dall learns to relax and you get your fifth teammate but it's short-lived. Basically, if you like Marvel humour, you'll enjoy it. Otherwise it gets old, fast.

review:
This is a disappointment for me. My expectations were probably too high given the hype and rave reviews.

What it isn't:
- Is it not an XCom-like were you own, equip and develop your team as you see it.
- Is it not a tactics-like RPG with any freedom, exploration or grand adventure.
- Is it not an immersive narrative experience. You are constantly taken out of the story, in and out of missions. Between the training missions, the gamy challenges and achievement-like objectives, you are constantly distracted and prevented from imbibing the narrative and universe.

What it is:
- A series of baked puzzles to solve. Those are not particularly challenging (even with the confidence challenges) and that get stale and repetitive fast. They are often gamy and sometimes only thinly representative of the narrative justification.
- A well written ensemble of quirky & snarky characters that doesn't take itself seriously.
- An underdeveloped but intriguing and distinct universe.
- In the end, it's a game where the player has very low agency and no long term decisions to make or strategy to have. You just read an average and static story, drudgingly unlocking it bit by bit by solving the puzzles like a good dog. I imagine some people feel smart solving the puzzles. I didn't.

What it tries to be but isn't:
- You can feel the desire to be a noir story a la Disco Elysium, with an immersive narrative and engrossing characters, but much detracts from that and it ultimately failed for me.

review:
Before you scroll past this negative review, give it a read. I've put about 9 hours into this game, and while it's really quite amazing at the start, it turned into frustration and restriction by the time I stopped playing. What do I mean by that? Well, let me explain. 

Early game is amazing. You have a lot of options, can breach with almost any order of characters you want and still come out of it a bit banged up, but still alive and victorious. The real fun is replaying the levels and finding that "golden idea", that crazy play or daring strategy that'll bag you a perfect victory. But that's where the fun ends, early game when you HAVE that freedom of choice.

Mid and late game is, quite frankly, restrictive. No longer can you survive and clear the level while losing a couple characters along the way. If you want to win the levels in the late game, you need to have the perfect strategy every single time, with little-to-no room for error. This involves a lot of trial and error, rewinding over and over because a character died on your last turn and made the entire rest of the level unwinnable. But you won't know that, you CAN'T know that, until you keep playing for another hour on the same damn level until you inevitably restart from scratch. This isn't fun game design, it's restrictive and demoralizing. I want to be able to approach a level from several different angles, have fun with different strategies and daring plays, not be railroaded into only being able to use the "right" solution halfway into the game.

review:
I didn't like this game, but lots obviously have. It's similar to a number of other mini tac shooting games where everything is broken into mini maps and short engagements and you're rewarded for how quickly/efficiently you clear a stage rather than your tactical approach. 

The writing is pretty good and there is a reasonable story that accompanies the action. It's just kind of dull, there is basically an ideal approach to each level and it requires trial and error to get right. I prefer a more traditional approach like Xcom, where there is value in taking different strategies that you prefer, even if they aren't ideal, but you can still achieve victory rather than being locked into one narrow box.  The engagements are so small and quick, there is no space to build a strategy and plan ahead. The units are also very narrow, each one does something unique so, again, you need to combine them to get the right pattern and outcome. I can see why some would like that, but it's essentially an overdone rock paper scissors game. It just takes all the fun out of it when you see the layout and know exactly what the game wants you to do to win. Not for me, refunded.
name: Tactical Breach Wizards

review:
Every time I try to play this, I find myself restarting levels over and over to try to optimize them. On the one hand, the game explicitly tells you to not do the challenges it sets out for you, but it also has the optimization conditions sitting in front of you constantly taunting you, plus the end screen that only gives you kudos if you're efficient. Theoretically you'd plan out your actions like a tactical shooter game, but you can't see what enemies will be spawning from which doors or when until you've played through the entire battle once. It just feels so confused and I don't really enjoy it. 

The writing is fun and I like the story, but on a moment to moment basis I'm constantly worrying about whether there's something I could have done better and I don't ever feel like I have enough information to decide if I have.

review:
The setting of the game is genius and the small stories and dialogues are really fun. The game also plays with stereotypes in Pen and Paper and RPG games. Have you ever seen a traffic wizard? Hilarious :)

Why the negative review then?

Because it is NOT a tactical game. Basically its a puzzle game with some chess-like elements. There is THE solution for many levels that require exact steps each turn. Yes, you have some freedom, but most time freedom leads to subpar results. So you basically solve puzzles the devs created for you, wrapped as a tactical game. And that's simply not what I wanted and how its advertised. For me a tactical game is a game that gives me the freedom to choose my team, my weapons, stealth or not, kills or not. It's definitely not "In Turn 1, you have to position char 1 here and shoot there, char 2 must move exactly here and push that enemy so that in Turn 2 you can....". That's a puzzle. Solving it means to play each move as intended. The little freedom you get are mostly sub variants of exact these moves. The rating of each mission reflects exactly this: how well did you solve the puzzle at it was intended to be played?

Compare this with the complete freedom for Jagged Alliance, XCOM or Shadow Gambit. These are great tactical games that make you think about how YOU want to solve a level/fight. There are no best ways or preferred tactics in these games and thats what make them a tactical game.

The writing is clever and it'll make you laugh, but also I felt like the story just pushed you through a very pre-determined path. I really wanted to get into the nitty-gritty of designing different characters, specialize someone in hacking abilities while someone else is a sniper, etc. There is some of that on leveling up, but the choices are very limited and the characters are pre-generated. I guess I'm in the minority on this one. I'm off to try out Cyber Knights: Flashpoint. Maybe that'll be more like what I'm looking for.
