review:
The design / pacing... -done by a monkey.

The game starts by not telling you what each difficulty does.
Then it tells you to use abilites (which you select with LMB) without telling you to 'activate' its RMB.

Next the tutorial forces you (twice) to RUSH INTO A ROOM and turn on a laptop WHILE ENEMIES ARE NEARBY AND POINTING GUNS AT YOU... - and only once you did that, can you take them out!

The tutorial is HEAVILY scripted and it took me 5 tries to figure out (or rather stubbornly follow) the things i need to do. Its not hard! Its just VERY specific. 

If games like SWAT or XCOM and others like this tought me anything is: NOT to give the enemy a great way to SHOOT ME...  - but that is what the game teaches you.

In 'stage 3' of the tutorial i was refused the option to take cover DESPITE me seeing the enemy behind the next door waiting to rush in. Yes, this had to happen for the ham fisted script, but it is so counter intuitive! 

The enemy who stormed in is used to teach you RETALIATION mechanics. If you get too close the enemy will prioritize you over other targets.(its almost as if good positioning is important). What a piss poor way to explain this to me. It is forced and feels bad- not organic.

--

But... whatever. Its "just" the tutorial and you have to LOOSE THE TUTORIAL mission. Sorta.

You save a hostage, lose a party member which gets kidnapped, and then its back to the police station. Not the SWAT HQ but the police station... because... reasons. 

At the station you get boring cringe dialogue with answers that may been cool in the 90s (at this point i already tuned out since all the dialogue was just so basic and boring) and you learn a few more 'cool moves' with a little more freedom but overall its paint by the numbers.

You go around and shoot up the cops because your pal that was kidnapped came back and TRUST ME BRO WE ARE THE GOOD GUYS AND WE GOTTA GET OUT OF HERE or something.

Then you go to your... idk hidehout? (seriously, NOTHING was established at this point, the game just rushes through! BOAT HOSTAGE POLICE KIDNAPP! TIME PASS DRAMA FREEEDOM FIIIGHHHTERS!)

Its like watching fucking StarWars on 20x speed! You see scenes and stuff but it means NOTHING to you - and again, the cool one liners don't help!

During the shoot out you get "How are you doing?" (remember he was gone for idk years? Though irl it was like 30 seconds) and you can reply: cool. / i get dental / something i already forgot.

urgh...

Anyhow... i was in the hideout and HAD to spend a skillpoint on a skill because level up (yay)

FAR LEFT on the edge of the screen is a character. FAR RIGHT of the screen his/her abilities.
(Why?! This feels very disconnected and they don't use the space for much other then your character who takes like 5% of the space! It feels like selecting skills in the next room, and they COULD have used the space for a visual demonstration of the abilities or something... or just bring them closer to the character!)

I had to chose 1 and give it a perk... i am not ver familiar with those abilities or what is useful later on or if i get to unlock it all over time and a hundred other things! So you read if you want idk hit 1 more target or have a bigger knockback +2 ... 

WHAT DO YOU THINK I USEFUL? Hit +1 target... or knock people back farther?
During the tutorial the entire games gimmick (knocking people out of windows) was done on EASILY 10 of 20 enemies. Something cool, that might happen, is now an ESSENTIAL MECHANIC.

Imagine a game like Overwatch, but Winstons ultimate is now a basic attack!
The game does move from 'abilities to characters' to a game of 'how to remove the most chess pieces' by pushing them back through overly convenient HUGE and badly secured windows!

Why bother learning strength or tactics or items or anything... if there is an automatic win by kicking someone out of the window? (which may be conventiently right there).
And what do you do if there is no window to exploit or door to seal shut hMMMM?

Seriously this might be the dumbest game I played in a while.

---

Just buy ANY OTHER turned based tactical shooter.
The 'fact' these guys are wizzards isn't even that important. 

Shooting someone or spushing someone or even teleporting... - nothing special any other game can do. More importantly: the game sucks ass at telling a story that goes with it!

> boat tutorial
> shoot up your police HQ
> level up
> go to the world map and do 1 of 2 quests!

All in the span of less than 30 minutes! NO PACING.
I doubt i missed much important information since the 'banters' you can go through are 100% skipable and the game made sure i wanted to skip a lot of them...

"OH YOU GOT NO PATIENCE"

>Helldivers: a squad based shooter where picking the right tools is CRUCIAL.
>2+3 most played: Factorio+Satisfactory, where you do nothing but figure out issues.
>165 hrs in Baldurs Gate 3 where i CRAVED to look at everything i could find! (in and out of game)
>5th Company of Heroes.
>More RPGS,RTS, and other slow moving stuff...
And don't get me started on my AdvanceWars addicition<.< 

YEAH.....

That is not a patience problem.
That is a BAD GAME problem.

btw: games such as Wandersong or Spiritfarer also have no voice acting and a LOT to read... and i read it... and i won... (and those were fun). Just to brush that off the table too.
Read more darn novels n fanfics than the game has pages worth of freaking code.

I don't care if the game gets better "eventually" (or so Stockholm people tell me).
I'v had better. I played long enough to know when i waste my time. 

First impressions matter and those devs can't get a basic start right... why would i trust them with 12 more hours of my darn life??

review: I have already put 6 hours into this game from initial launch yesterday so it may seem weird for me to say that I can't recommend Tavern Manager Simulator. There's just no replayability here. For some people, like myself, I'm sure the first jump into the mechanics will launch the dopamine sky high but as a well versed sim/video game player, I'm honestly disappointed with what this game could've been. The foundation is there but without much in the way of customization or meaningful interaction. I would've liked to see more food recipes and prep so players can change up the menu how they like, import other ales and drink, possibly brew their own mead or maintain a garden for fresh ingredients. The interaction with NPCs is non-existent for the most part and feels repetitive and empty. I don't mind so much that I don't have a huge map to explore but I wish I could rearrange the layout of my tavern, or even just my bedroom beyond the basic wall decorations. The only driving force is to see what else the game has to offer but at level 8 (out of 12), I'm not very interested in continuing on after I unlock everything. I had a lot of hope for this game and I think the base of it is there, it just feels extremely unfinished and lacking. I support the niche genre tho and I have gotten hours out of it so maybe get it on sale if it's your thing.

review:
Not a bad game at first, but after a short while (say 7 hours in) you realise it becomes a monotonous grind. For example you make so much food for customers like meat and soup, you make some money and improve your inn a bit. But then after giving you 2 tasks to do and you grinding them for 2 or 3 in game days, it just gives you yet another task which is serving the same type of food 60 times even though you just served it probably a couple hundred times already. This feels too much like the game is making you grind boring stuff to get to the next upgrade, and doesn't tell you until you complete a task, then it just gives you another one. Its at this point I just quit the game through sheer boredom.

I will also add that I really like these types of games usually and always wanted to play some kind of first person tavern manager. However giving us a set of tasks to aim for, only to then give us a bunch more to do after we have finished them (usually even grindier) feels too filler. I understand the devs are padding out some of the game but I do not think you need to do it this way as its frustrating knowing you have to spend another 1 or 2 hours minimum to do the next hidden set of tasks. And who knows, maybe more tasks after that before we upgrade! Also the 'helpers' will sometimes just stop working completely, making them kind of pointless some of the time.

review:
Bugs, bugs, and more bugs.

If this game released in early access instead of a full release, I would recommend it. But it is not anywhere near ready for release. Performance issues in late game is horrible, even on a powerful computer. Fairies getting stuck, requiring you to reload every 20 minutes is a non-starter. 

The fact that new stuff is locked behind a quest system also disappoints me. They want me to spend $200 on a fairy house that I know is bugged before I can use the boiler that works. I bought the boiler, then found out I can't do anything with it until I get to that part of the quests. I don't want to progress in a linear way that they designed. I want to progress in a way that I want it to. My reputation is at level 7, but my tavern is at level 5. I am currently stuck with needing to sell ale, and guess what item most customers are no longer wanting as much now that I have other items? So I am stuck for however long, and cannot progress until I do this. I cannot grow my tavern until I do this. 

I want to like this game. I want to enjoy it. And it has the possibility to get there. But it is not there. I guess if you have an extra $12 to spend to sit on the game to see if they fix the bugs, buy it. But I don't recommend it.

review:
I was so excited for this game. But after playing it the last few days, I've nearly reached the top of the upgrade tree and saw that there are no additional perks you can buy so either they will add some or that's it. Not only that, despite being level 12 in reputation, I can't upgrade more until I do these tasks that check off the random list ie; sell 15 sausage, 15 ale etc. And it's stupid. Not to mention, you can't hire people to help, instead you get these fairies that are, honestly just useless. They get stuck, they glitch out and visually stay over a table. Their AI needs work ie; I happened to be in the noble area and had some walk in. So I took care of it. Then I had two fairies fly in as I had already cleaned up another table and was walking out so I stopped to watch and yep! Grabbed the items and went to place it on the table. I've also seen them only take care of a table partially. Honestly, it's frustrating because they're super slow and carry one thing and will glitch out so you are left babysitting them. The one that has worked most is the dishwasher and that one sometimes needs to be reset. 

The amount of freedom you get to decorate is poor. I tried handing some stuff in my room and for the life of me, would not take it. Not to mention you only have so many items you can sell. And, as a manager game I should be able to change my prices. I honestly found it a chore to play towards the end and kinda boring. Which sucks cause I was so excited for this. Hopefully it improves and maybe after good overhaul of the system I'll try it again since I'm stuck with it.

review:
I played all through what was available. It's a hard okay. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed playing the game, but I'd not really recommend it to other people /yet/.

The game has a solid core gameplay loop of mobile-game level bartending and catering to NPCs. All that said, this game is not great. It needs work. It's impressive that it was made by two guys working on a game, and as a short little casual experience it's alright. As a basic management game, Tavern Simulator checks every box, but this game doesn't do anything innovative at all. 

I was disappointed with the Tavern upgrades at every turn. I spent hundreds of coins upgrading kitchen items with no difference made. I couldn't tell you after 13 hours the difference between quality of the created items in gameplay -- a perfect ale or a regular ale will make anyone throw up all the same so there's no real reason to focus on making anything perfect. 

I really wish that basic things were upgraded: Chopping wood would go faster, maybe some kind of magical well upgrade that auto-refills the wash basin when it runs out of water. No matter how advanced the tavern got, there are just a few things like the well and chopping block.

The fairies are practically non-functional half the time. The Dishwasher and cook fairies work, but the Cook fairies never produce perfect items (Not that it matters most of the time). Waitress Fairies will just break if you complete an order just a little bit faster than them. They move painfully slow in a game where you're juggling delivering orders as fast as you can. This game ultimately just tries to give you convenience in all the wrong places. 

I think this game has a lot of potential. There are some things that could be done that would make this a game I played long term obsessively:
1. More events. This game really needs like themed days that pop up every now and again like fairs or festivals or people coming in from jousting tourneys where you get bonus money for meeting certain demands and to mix up gameplay. It also just needs to up the percentage of unique events happening all around. I think I hit a thief twice with a pan in 13 hours. 
2. More exploration outside of the Tavern. The Easter Eggs were cool, but I'd love the option to buy tavern stuff from the town as well as cosmetics for the tavern. I want to put way more work in to restoring the tavern. 
3. Tavern Gossip/Bounty Boards...any additional flavor at all. Taverns and Bars are social places, and there are dialogue menus in this game -- I wish there was more to that than just welcoming people. 
4. A better Actionable goal than just "to be the best tavern" when there is no tavern in comparison. It's like you're just waiting for someone at the end of the game to tell you you're the best. 

tl;dr Game's got potential - It's very basic and needs some more love.

- If you were to quit and resume the game, the fariy helpers won't do their assigned tasks unless you manually assigning them again.
- Fariy helpers lvling system are bad, there are zero difference between level 1 or level 7. They will never able to make "Perfect" items or perform their tasks better.

- Lack of endgame content, you'll experience everything that the game has to offer at mid game around tavern 7-8. Once you reach max tavern lvl 12, you'll unlock 1 new guest type and then the game become a sandbox type and you pretty much repeat the gameplay loop you experienced around tavern lvl 7-8.

review:
*EDIT: After months, I came back to this game to see if anything has changed, and hoped to change my review.

To my delight a lot of the game break bugs were indeed fixed.

Other than that, all of the things in my initial review remain problems.

Over the last couple of months, no new content was made, just decorations that don't do anything besides look pretty.

A little disappointed, a game not being completely broken should not be the bar that is set for a "good game".

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Original Review:

After 11 hours I have beaten this game.

I have finished the quests, maxed out my tavern upgrades, furniture, and purchased all decorations.

Here is my synopsis:

1. This game is fun, but very very broken. I don't recommend buying this game until they fix all the literal game breaking bugs.

2. At around tavern level 7 money becomes completely obsolete, making progression purposeless.

3. Almost the entire game is made using pre-built assets, and AI generated crap.

4. The user experience is not well thought out, leaving many aspects of the game to be a practice of guess and check.

5. Poor optimization, I have an oc rtx 4070ti, I can run huge games at max graphics at at least 200fps, I was stuck at around 30fps throughout my play period, with it getting worse as I progressed.

6. The map surrounding your tavern is relatively empty, with a few fun exploreable easter eggs that may give you a decoration or a table. There is no lore, just Naruto, Dark Souls, and LOTR references.

7. Lastly, I did have fun playing this game, I've sent the developers a number of bug reports, and I look forward to them fixing this game, and expanding upon it. 

If the above problems don't shy you away, and you are willing to wade through the problems to have some fun, then buy it now. Otherwise, wish-list, and come back when it's actually ready.

review:
It is a cool concept but not amazingly implemented. Kinda feels like a random mix of Unity's game asset packages bunched together.

If this was an alpha I would, maybe, forgive it...  but it a game lost between simulator and fantasy styles.

- The bad
It is too fast paced to be a chill game, progression feels very empty... using fairies as helpers makes the world feel even more empty. Art direction is a mess, characters look like they came straight from WoW but other art does not match it, all your doors are open all the time which just looks terrible and lazy meanwhile displaying a very unattractive scenery. - I have to add that: damn the lighting sucks, it could be so much more but there are no shadows! - Character animation and dialogue is lacking, patrons even clip into one another while sitting. When you get your delivery it all becomes a big bag. Then the game loses itself between having to do things manually and having things "magically" done like changing the beer barrel. Putting the ingredients from the warehouse to your cauldron. Also there is no control over how you build your tavern. There is no control over sell prices.

-The Good
The concept itself is nice. Having to do things manually is very satisfying. Asking for a delivery and waiting for it is pretty nice too - I rather wait for a whole day or longer if it rains. Automation of some of the most annoying tasks. Cauldron produces a big batch of products and can be kept with firewood. 

Man it is sad, very sad. It needs to firmly decide between going simulator or going fantasy. I could understand fairies making low physical or magical tasks but... washing dishes... why isn't a high magic creature doing the whole business instead? Have a damn goblin or a respectfully earning humanoid. How the hell does the delivery man delivers me a single pint of beer instead of a whole barrel? Why do I see multiple barrels on my warehouse but my single barrel holds a hundred worth pints? Nights are not even dark... how come I can't clear the trash and add a little stage for a bard? I have to pay for an "upgrade" that just cleans some trash...

It is low priced but I see so little effort in this game it is hard to recommend without having a roadmap of improvements.

review:
In [i]Tavern Manager Simulator[/i] serve your patrons the best ale and grub in town while working your way up to owning the best tavern in the kingdom. 

[h3]Gameplay & Features[/h3]

The setting options in this game include; Language selection, resolution options, graphics quality settings, audio controls, mouse sensitivity and the ability to disable head sway (love this feature for those of us who get nausea in games). The game also supports widescreen monitors. Mouse and keyboard (no controller support). 

The movement of your character in this game is smooth as you run and jump. There is a whole map to go and explore, not just your tavern. This is such a nice addition to the game. Other areas of the map will also open up as you progress. During your exploring you can find some treasures along the way such as gold and items to decorate your tavern with. 

Now progression in this game is behind levelling up your tavern by doing objectives. Some of these tasks are pretty tedious. Serve so many ales, or sell so many food items. The typical objectives. So you cannot freely decorate your tavern or add additions until you unlock that level. 

I honestly do not care for this system. It makes the gameplay much more linear and takes away that joy of designing your own tavern. It becomes all about grinding out that next level. 

You are also limited to where you can place your purchased items, the game has already decided for you what areas are designated for decorations and table placement. Making the linear feel of this game much more noticeable. 

[h3]The Visuals & Audio[/h3]

Visually the open world part of the game is beautiful to look at. The NPC’s are generic, not honestly all that appealing to look at. They all pose the same way and all share the same animations. I honestly did not mind this as much as I was playing more for the immersion of designing my own tavern. 

The music is fitting, medieval, fantasy type music that you would expect to find in a game set in a fantasy realm. 

[h3]Overall Experience[/h3]

If you would enjoy this game depends on what you'd like to get out of it.  The price point is a highlight as a lot of sim games are much more expensive in this genre. What will probably hold this game back in comparison to others is how linear it is. You do not really get to design the tavern of your dreams. It is more levelling up your tavern through quests that become more of a grind as opposed to being rewarding. 

There are some nice touches like being able to explore the area outside of your tavern with loot to find but there is not enough there in the open world to keep that interest fresh for long once you have found all the goodies there is to find. 

The concept is a strong one but the execution is what holds it back. If progression was based on your reputation and experience earned and not locked behind tedious objectives it would be a lot more fun. If you do wish to pick up this game I would still recommend it on sale. It will pass the time for a few hours but I think eventually the linear grind will show itself.

review:
Tavern Manager is one of those games that can be enjoyed for a few hours. I don't mind it's simplicity, but it's certainly got it's fair share of redundancy. 

The biggest issue I have with Tavern Manager is it's longevity. At 1.8 hrs in the game, I had received 18 of it's 42 achievements and reached 1/3 of it's level progression, which is increased by a questing system. There's just enough meat on it's bones to make it fair for it's price point, but for me, I am looking for something to play more long term.

Tavern customization is limited and you'll always be customizing and expanding on the same tavern with no other options. I also wasn't too fond of the fairy system, which feels like a cheap way to tackle automation. There are just some things I didn't want to have to do myself. Like clean the outhouse in mini-game fashion and it's just far enough from your tavern to be annoying. Furthermore, there were other tasks that became so redundant, I couldn't see myself wanting to do them for the hours to come. Like washing dishes and sweeping the dang floor. Why can't fairies do that?

I like the concept. I like the art. I even like it's simplicity. But the honeymoon phase started to end before the refund window ended. So I am going to give it a pass.

review:
TLDR, this is a disappointing mess that gets boring after a few hours. Unless big changes are made, and the use of AI generated images is changed, I would strongly recommend against playing this.

While this was a decently fun experience with a very cute, almost world of Warcraft style to it. I have to say I cannot recommend this to anyone. It takes roughly 11-13 hours to finish the game, but trust me, past upgrading to tier 9 it is very boring. The fairies will end up doing all of the fun jobs, while you clean the toilet and the floors. 

There is also the glaring problems of it using AI generated images, which i only figured out after reading reviews to see if others were having similar issues as me. I never even figured out there was a bank with an ai generated goblin image to use as the banker, because theres not tutorial for getting a loan? Its apparently the safe in the corner of your bedroom, but i simply thought that was decoration. 

The world feels also open to the potential, or even teasing that there should be more there. But outside of the pointless eastereggs that, other than getting a decoration or a table, are just meh. you might think 'oh thats funny' at most and never think of it again. Instead of having a darksouls, wow, and other references littering the world around. it would have been nice to have a few farming or animal keeping mini games to get your own food for free instead of having to order it all. or maybe be able to unlock the town and walk to town to purchase your goods to get a better deal? you have the room for so much around your tavern thats just not used. 

there's a wizards tower on a hill that's just set dressing, there's the kings castle, there's a water wheel and a house across the bridge that's blocked off. there's a road that leads out to the world blocked by a tree. there's just so much more potential for more, that I'm honestly so disappointed that there's no road-map for future updates. This isn't shown as an early access game, if this is the full release, honestly, there's better simulator games than this. 

There's not even a point to decorating your tavern other than your own enjoyment, the customers don't give a crap about anything hanging on the walls or book shelves with plants on them. Its just something to spend your gold on, that they hope you wont realize that by end game your gold is useless anyway. 

TLDR, this is a disappointing mess that gets boring after a few hours. Unless big changes are made, and the use of AI generated images is changed, I would strongly recommend against playing this.

This game is cute and fun at first, but the more I play the more incomplete it feels. I keep double checking expecting it to still be early access and its not.
There's all these things you find exploring the map that you keep checking after each update expecting them to be something and they never end up being anything. Which isn't helped by the Goblin and Gnome side distractions that set up the expectation of more.

Village with the guard accusing us of a bad ale incident? I thought oh, maybe we eventually get to clear our names and unlock more content in the village. Nope, it's not even real. No people, just building shells with no innards.

Guy hanging from a tree asking us to tell his friend to come home? No sign of his friend. It's just an excuse to give you a random dude's picture you can put on you mantle.

Ogre's house? It's just a Shrek reference, never once actually had any encounters. I stole the fish off his door and never got a peep.

Helm on the alter? Just another decoration apparently. Just like the elf at the entrance is just there to be a WoW reference. Horde or Alliance? Whats the point in asking if it means nothing to the game I'm actually playing. I expected her to give me a quest, not ask stupid questions.

Can't go past the guards without an invitation to see the king? Where's my invitation?

Blacksmith over the hill? Kind of expected to eventually get tools from him. But no just a table his friends will never use because they went to a volcano.

Bridge I've never crossed blocked by debris? Where's my ax from the blacksmith to clear it?

Glowy Hero Sword in the tree? Just a fancy wall light for you bedroom apparently

Ghostly red knight with the ghostly red sword in the campfire? Who the F knows? Didn't want the sword or helmet I found. And never gave me any response to trying to talk to it.

Big field out back with the scarecrow? Expected to be farming at some point, but no.

Cave with the giant skull and the fancy hammer in it? Why can't I take the Hammer to? I kept expecting a quest that was going to send me in there and it never happened.

Got past the giant tree in the road just to find everything past it is just for looks, and the tower's just a shell.

So many potential quests and the only "quest" is to go catch a Goblin. And even that felt unfinished, I expected to do something more with it. Not just put it out as a decoration. 
Why are there a bunch of things to pickup that look like "Quest Items", but are just decorations? I kept expecting them to be something more. if they're not going to for anything but decoration, at least give me a reason to care about them by making them the reward of a quest or something. Not just random junk I find laying around that looks like it should have a specific purpose.

Don't give me expectations and leave me hanging.
No hate to the publishers, and not to demean the developer's work because I don't know the situation or who came up with the concept first. 
But In the end, between the similar and (in several cases) same assets and the unfinished feel of the game, I'm left FEELING like someone got wind of Ale and Tale and made a cash grab by rushing to get this out first. Whether or not this is actually the case.

review:
[h2]It's a nice time waster, but not a deep game.[/h2]

[b]GRAPHICS[/b]
I like the low poly style, but the character models are really ugly. The tavern and the environment do look nice, though.

[b]SOUND[/b]
Nothing to write home about. Some AI was used, but I play these games while listening to podcasts / music, so I turn down the in-game sound anyway. 

[b]CONTROLS[/b]
WASD movement, jump button. You click on stuff to get work done. Some jobs are mini-games / QTEs, but they're laughably easy. Wood cutting is a bit janky. The toilet cleaning mini-game is bad, because it's just an unnecessary element of additional tedium (see below). Generally, I don't like QTEs / click timers, because they offer no real mechanical challenge, they just feel stupid. Especially the cooking could be much more interesting. Let players combine ingredients to create special variants of foods. 

[b]GAMEPLAY[/b]
It's NOT a management game. There's ZERO economical management. You never really run out of money. As the tavern grows, you get more money, so restocking the shelves always stays on the same difficulty level. Gameplay mostly revolves about completing mundane tasks (preparing food / drinks, fetching wood / water, cleaning). It's a time management game, first and foremost. The core loop is fine, you never run out of stuff to do. But you do have to accept that it's a very simple game. 

[b]PROBLEMS[/b]
The fairy helpers are kinda useless, because the cook / bartender ones always create "normal" quality items. They should be making better items as they level up. The waitress fairy gets stuck at times. The dishwashing one works fine.

The main issue of this game really is the tedium. Many gameplay elements solely exist to annoy you. Cleaning is the most obvious one. The game turns into "footprint remover simulator" in the later stages, as the fairies do most of the other jobs - unless you insist on creating perfect food / drink items. 

There are some "special" encounters (beggar, traveller) and some funny interactions (people passing out, thievery), but these are only interesting for like 2-3 times. Then they start to be annoying. The map contains some secrets, but it feels like there could be so much more. Maybe they'll add additional elements with future updates.

There's also some padding, especially level 8 is insane. You'll end up with more than 4x the money you actually need to level up and buy all the upgrades. This needs to be rebalanced. I really don't get why you have to meet arbitrary requirements like "sell 30 soups & 30 steaks". It feels unnatural and forced. In my opinion, this "quest" system doesn't offer any real challenge. It would be much better if there was more emergent gameplay. Challenges should be created by interacting systems (cleanliness of the tavern, service / food quality, and so on). There's already a reputation meter (which basically is an XP system), so unlocking the next tavern level doesn't need an additional layer of requirements. 

The prices of food / drink items are predetermined, you have no influence on them. It would be nice to have at least some kind of control over them. Low prices could attract more peasants with more lenient quality requirements, high prices mean that you have to be a great bartender / cook to keep the rich people coming.

Decoration is utterly meaningless right now, it doesn't really affect client quality. Tavern Master does this MUCH better.

Oh, and please add a way to auto-supply water to the washing / cooking stations in the late game. Running to the well is just... well, you know... tedious.

[b]SUMMARY[/b]
It's good for what it is, but it could be SO much better. It's a shallow game, so I can't quite recommend it. I've had some fun, but there's zero replayability.

[h3]5/10[/h3]

Almost recommended.
It's an okay, chill game.

You prepare food and drinks through simple minigames, and then serve your guests in your somewhat customizable tavern. You also have to clean up and fill your tavern's inventory. Main progression is expanding the tavern and getting some new tools. You can also partially automate later.

In 12 hours I went through all the content currently in the game (there's also some idle time in that).
Everything worked as it should, but there's not much depth or variety, and zero replayability.
The minigames are good and satisfying, although the mechanics of them arbitrarily limit your speed. If these minigames were "unlocked" in a sense that with high skill you could achieve high speed and efficiency, that would add a LOT to the game for me.

I almost gave this a positive review, but the steam page seems to be overselling the game, which reminded me of my disappointments in the first few hours of my playthrough. - calling it a "fantasy tavern game" is sadly not true, a massive overstatement, it's not even close to how I'd imagine a true fantasy tavern. It's more like "tavern game (contains traces of fantasy)"
- "create a unique atmosphere" is also not there. Your tavern doesn't really feel "unique", especially when I played it with the forced chinese new year decorations, which overwhelm any decoration you can do. This game is just not alive enough for that.

I think with more content and some improvements it could be a neat game, and what is already there is enjoyable.

review:
Hello there,

[h1]Tavern Manager Simulator: A Frothy Mess[/h1]

I wish just like the curator page, I could give this information and tell you "maybe". Tavern Manager Simulator promises a delightful experience of running your medieval tavern.  Instead, it delivers a frustratingly buggy and shallow management sim that feels more like cleaning up a spilled keg than running a thriving business.  The core concept has potential, but the execution is so poor it leaves a bitter aftertaste.

[h1]Story:[/h1]

There are some dialogues with NPCs and Holiday Events but that's pretty much it. You are in the loop after that. 

[h1]Game Mechanics:[/h1]

♦Resource Management: You manage stock, finances, and staff. Sounds simple enough, right? Wrong.

♦Staff Management: Hire and fire staff and assign tasks. They'll mostly ignore you or get stuck on furniture.

♦Customer Satisfaction: Keep customers happy by serving them drinks and food. 

♦Tavern Customization: Decorate and upgrade your tavern. Because what's the point of a broken game if it doesn't look slightly less broken?


[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]

Pros:

+The idea is charming: The concept of running a medieval tavern is appealing. Unfortunately, the execution ruins it.

+Occasionally, it almost works: In those rare moments when everything clicks, you get a fleeting glimpse of the fun the game could be. These moments get quickly repetitive 

Cons:

-Bug-Ridden: Seriously, the bugs are a major problem. I was under the ground two times for no reason.

-Shallow Gameplay: Lack of depth in the management mechanics.

-Frustrating AI: Staff and customer AI are both terrible.

-Poor UI: Makes the game harder to play than it needs to be.

-Lack of Polish: The entire game feels unfinished.


[h1]Conslusion[/h1]

Tavern Manager Simulator is a frustrating and disappointing experience.  The charming concept is completely undermined by the numerous bugs, shallow gameplay, and terrible AI.  It's a game that's more likely to leave you with a headache than a satisfied thirst.

My recommendation would be;

Avoid this game like a bad batch of ale.  There are far better management sims out there that will respect your time and money.  This one needs a lot more work before it's even remotely enjoyable.


3/10

Until next time.
Take care everyone.

review:
Let's review this thang (for the second time, cause I accidentally deleted it when I switched my review from it's good to not recommended haha)

For pricing: I do not think it's worth the price. Maybe more around 5ish? Definitely wait for a sale. To be honest, there's not a lot to do. Not a lot of environment to explore, and it kind of feels like it should be multiplayer, despite there not being much to offer. There aren't that many things to cook, and every single mini game within the tavern is a time based one. "Let go when the marker reaches green or recipe is bad" type. I think there are quite a few games in this genre at this point, and they all just tend to use the same unity asset pack. Which is fine. Do whatever you need to make a game, but at least give it some substance. 

I will say, if it's on sale, the game is fun for people who like to run a little shop. I spent 12 hours on it just hunting steam achievements, and it was mostly just waiting for money. The quests do go beyond the steam achievements, so you will get more hours out of it if you are looking to complete it that way. 

*spoilers ahead* 
In terms of why I say it feels like it should be multiplayer, you can hire helpers. They are cute little Navi fairies that are happy to help wash dishes, and be your waitresses. They'll cook for you.. at a cost. Every recipe they make will be good instead of perfect. So yeah, you could automate everything except for ordering the food and drinks and a few other tedious tasks, but you would be sacrificing some decent money, and get bad reviews from the mean critic if you don't serve her perfect food. There is no upgrade to change this fact either. 

On another note, the water system also never gets a good upgrade. You're only allowed to run around with one bucket from the well, so the back and forth + jank animations to get more water really make it annoying. It doesn't get better, and you get no help for it. Even watching youtube videos on the game, I found that some people had a hard time figuring it out, but the second upgrade is a very wonky motion control system, where I find the water doesn't like to pour out half of the time. In fact, most of the animations in this game are just wonky in general haha. 

Cleaning is also extremely wonky, and footprints can get stuck under furniture causing you to have to move it away, and move it back. It doesn't matter if the furniture is close to the wall or not on some of the tables, so having larger tables are while necessary, also very annoying.

~A warning, some of the minigame sounds are so LOUD! Especially the chopping of the steak. Every clank of the knife on the steak that you have to chop 12+ times or something is like a ring to my soul. Turning the game volume down kind of takes away from the atmosphere, but if you are sound sensitive please keep this in mind.~

As for what I think might be my last spoiler, I think the player area is a bit too spread out. To get ice you have to walk a long way, and I even find that going to get buckets of water early, or bringing wood that you've chopped from outside is a bit far of a walk. There's no way to keep stacks inside to make it easier on you, so the running you do to get random things is added to the list of tediousness. 

(I love the little goodies and hope the devs don't get sued for the hidden item references)
*spoilers end here*

In the end, it's an upgrade game that seems overwhelming considering how little you make money wise, but it doesn't actually take that long to make what you need. So it is a decent little game to chase achievements on, I'll give it that. Unfortunately, I can't recommend it based on things I've said unless it is on sale. If it is, I recommend it for people who love simple shopkeep type games. I'm always stuck wanting there to be a neutral button unfortunately, because the game isn't bad, just a little wonky and tedious, and a bit too expensive for the value.

If you've read all of this, I'd say go watch a video on it. Don't watch it all in case of spoilers if you want to see certain things for yourself, but make sure you know what you're getting into! Also, there is a moment for sound sensitive people that I did include in the spoilers, which I marked with ~. Hope this helps!

review:
Sorely disappointed by this game. Could have been an enjoyable, cozy game for an evening or two if the developers had not chosen to artificially bottleneck playtime by omitting a considerable amount of QoL options. 

I am a fan of unlocking stuff, but I am also a fan of leveling up - that is leveling up and actually getting a sensible reward for the grind. I level up the character, but there is zero reward or any buffs to it. He just levels. That's it. There is no increase in quality of the things you produce, there is no increase in speed, there is no increase in "ease" of the minigames or anything. 

The fairies that are some alibi help later on can "level" as well, but (probably) other than speed for the tasks they are to fulfill, they also do not actually "grow". They can never cook or tap a high quality item and are thus utterly useless, other than for washing dishes. You lose out on a huge amount of money if you let them cook or tap, thus bottlenecking play time even more, since you need money to unlock tavern growth.

Fairies are not even good at serving or emptying tables or tidying the inn. They are just too bad at those jobs and you are about 500 % faster at everything if you do it yourself. Why is that such a disappointment then, just don't use the fairies? It wouldn't be so bad if the minigames that you are FORCED to play to actually craft stuff weren't so utterly HORRIBLE. And BORING. Tapping the drinks: Hold mouse button, release mouse button at the correct time. Imagine fishing in SDV and the bar never grows larger with experience or a better rod or anything. Yes, the miniscule space in that bar never grows, making it easier to tap beer or wine, ever after you have tapped 200 of them. It only ever stays the same boring Hold-Release "game" for the rest of it. 

So, if you do not want to lose out on money, you have to do those tasks yourself. And for the most annoying tasks like drawing water from the well or cutting firewood - something that wouldn't necessarily need quality - you cannot even employ the fairies. Drawing water is a HORRIBLE minigame: You either click and hold if you don't want to puke or you click, hold and violently circle your mouse button while the whole world swings around you. Like playing old school DOOM and getting motion sick. Later on, the minigame changes and you have to figure out how to actually position correctly to draw any water at all, with a kind of crescent moon like action. Who designed this xxxx?? Cutting firewood is so stupidly dumb, you don't even need to actually aim with the mouse, it doesn't really matter as long as you don't actually pull the mouse out of the screen, you will always hit correctly. You could probably program some macros for the most annoying of those games and then just play walking simulator. How is this enjoyable??

And no, just putting in some references to other games or shows doesn't cut it. Just make a decent game, Jesus Christ. And keep your advertising for your stupid soft XXXX anime game out of the loading screen. I don't need that filthy trash.

review:
I love the concept of this game, but the execution is lacking currently.  Yes, it is early access, but based on the demos, it seems like the time since then has more been spent on additional content rather than expanding or fleshing out the core concept (imo).

Up front, The biggest issue is there is not really any "game" to be had here.  There are no fail states, no impactful decisions (whether that be time management, conversation or gameplay choices), no true "game".  From a gameplay standpoint this is essentially just an extremely low budget, bare bones VN with some busywork thrown in.  You might think that this is some sort of puzzle game based on the screenshots and trailer, that you get these objects that you need to figure out how to identify, clean and sell, but not really.  That's the busy work.  When chiseling a new object, there is no way to fail, no way to do it "correctly", no way for you, the player, to effect anything.  All you do is mash the cursor on anything and everything.  You can't damage the object, you can't do it wrong, you can't make a wrong decision via your actions.  You just keep clicking until it's done.  THAT IS IT.

Outside of the chiseling/sponging "minigames", you are clicking through typical text fodder between customers and your shopkeeper.  To be frank, these characters are low quality, flat JPGs.  I had hoped that some more effort would go into the NPCs after seeing the demo, thinking that these cardboard cut-out looking characters were placeholders, but that doesn't seem to be the case.  The conversations between you and NPCs, if it can even be considered conversations, is extremely basic and safe.  It is genuinely suitable for a children's book, that's how basic we're talking.  I'm not advocating for a complex novel of dialogue here, but something that doesn't feel like it was designed for literal 5 year olds.  Maybe that explains the lack of a fail state, or any real gameplay to speak of.  It would certainly make sense why this game could be described as little more than a digital fidget toy rather than an actual game.

A good comparison would be Potionomics, which I suspect the devs of this have played and used as some level of inspiration.  Potionomics has things like VN style conversations, time management and actual player agency, decisions and interactions.  If you spend too much time doing things that are unproductive, you suffer and will fail.  If you don't make intelligent, planned decisions in your potion brewing or customer interaction, you will suffer and fail.  This is what game design is, and it's where the "fun" comes from in a game.  The ability for a player to test their wits and understanding of the games mechanics and suffer or succeed.  Without consequences, it's not a game, it's a toy.  That's what Trash Goblin is, in its current state at least.  On top of those things, Potionomics has quality 3D models and animations for their characters, whilst Trash Goblin...does not.  As I said, they are relatively low quality looking jpgs that look distinctly out of place in the 3D modeled environment.

Most worrying on this aspect is I think I've seen others mention this and the dev has responded that this is how they want the game to be and don't have plans to really deviate from this path(?).  If that's the case, it's unfortunate.  I couldn't recommend this game in any capacity if this is the intended design.  I was really hoping this would scratch that 3D Picross itch in SOME capacity, but it doesn't.  

Ignoring design issues, there is also the added fun of the game not saving, so twice now I've gone through the mind-numbing tutorial.  I'm not going through it again.  I don't think this game is ready to be released even in early access, and given the core design of the game, or lack thereof, I don't think it ever will be.

For starters this game seems very Well made and like it has a good team behind it that put some care into it.
I do not know much about the developer or the future plans for this game at this time.
I understand that this game is in early access and will most likely receive updates to improve on its gameplay.

With that being said.

Core functions of the game 
you start out clicking through a barrage of text as there is No voice dialogue from what I experienced there are only groans when you 
click to your next text box. then it proceeds to show you, your four "Stations" the workbench, the customer table, the bed, and your staircase where you talk to the, idk owner I guess. Hope you like these cause its where you spend the whole game from what it seems. It prompts you little text boxes telling you what these stations do and are used for. then you get to test them out in the tutorial by serving a customer who needs an item that you must clean up to sell to him. the basic function of this game is to hear what a customer needs then go open a bag that will likely have that item in it, get the dirt off the item with a chisel tool, clean it with your sponge, then sell it to the customer and maybe you upgrade it. that's the entire game. there does not seem to be a real "Shop" element to it where like you can put items on a shelf and customers can offer on them or anything like that yet. these chisel and cleaning "minigames" feel mindless and boring and don't really add any kind of fun factor to the "Game". there does seem to be a lot of items to discover and maybe new shops to be seen further down the line but the desire to progress in this gameplay is just not there for me its not keeping my attention or scratching what I wanted out of this game.

Time management system
they have opted to go with this odd time management system that feels as if it was pulled straight from a mobile game where you have time blocks for your day, and certain
actions require certain time blocks. Lets say I wanted to chisel a trinket and clean that item, Well that just took 2 of your 5 time blocks away before you have to go to bed. so it makes it near impossible to serve 2 customers in a day this system gets old real fast I played this game to run a shop not sleep every 10 mins just to get to help 1 maybe 2 customers. I think surely they could find a better system to implement here.

Play-ability 
I really loved what they made this game sound Like, Honestly. I have not even 30 mins in the game as of this review and I'm having to have a youtube video up on another monitor just to keep my entertainment up. I sure hope they add more of a Game in future development. sometimes you are just kind of sitting there cleaning items cause customers are few and far between at times or at least very slow to come. leaves a empty feeling in the game world no consistent flow and in all honestly not sure how you could manage a consistent flow with the time management system. NPC's in the game are these 2D PNG images that just kind of shake and groan at you and don't do any real movement or talking.
If you need a mindless game to play while you are doing something else I guess I could see this being something, but for me I just do not enjoy it.

seems to be a few issues but the development team seems to somewhat be responding to those in the discord, I hope the team keeps up with development and maybe moves in the right directions, But from how it seems this is the game they wanted and may not deviate to broader shop style concepts. If you are looking to me to give a recommendation on this title, for me I'd say avoid this game or at least give it some time to add more to it If that is something the development team plans on even doing.

review:
Needs more time to cook.

Fun concept but has too many rough edges to recommend right this second (day of release). 

First the good. The game is fun and cute. It has that relaxing, doing chores but don't have to move to do them, gameplay loop. There is a promising game in there.

Now the bad.

-The story is meh. Nothing amazing, nothing terrible. But a game like this, I'd prefer a little more story.

-Controls and hit detection need work. Things like setting your tool down after chipping or cleaning a relic is way too fussy. I don't like that you have to hover your mouse over the "Continue" button do advance dialog or tutorials. It would be nice if you could just click anywhere for next.

-The cleaning in particular can be bad, especially if you have another item on your bench. The game is extremely picky about where you can touch relics to clean them. It's not so bad on the larger objects but the skinny ones like the magnifying lens or a hair pin are downright painful.

-It's annoying you can't sleep without using up all of your energy. Sometimes I just want to put the game down but there's no way to go to bed early. Maybe that's not really a problem, but see my point below.

-Perhaps worst of all, the game gives you no indication of when it saves AND you have to finish the tutorial before you can save your game AND the game doesn't indicate that at all. I ended up having to restart the game because I didn't cross the invisible line between the tutorial and the "proper" game. Likewise, I don't know *when* the game saves so I don't know if I can just stop and quit with one time segment left in the day, and I can't sleep without completely using up my time, so I end up having to keep playing until I can go to sleep so I don't lose any progress.

So I think this is a game worth watching and I'm not going to refund it. But if you're reading this at release and the game hasn't been updated, I'd wait a bit before buying it.

In its current state I can't recommend it.  It is an interesting concept, but is just missing any sense of progression or achievement.  The gameplay loop gets stale after about 1 hour.

From my perspective, the following game mechanics would be expected in a game like this and they're just missing:
- Trinket gathering minigame/dungeons (just having it magically appear on your bench is really weird).
- Regions to gather trinkets which have different loot tables to try to get specific items.
- Bartering with customers (many others have mentioned this)
- Upgrading tools to be quicker/more efficient.
- Ability to expand number of "active customers" at a time.
- Ability to put items up for sale for "window shopping" with different components having different values that change like an active market. This would also open up "rushes" of demand for a specific object.
- Regular customers that come more frequently but expect better prices.
- Customers have a specific amount of time they're willing to wait.
- Different unlocked decorations change variables like demand for objects, customer patience, rate of finding "rare" trinkets, etc...

Those features would at least put this game in line with its competition. 

I'll keep my eye on development, but this release plays more like a rudimentary demo. The only thing you can do is chip away relics, clean them off and attach random things together. Customers are more of an inconvenience than part of the game, unlocking new decorations in your shop is meaningless and just a money sink.

review:
There is an increasing trend in the popularity of cosy games. For many, gaming is no longer — or never was — about hacking and slashing through fantastic worlds, or shooting past wave after wave of enemies. Rather, gaming is about a sense of escape, and a chance to relax and decompress from the stress of the world. 

Cosy games can be best understood as games that don’t necessarily require much thought or planning, aren’t particularly ability or skill-focused, and are very forgiving of mistakes. This isn’t to diminish these games, or to diminish the skill of the people playing them. It is, however, to say that there is a world of difference between the consequences of a mistake in Cat Cafe Manager and, say, Counter-Strike. 

With this focus on accessibility, there comes a point where a game can be excessively accessible, to the point where it is nothing but mindless repetitive actions with no challenge or interest to be derived from it. This is especially true in job sims, and is what I’d argue is the fundamental failure of a game like Plane Accident. 

It’s also the fundamental failure of Trash Goblin. Trash Goblin veers too far into cosy, forgetting that it is also meant to be a game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3362633511 

Trash Goblin is a cosy job simulator. You play as a goblin, collecting, cleaning, and refurbishing trinkets to sell in a fantasy junk shop to whatever fantasy customers happen to pass by. As the days go on, you get brief glimpses of your customers’ lives, colouring in the world beyond your walls. 

To be clear, despite taking place in a shop, this is not a shop simulator. This is a cleaning and assembling game. There is no real way to set inventory, no way to set prices, and no way to grow the stop. While players do have the option to upgrade their tools, the tools upgrade in a fixed order, leaving no room to think strategically about which skills to upgrade, or whether to upgrade a skill at all. 

Indeed, calling the actions in Trash Goblin “skills” is itself a bit of a stretch. The goblin’s day consists primarily of cleaning and chipping away at objects, then hoping a customer interested in that object comes along to buy it. However, rather than the process of cleaning being based on the player’s own skill, the size of the object, or any external factor, the game instead assigns a fixed amount of time to each cleaning or repairing action, limiting what can be accomplished in any given day. The ultimate impact of this is that the player has no real agency. They, like the goblin they play, are trapped in an endless loop of grabbing an item, discovering it’s not what the customer wants, and being forced to waste more time grabbing another and another and another, with no real way to improve or break out of the cycle. 

So it is a job sim, then. Just maybe less cosy than the devs intended.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3362633348 

Beyond the lack of ability to change anything about the gameloop or the shop, save for its aesthetics, Trash Goblin has no plot or progression. While a customer will sometimes show up at the window and not leave until they get their single, very specific item, these customers have no real bearing on the shop. The brief glimpses into their lives based on the items they buy are too shallow to give them true character, and the fact that they gum up the store with their demands made me dislike when I saw one showing up. 

With no way to improve and grow in a way that meant anything to the game, and no reason to distinguish one day from the next, I got bored and frustrated very quickly. Adding in the various bugs I encountered (one of which made the entire cleaning and chiselling loop impossible by disabling my left mouse button), and the entire experience was a far cry from cosy. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3362633095 

The most tragic element of Trash Goblin, though, is that it didn’t have to be this tedious and dull. There are some fantastic elements throughout that made me want to believe there was more to it than what I’d seen. The art and design of the world, for example, are beautiful. The trinkets are fun, and I enjoyed what few snippets of story I did get. There is the potential for a good game in here, one with a dynamic shop and the ability to actually have some degree of agency over the game. Currently, Trash Goblin is not that. Instead, it is a tedious, monotonous experience, riddled with bugs, and failing to answer the question of why I should press on through any of them. 

Throughout my playthrough, I was reminded of another disassembly-based job sim that illustrates why Trash Goblin doesn’t succeed, that being Hardspace Shipbreaker. While the settings and gameplay loops are wildly different, the fundamental philosophies undergirding them are not. Both are games being in a world centred around one’s work. Both are cosy job sims, focused on the player doing the best they can with the tools available to them. Both are games fundamentally about capitalism, the whims of a system beyond our ken or control, and building ourselves a world that works for us within it.

Where Hardspace Shipbreaker succeeds and Trash Goblin fails, though, is in giving meaning or purpose to the job. Hardspace sees its job accentuated with a plot, mystery, and a sense of progression and choice. The player shares their world with three-dimensional characters, choosing how to approach their work, and becoming better and better at it over time. The player’s skills build with the character, giving everything a meaning, a purpose, and a sense of something bigger than just clicking buttons. 

Trash Goblin does none of this. It traps the player in the same actions over and over, with neither meaning or control. If we call both job sims, Hardspace is the job sim for the job we wish we had — something satisfying, meaningful, and not too overwhelming. Trash Goblin is the job we actually have — rote, boring, and a reminder that, even though life is finite, we’re trapped in the limits of our rooms, with no real prospect of ever getting out to actually live. 

I’d rather play in a world of imagination, personally. As such, this goblin does not recommend perusing through this particular bag on the workshop bench.

review:
There's something therapeutic about chipping away at the little puzzles and popping blocks until an item comes out, cleaning it... Kinda like a youtube restoration video.

The problem, however, is that in this early access phase, there's very little to do. I went to about day 45, at which point the regular customers with a name, the interesting ones, had stopped showing up. I stopped getting new items. The only tool you can upgrade is the one that lets you attach more trinkets, but there's a limited number of slots on the items available, and I struggle to imagine attaching more than 4. It's also not really intuitive what can be attached to what.

The trailer says something about taking the shop on the road, but that didn't happen, and my patron who lives upstairs in the antique shop stopped showing up long ago, even though the bell says I can ding it to talk to him.

The loop, unfortunately, dried up, and the sense of exploration I had at the start didn't linger. There's a lack of strategy and interest in the current content, and no real lore to explore, and not enough content. Once you've exhausted the items and all the customers that show up at random strangers who ask for a random item ("in any condition" every time), the loop then becomes repetitive and drab.

Come back in a couple content updates, I think. I still enjoyed the first couple of hours I put into it, but it's a bit early in the early access to get a recommendation.

review:
No stakes, no skill or strategy involved in any way. You simply exist in a small building, randos come by and demand something from you that you might or might not get based on RNG, if you don't get it you lose time and eventually have to start a new day until you finally get the thing you need and then you can sell it to the rando for a fixed amount which you don't control. You do not price. You do not walk. You do not do anything that could bring any sort of gameplay aside from the repetitive drudgery of pick pick pick, sponge sponge sponge, maybe glue something together that nobody will buy. The rando will also take 5 seconds before you can dismiss their dialogue box as well, so you'll be furiously clicking until they finally decide you can close the box, and they won't leave until you fulfill their order, regardless of how long it takes or what you may want. You are not in control. You have no agency.
You can experience nearly the same thing you do in this game at your regular job - repetitive drudgery with no end or goal in sight. Maybe you can earn enough to decorate your workspace a little, just like IRL. You don't get to go out into the possibly colorful world hinted at by smatterings of dialogue from two-dimensional randos, but no, that's for other people. Not you.
Stay in your little hole, Goblin. Dig through your trash. You have no value aside from what others ascribe, and there is nothing you can do about it. Your world is your four walls. 
I could have saved money on kickstarter if I'd realized that there would be nothing else to the game aside from a depression simulator.
The game brands itself as "fantasy powerwash simulator." However, they missed the part where it's actually a game, you can move around, you can choose how and what you do, and you can choose where you go and what missions you take. They missed that purchaseable upgrades should actually affect gameplay, or that skill could factor into how a person plays. Each person has a different way they approach powerwash simulator - there is only one way in Trash Goblin.
Don't waste your time.

review:
A decent core attempt at a 'cozy' game but I cant recommend it as it is now, It's just missing any true depth unfortunately, which is a shame because I was really excited when I first heard about the game. As it is, all there is, is the primary game loop, get given a quest, dig through trash till you get said item, wash it and sell it for the given price, seemingly no haggling allowed. meanwhile you end up with mountains of trash you can do nothing with until a random npc (which you can only have one of at a time) requests it. This makes the game deeply unsatisfying as time progresses since you ahve no agency, all the money can be used for is buying more worksurfaces to put more trash on when your bag overflows or to upgrade the combining tool, the only tool that upgrading doesnt make the primary loop more efficient.

I dont want the review to be all negative because as I said at the start of the review, theres a great core here and with fleshing out the game could be something awesome. The main requirement as far as i can see is fleshing out the secondary and tertiary loops. Firstly the secondary loop, I want money to mean something with useful upgrades (bigger/faster sponge, slow auto cleaner/chipper that i have to load up and keep an eye on, etc.) and for more agency in how I make money, its a shop, why cant I put items on display to sell them? then have the character npc's make special requests, this immediately makes the player choose whether to sell something for temporary gain or to save it for a bigger combine and money boost later, or to just stockpile for a potential quest. Money can then also be spent on upgrading the shop, more selling shelves, higher quality shelves to sell things for more, etc.

Then the Tertiary loop, what are my overarching goals? why do i keep coming back to play? Having meaningful upgrades to the shop and tools will help as then I can aim to maxing out the shop, but maybe also a collection log, that way holding on to pieces to see if they will make a unique combination enters the agency argument from before. The game doesnt need to be challenging, I understand its meant to be a chill cozy atmosphere kinda game, but these games still need a destination otherwise players will just stop pretty quickly.

review:
Editing review because the game has released and I have very strong thoughts about how it's been 'improved' since early-access. It's still a cute game, but the issues definitely outweigh any fun to be had, and considering the game has been fully released for a while now there's been more than enough time to address the problems it has:

PROS:
- Super cute artstyle
- Unique NPCs you'll (usually) recognise whenever they pop-up again
- Simple but fun puzzle-based gameplay to uncover the trinkets
- Tool and workspace upgrades you can get throughout the game
- Almost-fully customisable rooms and furniture

CONS:
- The RNG is absolutely atrocious - a customer will ask for a specific trinket and I'll spend at least two or three in-game days to find it, which creates a massive backlog of dirty trinkets everywhere, and then the customer will leave at the end of the day anyway so my efforts were wasted, PLUS the replacement customer won't want anything I've got lying around so I end up either repeating that same experience or just refusing anyone service unless they want what I already have
- Most new equipment and upgrades won't say enough about what they do before you buy it - a couple examples are that the pay-what-you-can box doesn't say it initially only holds one trinket at a time, and the soap bucket doesn't say it only works overnight
- You can upgrade more than just the attachment tool now (I still can never remember the name) so they actually feel useful and fun to use, but there's other stuff to spend money on so you have to weigh all your options and figure out if breaking blocks easier is more important than being able to store all your random trinkets no one wants
- The sponge works well on about half the trinkets, while the other half it cleans much slower and harder with no indication of if it's related to size or material or whatever, so only at max-upgrade does it feel any ounce of ease
- The only way to 'dispose' of trinkets you don't want/need is a limited-slot box that you have to wait overnight to see any results from, so you very easily get a massive backlog and have to spend all your money on shelves and stash upgrades to hope to hold it all, which obviously cuts massively into the money you could otherwise spend on tool upgrades or customization

I can't say it's a fun game at all, as there's way too many problems that remain unaddressed that massively cut into any fun you could have. I wouldn't recommend this game at all, as the developers don't seem to understand the massive RNG issue that's ever-present throughout the game so there's no hope for them to fix the foundational problems, instead focusing on letting you make your workshop slightly prettier while you drown in a sea of unwanted and unremovable trinkets.

review:
I am a couple hours into the release of the game after playing the beta very thoroughly and I gotta say I feel like... The game got a little worse after launch. Progress is abysmally slower than it was in the beta due to the changes in how customers work and what they ask for. Before that I'll just start with some positives, despite my review saying no. 

First and foremost the game is very chill. There is no pressure, no time constraints, and you're not expected to do everything right away. You take it at your own pace and do things your way. You can ignore customers at your window and just focus on gathering trinkets or keep turning the nameless ones away hoping one will come asking for something you already have for a quick sale. Named characters, thank god, were changed to allow you to send them away and then call them back when you're ready with their item. In the beta you could send them away but they might not come back until the next day or the day after sometimes. So really that was an improvement. 

A lot of the bugs in the beta were polished up and fixed when it comes to moving items around, but it is still a little janky. Way better than before but the change in how you hold items does make things a bit funky. There's an item called a teapot that looks like a genie's lamp and while you might want it to stand upright, the thing just slowly turns until it's completely upside down because I assume it's a top heavy item in the physics engine so certain items just... look weird if you want to display things for aesthetic reasons. Still, I haven't had any items just glitch into the walls or lose their interaction completely, teleporting into the abyss or thrown into your bag for no reason, etc. 

With that said I'd like to air out the problems I personally find this game has. The biggest thing you might notice is how abysmally slow this game is. I played the beta so I already had just about my entire shop maxed out before the release and my reward was having like 30k gold in my new game the moment I opened it up which was nice, since old saves were made incompatible with the release. Yet despite this I still have to play until like day 12 before I'm finally allowed to upgrade something, and even then it wasn't what I wanted. You cant upgrade your sponge, chisel, or upcycler whenever you want and you gotta get a decent way through the early game before you can, and let me tell you, the base level tools you have absolutely suck. The chisel is super weak, the sponge's area of cleaning is microscopic, and the upcycler is borderline useless at level 1 since you can only attach two things. The game forces you to play the same gameplay loop for days and days and days on end before its suddenly like "oh, by the way, here's the sponge upgrades if you have the money for them." Granted, you're not gonna have 30k gold burning a hole in your pocket the moment you start a new game, but you might find yourself wishing you could upgrade your tools because of how painfully slow it is to use them. 

Speaking of slow, the entire gameplay loop is basically just using your chisel on the bag to poke at cubes to reveal a dirty trinket underneath, use your sponge (or soaking tub if you can afford to buy one) to clean said trinket, and then hope to god someone might ask for it. The trinkets you get are completely random so while someone might want a lich crown, you might not find one for weeks. In my opinion this becomes very problematic down the line when you're looking for ONE SPECIFIC ITEM and you play through days or even weeks and just never find it. You might have a lich's crown and you want a lich's gem and then just literally never find a lich's gem. Play for 10+ in game days and never find it, doing nothing but chiseling all day every day to never actually get one until one day you finally get it and at that point you don't even care, it took so long and there is no relief, its just... "eugh.... finally i guess..." 

Another major problem I have that ties into the slow progression of the game is the change to NPCs and their requests. Before in the beta 99% of characters that came to your shop usually asked for one item in any condition or clean, and then didn't care what was attached to it. Your money maker was your upcycler because you could be asked for a glass eye, so you give them a glass eye... attached to a mask... that also has a human fist made of wood, a goblin lantern, and a gem attached to it or something, and you'd charge them like 500 gold for all the items you used. You could push out a lot of stock by doing this regularly and you'd make a lot of money which was needed cause every upgrade for both your tools and your shop are as low as like 150 a pop and as expensive as 1500+ a pop. [b]But now?[/b] Every character except named ones seem to almost always ask for ONE VERY SPECIFIC ITEM, which means the money you make is going to be absolutely tiny a majority of the time. With only so many time slots in the day and people asking for something like ONLY a magnifying glass, or ONLY a bent nail, you're gonna have so many days where your profits are gonna read like 30 gold in the day when a pot of coffee costs 20. I was glad to have the money to upgrade my shop to full but personally I'd hate to play a fresh save now with how little gold you make at the beginning, but maybe it gets easier in the late game, I can't say quite yet. 

This game serves its purpose in being a slow chill game you can take at your own pace, and if progress isn't something that bothers you then maybe you'll like it. I find that it being mouse only controls is nice though because I can just lean back in my chair with a show on the side and only needing to use my mouse for everything. If that's what you're looking for then perhaps you'll like it, otherwise who knows if you'll like it at all. I want to like it more but with the way it's designed I honestly don't even know what I would want to change that wouldn't alter the game drastically so or without making it absurdly too easy. It just feels like it's missing something and needs a bit more polish. Although apparently you can go out of the shop now and I havent unlocked it so maybe I'll have to update my review again. Right now though? Playing through the beta and finally getting into the release version has left me feeling a bit disappointed. Not much has changed since the beta other than it feels like it was made so much more slower.

I have to hope that the issues are just symptoms of Early Access, and maybe the full release will be better, but as it is, I just don't find it fun. In its current form, it may be, dare I say, TOO cozy? Which is to say, there are mechanics that some games use to create pressure and difficulty, but in this game, the consequences are removed while the mechanics remain. Why does performing certain actions (but not others!) consume a unit of time, if the passage of time doesn't impact anything? Either remove the clock, or add something of interest to the schedule (and it doesn't have to be difficulty! maybe there are pronounced atmospheric changes, maybe certain customers arrive at certain times, maybe some gadgets change if you look away at night, or it's easier to wash things in the morning, etc).

The other big thing that I can probably attribute to Early Access is that the controls are slightly jank, and there's no controller or remapping support. I'm begging you, do not assign important controls to the scroll wheel.

I know there are some people who are gonna be wild about this game regardless. The aesthetic is cute, and it's a nice concept. It could be helpful if you're someone who needs a hand debuff while listening to podcasts or something. But right now, it's not actually fun to play.
