review:
Even in its Early Access phase, this game fails to deliver any value commensurate with its price. From the very beginning to the end, the game balance is severely flawed, making it virtually impossible to enjoy any aspect of gameplay.

* A message for the developers and my own reflections are included at the end of this review.

[h2]Expectations vs. Reality in a Movie Theater Management Simulator[/h2]
Movie Selection
Although the game is marketed as a movie theater management simulator, the option to choose which movie to screen is merely superficial. The films available are actually AI-generated content created by others, and the original credits remain intact. This lack of originality and disregard for creative ownership is a major drawback.

[h2]Hiring Staff and Delegating Tasks[/h2]
The concept of hiring staff to manage screenings and operations sounds promising at first. However, once you delegate these tasks, you as the player are left with nothing substantial to do other than watching a simulation. The interactive and engaging aspects are completely lost, reducing the experience to a monotonous series of automated tasks.

[h2]Lackluster Expansion and Repetitive 3D Graphics[/h2]

While there is a feature to expand your theater, the core gameplay itself barely changes. You’re just repeating the same dull tasks: assigning seats, selling snacks, cleaning, and dealing with troublesome customers. On top of that, scheduling essentially boils down to deciding how to fill a 14-hour daily slot. In the early stages, you’re stuck with three- or four-hour films that aren’t very popular, but before long, you can easily license far more popular one-hour films, so there’s virtually no strategic depth in planning your schedule.

I only watch around 70 movies a year myself, but I still think there were better ways to simplify this concept into a game. For example, rather than limiting movies to a single genre, they could’ve introduced multiple genres and given users different preferences. If all I want to do is run a money-making simulation, I might as well play a clicker game instead of something branded as a simulation game. There’s also an option to place arcade machines, but they just sit there unused.

The short animation of loading popcorn is the only thing that feels even slightly cute, and overall, the experience boils down to tedious routine work.

[h2]Additional Grievances[/h2]
[h3]Bizarre Beverage Skill Check[/h3]
The game includes a skill check related to beverages that seems tacked on without any meaningful integration, leaving one to question whether the developer even played the game themselves.

[h3]Tedious Cleaning Mechanics[/h3]
Cleaning is unnecessarily cumbersome as the dirt on the floors does not disappear with a long press; you have to click repeatedly, which only adds to the frustration.

[h3]Rigid Object Placement and Poor Quality[/h3]
Objects can only be placed in predetermined positions, stripping away any sense of creative freedom. The overall quality is so low that it feels as if a novice student, armed with generative AI and readily available online content, hastily assembled this crude simulation software.

[h3]Mostly Positive?[/h3]
Don’t be misled by the current user reviews. As of February 28, 2025, 83% of the 154 posted reviews are marked as positive, but the unlock rates for achievements that should be easily attainable in this game are only a few percent. For example, only 3.5% of players have earned the basic “Hire One Employee” achievement, and an ostensibly easy goal like “Achieve 100% Customer Satisfaction” also has a similarly low unlock rate.

Furthermore, the customer satisfaction score fluctuates wildly during film screenings. It appears that instead of calculating an average among everyone in the theater, the game uses the satisfaction of only those who have just finished watching a movie—likely a bug.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]
In all honesty, it appears that the developers lack sufficient experience in actually playing and refining a game—or they are simply understaffed, leading to inadequate quality assurance. Having played a fair number of indie games, I can confidently say that this is not a game at all, but rather a shoddy simulation software produced by a small-scale company. For a price tag of around $10, there is no justifiable value here, especially when compared to the wealth of far more engaging titles available. Save your money and look elsewhere.

[b]Note: This review was summarized and translated from my rough notes using generative AI.[/b]

Unfortunately, it seems generative AI still isn’t quite ready for game QA testing. While Claude 3.7 Sonnet appears to be getting better at playing Pokémon, thorough QA testing apparently still requires human effort. I'm sure the developers eagerly await the day AI can fully handle QA tasks—and frankly, so do I.

Making a game is incredibly difficult. I’ve dabbled in it myself, and I’ve spoken with friends who work full-time in game development. I also write code for data analysis, but the volume of code and techniques used in game development are on a whole different level. Even with that in mind, this is just terrible.

I understand how hard you must have worked to try to make it good. And no matter how much you push your limits, hearing comments like mine must feel demoralizing.
However, I believe the developer must not forget their own inner “user” perspective. Don’t betray yourself.

Have you had many people playtest it? I’m not sure how many hours they’ve spent playing, but please have as many people as possible try your prototype and sincerely take their feedback into account.
A movie theater simulator is a great concept, and I was excited at first. I was also thrilled that you could choose from so many movies. But the footage includes credits that can easily be traced back to the original creators if you dig a little. Since it’s generated by AI, the question of whether it’s subject to copyright varies by country and era. Maybe keeping the credits is more ethical. Still, as a creator, why not at least use AI-generated content you’ve created yourself?

I do understand the game’s system. However, even if the idea is good, it will lack potential to grow—both as code and as a game—if it’s based on random spur-of-the-moment ideas or sloppy design.

I noticed that the developer of this game responded only to negative reviews, sometimes asking, “What is the reason for your negative rating?” That’s why I wrote this detailed explanation here. My intention isn’t to be hostile, but rather to encourage the developer to take user criticism seriously—not to brush it off with superficial questions—and to engage with users humbly.

I truly hope this game becomes something genuinely worthwhile.

review:
I understand that this game is still in early access, so I'm willing to be gracious about some of the things I've experienced.

This is a very middle-of-the-road game as far as simulators go. Obviously, with full automation unlocked, there isn't much to do but turn your brain off and occasionally buy products to restock your concessions. Honestly, this isn't a huge issue for me; though, I understand some peoples' frustrations with a lack of further game play.

My biggest gripe with this game is the sheer amount of AI generated content. Again, I understand that it's in early access, and I do hope that the AI content will eventually be replaced; however, if the devs intend to leave or expand the AI content beyond what it already is, it reeks of laziness and an easy cash grab. There are a small handful of movie titles where it's obvious that the devs crafted original scenes using the assets they had, which stand out as better content than the AI generated loops. I know it isn't cheap or easy to create original content, but it would at least justify the price paid for the game, overall, if there was more thought and effort put into it beyond the AI.

For me, the game is a solid 5 out of 10. I don't love it. I don't hate it. I'm interested to see what more may come, but I'm not holding my breath for a miracle.

review:
I had great expectations for this game, yet I find myself completely dissatisfied. I understand that it is currently in alpha, but it is quite disappointing. I played for just over an hour, completed all the initial quests, and experimented with the building features.

   I would create a list of pros and cons for the game; however, unfortunately, it only presents cons for me. The inventory system is poorly designed; assigning items to quick slots is cumbersome, and there is no scrolling option available. The map is also inadequately constructed, lacking a scrolling feature despite the indication of a zoom function in the bottom right corner. The quests were manageable until I reached a task that required hunting raccoons. Given the graphics and the absence of any indicators, I anticipated that this quest would be nearly impossible and chose not to invest any further time in it.

   The crafting, building, and gathering elements are arguably among the worst I have encountered. Locating suitable placements is challenging, there are no snap points for construction, the hitboxes for gathering are poorly designed, and extremely limited building options.

   The combat system is significantly underdeveloped; some zombies require a headshot and body shot to defeat, while others can be taken down only by expending an entire magazine, even without a head. The portrayal of the zombie movements was also disappointing. The hitboxes for both firearms and melee weapons are also poorly implemented, and I refrained from trying the bow, suspecting it would perform even worse.

   The graphics are notably underwhelming for a game utilizing the Unreal Engine 5 in the current era.

it looks good in screenshots and mostly runs well on an RX 9070, but it just has some of the most baffling design decisions i've ever seen in a video game

-chop trees, return to quest giver, make campfire, return to quest giver, go back to campfire and cook meat, return to quest giver, make shelter, return to quest giver, and on and on and on. i have a GPS map device but not a walkie talkie?
-Q and E only rotates your gun in your hands without leaning or rotating the camera. why would this even be an option? i genuinely don't know who this is for
-shooting zombies in the face blows off their head but they still grunt and attack you for way longer than you'd expect or is reasonable
-animals running through the forest make no sound whatsoever
-can navigate only certain menus by clicking the buttons at the top, others need to be navigated with Q and E
-no field of view slider, no option to turn off head bobbing while running 
-unable to click and hold to swing axe/pickaxe
-quest tells you to drink "fresh water" from the lake but then tells you that the water is contaminated after you drink it
-random NPC survivors' character model faces look like they're from a cartoon and completely clash with the otherwise realistic visual style
-handgun UI element aspect ratio is off, making the gun look squished
-the "voice acting" is all over the place, which makes sense when you read the disclaimer that it's AI generated. one guy sounds like he's from louisiana, one guy sounds like he heard a russian talk exactly one time 20 years ago and is trying to do an impression of the accent

i know it's early access, of course there will be bugs, and it's not supposed to be representative of the final product. however, the devs said they expect it'll only be in early access for 3-6 months, which is an unrealistic amount of time to address all the things they'd need to make this game playable. i don't see any way in which this game has a full release within 6 months

review:
This game is more of an alpha than an early release. The movement is clunky. Animations for swinging weapons needs to be smoother and register the hits better. I think the melee needs some more range so there is any chance to kill zombies. Leaning with guns needs to include leaning with your body... not just hands. I think it would be good if people in game can see aiming and leaning animations of others. The map on the GPS looks horrendous and should be either simplified to show a basic terrain and topography lines and POIs instead of the green mush it currently is. The item icons also should have some rework because it looks like not much design was put into them and they were AI generated. More NPCs with more quests and more interactions would be cool and give the game some sort of story mode. The building system is fine but I would enjoy a more interactive and customizable system like RUST or sons or Ark. The crafting system is fine but it doesn't show whether or not you have the materials needed to craft anything.

I would love to say the game has potential but I could just go play STALKER and would have a much better time. There is just no obvious direction this is going. This seems more of a game concept that never should have had an early access at least for another year or 2 of development.

review: I was a fan of this game and had been waiting for its release for a long time. But I was extremely disappointed. I want to tell you the positive and negative aspects of this game after playing it for 7 hours. Positives: 1: Very attractive graphics and realistic lighting 2: Generally good sound. 3: It has a variety of items and a lot of variety in building. Overall, this 20% of the game is positive. Negatives: 1: The game environment is very full of plants, which will give you very little visibility, and the density of plants and the height of flowers and plants is very high, which makes you feel crowded and tired, and the visibility is low. 2: The time from morning to night passes very quickly. 3: The use of weapons is very buggy and shooting does not hit the target. Especially at the commando bots. Shooting at zombies is a little better. 4: There is no map and you can only navigate with GPS, and this is very confusing. 5: The items in the inventory and craft sections are black and white, and finding the desired item is very confusing and difficult. 6: The environment of the buildings is more like historical times than a survival game. It could be better. Okay. 7: Looting is only in containers and there is no chest of drawers or anything like that. 8: A very important thing that made me stop playing was that there are a series of commando bots that attack you. They shoot as if their weapons are locked on your body and they follow you for kilometers to destroy you, so that with all this grass you are not able to see and engage with them. 9: You have to go everywhere on foot and there is no mention of motorbikes or car or even horses. The walking speed is very low and you can only run for 5-6 seconds and after these 6 seconds your operator stops breathing and it is not realistic at all. Even a smoking person runs faster and more. 10: It would be good if plants could be used for construction, for example, making bandages. 11: Battery items cannot be found. I don't know if this is normal or not. A simple conclusion is that I don't want to say that this game is not worth buying, but serious changes should be made to this game very soon so that the player doesn't get bored and is attracted to this game. 12: You You will not be able to change and customize your player, and it is not even possible to change clothes. 13: One of the attractions of survival games is surviving in the night, but in this game, if you sleep, it will be morning. This sentence for the game developers: Please design with a more open and broader vision.

review:
Overall this game feels way more like a UE5 tech demo than an early access game. Everything that isn't baked in from UE5 is kind of awful.

The game looks VERY decent at first glance because of all the UE5 shenanigans like nanites, vegetation, and godrays but the moment you interact with anything the developers actually made, it falls apart super hard. Strong UE5 Asset Flop vibes.

[h2]Zombies & Combat[/h2]
These aren't zombies, they're just [b]kind of walking health bars[/b]. Super wonky hit differentiation:
[list]
    [*]Headshot? Same damage as shooting the torso
    [*]Blow their head clean off? They keep chasing you
    [*]Bleeding system? Only a visual effect, they bleed infinitely with no effect
[/list]

[h2]UI/UX & Menus[/h2]
The interface feels like [strike]early access[/strike] pre-alpha placeholder. Think like Garry's mod but magnified to shits for people legally blind. Everything is clunky, poorly organized, and missing basic QoL features. Even simple inventory management is honestly a big chore. No way to search through to avoid the tabs either.

[h2]Core Systems[/h2]
[list]
    [*]Movement: Very "Wobbly", I guess it's passable?
    [*]Mining: Really annoying trying to figure out which rocks are real vs decorative asset flips
    [*]Crafting is very meh, some recipes make 0 sense like 2 leather = bandages. [i]Sure, why not? I guess [/i]
    [*]Woodcutting is a bit dank, cutting the tree, hearing it fall down but it's in one piece after wood magically spawns in your inventory
    [*] Everything else is in a meh state
[/list]

[h2]The "Tutorial"[/h2]
It [b]REALLY REALLY[/b] feels designed to waste your time and push you past the refund window.

Every. Single. Step:
[olist]
    [*]Mine rock → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Cut wood → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Make campfire → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Place wood → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Place food → run back to base and tell NPC
    [*]Light fire → run back to base and tell NPC
[/olist]

God forbid you combine some steps together.

[h2]Technical & Game State[/h2]
[list]
    [*]No dedicated servers
    [*]287 players on launch day (honestly feels a bit DOA)
    [*]Visual issues on ULTRA despite UE5 is kind of crazy lol - shimmering on weapons, blur despite motion blur off, all puddles are mirrors, unless staring 90° at it
    [*]Audio: No directionality - zombies always sound like they're breathing down your neck
    [*][b]AI:[/b] Wildlife attacks trees in circles, NPCs shoot the ground while bears maul them, big oof.
    [*] Meh performance, but that comes with UE5 as a whole and Early access game so I won't really ding them too much on that
    [*] Dev and Community Managers are going on the Steam Discussions
[/list]


And honestly all of these things would [b]BE OKAY[/b] if it weren't for the fact that they're asking this much money for this thing. $38.99 CAD for this is [b]OUTRAGEOUS[/b]

Maybe $9.99$ or $14.99 sure. $38.99? Lmao. 

I'm not sure what I expected from a trailer filled with AI-generated slop.

May come back if the value proposition gets better.

review:
I enjoy this game! I want to recommend it! I really do! It's SO close!!!

There are plenty of reviews that rightfully point out the game's glitches. The developers seem to be on top of things and I don't doubt a future update will flip this thumb around. Seriously, if there was a maybe thumb, I'd do that. Alas, Steam be Steam.

The game, at its core, has three issues that hold it back more than even the glitches.
 
The first might be a minor or major issue depending on who you are. While the beginning hints at some kind of story or narrative to encourage you to continue growing your business, this kind of just vanishes after the tutorial. While this isn't a deal breaker, it does make any failures of the game's other systems stand out all the more blatantly.

The second is the gameplay loop. The overall flow is: Go to site, collect as many materials/valuables as you can, break everything else, clean up, go home, sell what you brought back. The primary issue with the loop is that the "sell what you brought back" portion lags far slower that you are going to be getting materials and valuables. You sell the items in the form of requests that are fully random both in how close to full value the item is, how many items they want, and what kind they want. That means that you will VERY quickly accumulate a ton of inventory and seriously struggle to get rid of anything.

To clarify why this becomes a problem, let's say you treat a home like a Buffalo and carefully break down everything you can and bring back everything you can as I started doing early on.  If you get unlucky, you might never seem to get a request for lumber and even if you do it will only be for one particular kind meaning you will accumulate a ton of one specific size that you can never seem to get rid of. All of the items you can bring back and sell have this problem and you could go several in game days of nothing only to have one order asking for a ton of stuff but they just HAPPEN to be asking for the ONE thing you don't have and there's no assurance that the next few contracts you do will have what they are asking for. So you just end up accumulating more junk hoping desperately you are hording the right stuff.

The third is probably the biggest disappointment: Lack of hazards. Hardspace: Shipbreaker is probably the abject best example of how to handle games focused on deconstruction and has a feature that easily puts it ahead of the rest are hazards. As you are working, you actively have to consider what you are tearing apart and how. Without hazards, games centered on deconstruction inevitably just boil down to a very monotonous cycle where you smash stuff until it falls over. There's no fear of being under the roof as it collapses, no pipes you need to close off, and, heck, you can literally smash the power bank that provides the building electricity hard enough to make it explode into sparks and nothing happens.

The third point is honestly the biggest elephant in the room for me. Ironically, Ship Graveyard Simulator 1 had this exact same problem and even the sequel doesn't really utilize hazards enough to be a huge challenge. As it stands, the most efficient method of playing this game is to recover any item people want, smash the two edge planks holding walls up until all of the walls come down, pack up the mess, and leave. Without any risk to smashing buildings apart like a maniac, the game just turns into one of those rage rooms where you smash stuff to let off steam.

Great fun in the flesh. Digitally, it gets dull very quickly when you realize everything you smash just feels the same.

review:
[i]TLDR will be at the bottom for those who want to skip the reading[/i]

[h1] Deconstruction Sim Review [/h1]

[i]This Game has some [b][u]AMAZING[/u][/b] Potential. However that means there's currently [u]LOTS[/u] of improvements needed. I want to preface with saying that I REALLY like this game, and WANT to make it the most enjoyable experience I can. so let's start off with the core premise of the game.[/i] 

[h3]Deconstruction.[/h3]

The ENTIRE game is about demolition, yet a majority of the time you are dismantling objects because customers want to save stuff or because there's a premium item you want to save to sell later, the only downside is. You can't. You see, you can only sell items with random contracts, these contracts decide which of the items you can sell to them, only problem is, most of the time it's something you don't have. in my playthrough so far, I have almost 200 pieces of beams/wood that I salvaged from houses, but not 1 of them has sold yet, because there are no contracts for them. If there where  ways to sell items individually, for the price that the scanner claims then it would improve the gameplay but a LOT. In my opinion, I feel like the scanner should have more uses [b]LIKE[/b] selling the items you click on [b][u]ONLY[/u][/b] in the warehouse.

[h3]Optimization[/h3]

The game runs fairly solid on my PC, but I'm an outlier as I have a fairly beefy setup, so why am I talking about this? because the game TANKS due to the amount of entities while dismantling houses. I have a 3090ti and top of the line CPU and I will tank down to less than 30fps when the wrecking ball hits the houses due to all the debris flying. if the amount of entities could be lowered or some more time spent on optimizing the game, I believe it could honestly make for a fun and engaging time. However, in its current state, the FPS drops make it difficult to want to keep destroying houses.

[h3]Economy[/h3]

Okay, this is my biggest gripe so far. I haven't delved TOO deep into the game yet, but the prices of items compared to what each contract pays is ridiculous. It takes three to four contracts + rubble from those same contracts, to gain MAYBE 3-4K. This is a problem, due to the cost of tools, which you have to buy [i]INDIVIDUALLY[/i] may I add. increasing each upgrade until you max out the tools. That of which ranges from 1.5-2k [b]PER TOOL[/b]. Not to mention upgrading you vehicle which you then need to spend 1K to unlock the Garage, then 3-4K for the next Van, on top of buying new permits to unlock better contracts. Also, why is the wrecking ball $600 to rent when a contract only gains me $200??. The only thing I found that works is to not even bother with the warehouse mechanic and just destroy [b]EVERYTHING[/b] and sell the ruble. it's saves time and gains me Guaranteed income compared to selling items. This, by the way, includes stuff like, walls, bricks, wood, windows, doors, etc. just destroy them all and you'll make more money than individually selling them.

[h3]Warehouse[/h3]

As stated before, I fail to see a reason to engage with the warehouse at all. sure, you can take the time to dismantle items,w store them in your van/truck, and store them in the warehouse, but at the end of the day, you rarely sell items you have. my warehouse is FULL will walls, bricks, wood, windows and various premium items and I can't get contracts to sell them to save me. it makes the entire premise of the warehouse pointless, you're better off just adding a dump truck to the game and a landfill to sell rubble as that's more profitable than taking the time to take a cabinet apart, piece by piece and storing it to sell whenever the games lets you. In my opinion, I feel like this mechanic needs to be looked at and reworked to make us WANT to fill it up and sell things, but at this point in time, it just feels pointless.

[h3]Vehicles[/h3]

Im just gonna say it. why do I have to buy a garage in order to buy better vehicles? why can't I just sell the starter van and replace it with new vehicles? it's stupid and a waste of money to HAVE to buy a garage to THEN buy a new truck. it's unnecessary.

[h3]Closing words[/h3]\

There is still plenty I want to say about this game, and I may even be wrong about much of it, like the economy and warehouse functionality, but I just can't seem to enjoy these premises. The amount you make is minute compared to what you spend to upgrade. The warehouse feels pointless and just another cash dump to upgrade. And the game's performance, while good, tanks when too many things break or are destroyed at a time. I believe this game can become amazing, and I enjoyed my time playing it, but it needs to improve and touch on some of these issues because it causes it to feel stale and hollow. you can only destroy the same house, store the same items, and play Tetris in your van so much before you get bored and leave.


[h3]TLDR[/h3] 

This game can become a great demolition game, the physics and contract system are fun but carry a lot of issues like performance hits, and entity overloading causing game crashes, the warehouse feels empty and pointless leading to no reason to fill it up. Contracts rarely asks for items you DO have, and selling the rubble from houses makes more income than selling items individually. This game has plenty of issues but if worked on and optimized, even reworking some systems, can become a great  game to play. At it's current state [u]DO NOT[/u] recommend the game.

I actually enjoy this game and plan to keep playing, but in its current state I can’t recommend it. It feels like one of those 50/50 games where some people might like it, but right now it’s closer to 90/10 against.

The biggest issues:

Warehouse feels pointless – customers almost never buy what you have in stock. I’ve gone 3–4 in-game days without selling anything, even with the knick-knacks box.

Disappearing items – things vanish overnight or when you return to the warehouse. Example: I stack sheets, run out of truck space, head back to drop stuff off, and by the time I return the sheets are gone.

Floating objects – tearing down a two-story house from the first floor leaves the second-floor doorway hanging in mid-air.

UI glitches – if you bounce between the warehouse and jobsite, the house destruction percentage can turn from green to blank, even though it still shows 100%.

If the devs fix the warehouse system, disappearing items, floating pieces, and UI bugs, I think this could turn into a really solid game. But right now, it’s rough.

I endured this game as much as I can and now I think I can say this game sucks. I got the last permit, upgraded tools and warehouse and bought the big truck, but I did most of it just for the sake of it and see until the end if the game gets any interesting with new permits and more item space.

1- It's a high when you first get into business, then it's downward spiral. There is no joy in this game, you can get more satisfaction and joy if you actually deconstructed a building yourself. Really, really boring.

2- There is no music, no story, no end goal, nothing. Intro starts like you are on a revenge mission, you have a story, a target. But nope. After the tutorial you are on your own and only thing you see is the mission descriptions. No secrets, no easter eggs, no fun. You just go through the same dozen of houses over and over and over and over...

3- There are some concepts they tried, like customer types, but it's shallow as a pool of piss. You can't set a quality for your products, you have to collect EVERYTHING or you miss the most profitable contracts because that wealthy customer wants a premium TV, a premium couch, coupled with some stupid common walls or bricks. You can't just focus on most valuable items, unlike what game tells you at the beginning.

4- That cool wrecking ball in trailer? It's not free, you can't buy it, you have to pay a hefty amount at the beginning of the mission to use it and it's not cheap at all.

5- Game has a lot of jank. Not only a couple of assets, whole second floor doesn't even collapse if you start hitting the bottom floor first. You will get used to see floating pieces everywhere.

6- IF they implemented a "set item" system to contracts, that would improve the experience. Like, you see 8-pieces-premium kitchen set, well, tough luck, you sell each piece randomly. But if you could get a bonus for set items like chairs and tables, bed and wardrobe, TV and coach whatever, that would be great. But of course, it's way beyond the bubble of thought of these devs obviously.

7- I mean, that's pretty much it for this game. There is nothing even exciting to complain about. It's THAT boring, shallow, poorly implemented and isn't rewarding. Stare at a wall instead.

This one’s right on the edge of a “yes” recommendation, but since it’s a binary choice, I’ve gotta go with “no.”

The game nails the demolition part — it’s simple but fun. Knocking out the right beams and walls just to watch the ceiling come crashing down is super satisfying, and the physics are great to mess around with.

My issue is with the so-called “career” mode. It’s not really about running a demolition business. You make a little money from demo jobs, sure, but most of your time is spent scavenging and selling furniture or random junk from the houses. It ends up feeling more like running a secondhand shop than tearing stuff down.

review:
There's some 200.000 games on Steam right now. You could be exploring faraway galaxies, leading vast armies, saving a beautiful dragon from a horrible princess, you could be building magnificent cities, or perhaps entire civilizations that will stand the test of time. You could be securing the future of your royal dynasty by getting to know your sister better. You could be a master assassin, or an ancient vampire, heck you could run around and cause mischief as a goat. Either of those would be more fun than what the devs, appropriately named Incubator, are expecting you to spend your limited time on this planet on. 

This game lures you in with a promise of explosive action - something that could help lower your cortisol levels after a stressful day job. Instead, it offers an exciting opportunity to do a second job in your free time. Indeed, the Destruction tag in this mostly refers to your sanity. You get half a dozen tools in this game - screwdrivers, saws, you name it. And all of them but one you can upgrade many times. The one you can't is the sledgehammer. You nominally have it, yes, but the game goes out of its way to discourage your using it. That's because it wants you to spent 10 minutes carefully dismantling a wardrobe - one screw at a time - because you can then sell it for more than the entire contract's worth... And the wrecking ball? Well, it costs $600 to rent one, when the contract to wreck the house pays... that's right, $600. Mic drop.

review:
If you're thinking about getting this game, download the demo and play it through a few times until you're bored because there really isn't much more content that's worth it outside of the demo itself. 

This game was initially a lot of fun, it felt like there were clear objectives and lots to look forward to, but it feels like I've reached mid-game about 10 hours in, and there's no real urge to see it to completion. It's repetitive. 

The idea of the game is neat, but what it really lacks is any sort of tangible progression or end state. Later game contracts are made arbitrarily harder by implementing a "day-tax" penalty and making the contract 200km away. Being able to only sell collected items as part of bundles means you spend hours painstakingly collecting items that likely never get sold and just take up space in your warehouse. Overall, the upgrades just feel like something to waste money on to flesh out the maybe 5-10 hours of gameplay this game has than something that makes any tangible difference. 

90% of your in game time will be spent fighting the punishing mechanics of trying to fit items into your van. You can see the silhouette, you can see that it fits, but the hit markers won't let you place anything. This is especially frustrating when the later-game contracts take 2 hours each way to get to and you have to make numerous trips. 

Overall, fun at first, but if I had to do it all over again I'd wait for this game to go on sale for $5, play it on a rainy Sunday, then forget about it.

review:
Currently feels still like too much of a tech demo and not enough like a game.

From limited experience and a lot of youtube, my issues are:
1) Control scheme needs to be looked at again. Why not left click for nearly everything (incl pick up objects when you have your hands out)? Why not have a different button for doors so that you can open stuff whilst holding it? Esc in computer should escape, not menu. 
2) Buggy noises and textures.
3) Cannot move dismantleable furniture but this stuff can still be destroyed when you destroy a nearby wall (tutorial bed exploded from nearby wall). No way to prevent that except dismantle bed and remake, PITA.
4) Exploding rubble. Rubble from demolished walls is extremely volatile and breaks stuff very easily (brick wall in tutorial exploded and destroyed the light fixture).
5) Unclear how best to remove all wood slats from the wooden walls. Half the time it ends up collapsing and breaking.
6) In general, game play is still quite shallow. Deconstructing a house should include utilities (wiring, plumbing, gas, etc). You should be penalised for how much 'trash' you create, thereby incentivising proper deconstruction. Different material types would also be good and better sales of items to third parties. Random orders right now feels to RNG. Would like to see incentives for roof dismantling - metal roofs? Would be good to also have to jackhammer concrete base etc to completely remove the building.
6) Pallets for reclaimed items should be on shelves or something. No one would store stuff like that. Also, should probably have the option to scrap stuff for raw materials cost. Maybe different sized pallets for different stuff.
7) Object placement in trucks is jank. Free 3d rotation would be nice and better valid placement checks. Adding multiple plasterboard to the tiny truck is not viable even if you don't take anything else! Chair stacking FTW!
8) Stuff inside houses is too RNG. Trailer should not contain premium etc. More 'types' of furniture would be good (common, uncommon, etc etc), also premium should be high value, is currently meh?
9) Starting warehouse is actually quite big? If stuff is tuned, could start off with a crappy storage box or something and grow.
10) Order a skip (trash truck) to the site?

Has potential though depending on what the developers do. Will revisit in a few months.

I love these kinds of games, but many of the reviews are correct.  Play the demo 3-4 times and its the same thing.  The only difference is later contracts are worth more to make up for the upgrades costing significantly more. It feels like time gating to make the game feel longer than it really is.   You have the whole game at about 2 hours of play, but to get all the upgrades i would assume you have to play those 2 hours around 25 times to complete it. 

The speed increase you get from several thousands of dollars of screwdrivers/chisels/etc isn't really worth it because the mechanic of selling the things you salvage is so frustrating because customers only want them in bundles with things you probably didn't save and theres no way to check contracts customers want when youre on the job site so you have to memorize or, more likely, ignore the mechanic. 

I made it to tier 3 contracts before giving up.  The upgrades are so expensive and the contracts only increase a bit.  I wanted to save up for a bigger van which is only $5000 but it felt like such a grind for a small payoff i gave up.  I am sitting on like $5000 of salvaged items i cant sell because i am missing 1 of the things the customer wants.  

It would be nice to see employees who could autoship what you already have so you dont need to look up and down your shelves to find the right item with the right rarity and move it to a van. It would also be nice to get a more powerful sledge hammer or different tools to bring to the site to help destroy small houses.   Would also like to see the base tools start at the level 3 tools speed for disassembly. Its an interesting mechanic, but it is such a carpal tunnel trap as it stands.  

I hope that there will be more updates to bring more content to make it more worth the purchase

Review of Deconstruction Simulator

The game is genuinely fun and has a lot of potential, but in its current state I can’t honestly recommend it.

Issues I’ve encountered:

Contract payouts: All contracts have started giving extremely low payouts, even though I have a 5-star rating. This makes progression feel unrewarding. 

Lack of incentive for full deconstruction: There really should be a bulk goods buyer who lets you sell collected materials, even at a reduced price. As it stands, there’s no reason to carefully deconstruct and transport materials home, it’s simply faster and more efficient (and more rewarding) to demolish everything outright.

Limited content: I’d love to see more buildings available for deconstruction.

Controller support: Better controller integration would be great. Let me use my PS5 controller so I can comfortably play on my TV.

I know the game is still in active development, and it’s clear the developers are putting effort into improving it. I’m hopeful that future updates will address these issues, and if they do, I’ll be happy to update this review.

review:
The game is buggy as hell. This isn't a "released" game, it is barely a beta version.
Some of the bugs: (not comprehensive!)
- Items disappear randomly or change shape or design after changing locations.
- The warehouse doesn't calculate available stock correctly (sometimes it shows items as available, sometimes not).
- Interfaces often glitch and can only be reset by reloading or changing locations.
- Hinges and screws for disassembly often float in the air near the object you are trying to disassemble.
- Indestructible items like chimneys float in the air after a house was demolished.
- Some items respawn when revisiting a site.

Annoyances:
- Interface for selling items (called contracts) is overly click-heavy and the contracts are so randomised, that 90+% of them could never be fulfilled (like 10 sofas, that would never fit into a single transporter) and therefore clutter your screen, making it just a bother to interact with it at all, even though the VAST majority of money is gained with it.
- Contracts rarely ask for wood, bricks or drywalls, which is the stuff you typically have the most of.
- Upgrading tools is expensive and barely increases speed.
- The devs would rather add new fancy features that were barely asked for than address or even fix the issues that were in the game since the beginning.

review:
This game isn't terrible, but it's also not very good. It's extremely repetitive, and the mechanics seem half-baked at best.

Repetitive: Some reviews mention how this is to be expected with this type of game, but I played Hardspace Shipbreakers, and it was an example of how this can be done extremely well. I continued to play after getting all the achievements, but I immediately uninstalled this after completing it.

Warehouse: You can't choose where things like loading/unloading zones are, which means you have to design your warehouse around being able to move the entire shelf closer to you to fill an order and then move it back.

Orders: Honestly the most infuriating thing about this game! Truly unhinged requests for things like 15 small windows... there is one small window every 2-3 houses, meaning it would take 50-60 jobs to complete that one request. You also end up having to maintain stocks of things you don't want, like a 20 dollar lamp, because the orders need a 20 dollar lamp to go with their 29 walls and premium television.

Upgrades: None of the upgrades to your character really matter; things get slightly faster, but it does nothing to alleviate the exhaustion you feel after taking apart your 90th dresser. The exosuit is probably the best one, but I can't use the sprint because you can't remap the key.

Vehicles: The difference between the first three vehicles is almost nonexistent, and the final two are better but still aren't wide enough to really allow you to stack things properly, and for some reason you can pay to upgrade your warehouse to hold more vehicles, which seems pointless.

Destruction: There is no wrong way to do this; almost every contract has you destroy the entire house, and there are no repercussions for collapsing it on yourself or leaving the electrical and water hooked up. There was an opportunity here to play with hazards, but it's completely ignored. The destruction does feel fun, but you'll dread it because of my next point:

Recycling: This is the longest part of every job, and there is NO way to upgrade your bag size or carry capacity or to buy a garbage truck or improve this element whatsoever. Some houses are like 30+ bags, and you need to deal with each one of them individually on both the gathering side and the unloading side.

The wrecking ball: It's way too expensive. A really good contract pays maybe 1300 dollars, and the wrecking ball is half that! (600) It also isn't hard to take down a house without it; it's the difference between doing it by hand for about 3 minutes or doing it with the wrecking ball for about 1 minute and then still having to clean up the area by hand.

Overall this game was a good concept, but it was poorly executed. I wish I had kept better track of my 3 hours so I could have returned it.

review:
Could have been a fun and cozy game if they wouldn't limit you so much. Let me explain.

You can gather furniture and take it back to your warehouse. You can also do this with things like wall pieces, windows, doors and even the bricks and wood the house is build with. And in the beginning I started gathering as much as I could. But here's the limiting thing: You can't really do anything with it.

Yes, there are orders you can complete but the bigger ones don't really make sense. There are three different rarities and a lot of different items you can collect, so you always miss a few of the items to fill a bigger order, so you end up doing the smaller ones. And yes, there is a trader that takes items from you but you can only sell 1 or 2 to him a day since as soon as you put more into the truck the discount he expects rises to 80% and you get less money for more goods, which is just absurd.

The contracts you get usually involve destroying the entire house so destroying everything, including the furniture, is a better way to make some money since you can collect the garbage into bags that you then can take back to recycle, getting you money at the end of the day. And you can't even upgrade the trash bags or how many you can carry so you end up just running back and forth a lot.

And thus the game is just way too repetitive: Destroy everything, gather trash, get trash to warehouse to recycle, repeat.

I like the game but I would not recommend it in its current state for $20, it lacks a lot of polish as far as SFX, and the system of directing 5 MOBA players what to do using a random hand of cards is clunky at best. You don't have a lot of control over modifying the decks your players use between fights. Another small gripe is that some keywords are not explained and you cannot hover over them to see what they do. 

Example A: You see one of your heroes is getting collapsed on and want them to recall or retreat but if you didnt happen to draw a card that turn that gives that command, there is nothing you can do to prevent it from happening.

Example B: My top laner started with a "roam together" action card that is useless on a solo laner and every time its drawn its a dead card in hand. 

Another problem is not being able to give macro instructions to your team. Your top mid and jungle could be pressuring the enemy nexus towers or nexus and your jungler is farming camps, theres no way to get him to group or assist in pressuring one of the lanes. 

The game has a pretty lazy way of handling the issue of all your heroes being at random places all the time, by having teamfight cards or teamfight events that everyone participates in automatically. 

The shell and general concept of the game is addictive and the core gameplay of watching your heroes automatically do stuff on the map is very fun and satisfying, for a game like this the devil is in the details and a bunch of small problems add up to an experience that isnt worthwile and doesnt feel like a finished product worth $20 sticker price.

I can only really recommend the game on a sale, at $20 I think it's still too unpolished to justify that price.

The main aspects are unclear mechanics and missing information. Despite getting to the points threshold to start actions at the same time, one team will always go first, with no clear determinant. Stats such as health, AP, how they scale, and even what order the heroes attack in a fight are all missing and this can be frustrating. This sort of information should be given in-game so that drafting isn't a coinflip as to whether you've screwed yourself because all your heroes go last in a fight. Some more granular information (and control) over what your 'athletes' do would go a long way to making you feel like an actual manager. While there are some nice updates planned to make the transfer system better (a sore point right now, your youth academy and scouting are essentially pointless), I do hope this gets looked at.

My main point of frustration with this game, however, is having moved onto the higher difficulties, the game starts to utilise scripting, when the probabilities start going wack mysteriously more often ([i] especially [/i] when one of the only stats the game purports to show you is probabilities in the first place!), rather than the having the AI make smarter decisions. It truly is wild just how often suddenly you'll find that your side will stop hitting the low health target with a 40% presence, or the enemy repeatedly beats the odds and keeps attacking your carry with a 8% presence. Overall, this has made what was an interesting concept into a frustrating experience, and unfortunately just going back in difficulty isn't really worthwhile when I've been smashing the AI throughout. Then again, I've been smashing it in the harder difficulty too, just having a more frustrating rather than enjoyable time while doing so. Guess it's not that different from actual MOBAs. Genuinely, just stop lying about the presence percentage and this would all go away, it's ridiculous having a 0.00005% chance scenario happening every few games because the AI is clearly not following the shown percentages.

So overall, I'd suggest either waiting for a sale, or for the game to reach a better state. Don't get me wrong, it's an excellent timesink if you wish, but once you get into it, you realise there's quite a gap between its current state and what it should be.

review:
There are 3 core things holding this game back from a recommendation. 

1) Tactics cards:
RNG! 2.5 seasons (15-25 hours of gameplay) until you have the OPTION to manually have access to the cards you need. This hurts the game in a few ways. It restricts players effective hero pools, shrinking the game. Artificially inflating the learning curve and forcing the player into learning bad habits. Which creates an infinite amount of jumping off points. That kind of frustration leaves a bad taste in players mouths and can prematurely put them off the game. And not ever feel the need to return.

2) Scouting players:
RNG! This one is really bad cus they did it well in version 1 of this game. Then they changed it for no reason. And now it is trash. 

Before you could actually scout for traits you'd actually want. Then develop them further into players that can become champions...

Now? Now it's entirely RNG. A gotcha mechanic spits out random players. Then you have to spend, and I kid you not, casino tokens to 'influence' them. fighting every other team in the game for them. Okay. Why not. Ignore scouting. Trade for players you want, if you can afford it.

3) Translation? Not even once.
I've played and understood many Machine Translated games. This game has to be poorly translated on purpose. Everything is nonsensical gibberish. Meaning even the dialogue trees are RNG based.

If these core issues get fixed the game will transform from another shitty casino rouge-lite into one of the best team fighting strategy and management games ever.

There are a few more things that bother me personally.

-Versatility. 
When the game launched players only had access to one trait. So. That is why this goes here instead of being an insurmountable problem. Cus this shit sucks. It is RNG based. Do you have an idea for a player with 3 different play styles to seamlessly assimilate into every meta? To bad. You'll have better luck scouting them then spending 2 seasons bringing their stats up to game speed... Yes. That is a joke. 

-The A.I. 
Playing on hell difficulty. In game 3 of worlds. If the CPU loses here they lose it all. They spend an entire turn playing gathering momentum. Their next deployment phase comes up. 23 strategy points to spend... My butthole puckers. Then the A.I. proceeds to spend all 23 points to move all their players to gank my solo lane... while I had two of their players over-watched. So it was a 3v5... Where they were attacking a player not involved in the objective fight that was happening the same turn... They lost 2 players in that fight. Which caused them to lose the 2v4 for the objective... My Mid lane made 1,500 gold in one turn. And it wasn't even my turn... Causing them to snowball. Giving me the win. Great job devs. Nailed it.

All that nastiness aside. I love this game. While it does fail as a tactical team fight management game. It does succeed as a casino rouge-lite, tactical team fight simulator, simulator. Basically. If you like thinking about playing games as much or more then actually playing the game. This game might be for you.

-The graphics, sound design and U.I. are well done and charming. Yes. There is A.I. art. And what is worse is the fact that not only is it extremely poorly done. It is also completely unnecessary.

-The base heroes are great. A few duds. But with enough foresight and creativity you can turn them into hyper-carries.

-The rest of the management outside of what has already been mentioned is amazing and flawlessly implemented.

-They finally got picks and bands up to a Gold rank moba standard. At least on very hard difficulty. It is genuinely fun now. Before you just banged your head against the wall until your opponent beat themselves.  

-There are about 4 billion options. You can, almost, completely customize your entire experience in this game.

-The newest Rouge-lite mode. ;) It is really good. Player development is based off winning only. No worrying about trophies, KDA or MVP scores. 

-Worlds is meh. The teams in premiere league are so poorly translated their player names just appear as empty boxes. And the World rankings info tab is also glitched to where every player is shown to have lost 99 games, each season, every season. BUT! Tier 4 skills are cool. And being recognized as being #1 is always very nice.

-Building unhinged team comps of the most absurd heroes. Then going 90-0. The synergies and counter-play in this game is spot on... I just wish the CPU understood more of it.

Fin:
If you love spreadsheets, senseless min/maxing, and/or theory crafting. AND don't mind having the game continuously demean and disrespect your time and intelligence. Then you could consider picking this game up on a severe discount. If you are looking for a fun, casual single player MOBA experience. This ain't it chief. This game is less strategy and tactics. And more RNG and risk management. 

P.S. DEFINITELY Ignore the DLC's. I bought the 1st one and immediately turned it off. Lazy, thoughtless greed. Heroes and items thrown at the player that don't fit in the game. They feel like they are from a different studio. It is bad. One of the heroes has an ability that just feeds me free kills while costing the CPU 6 sp. Foso's Libra record against me is 0 kills for her to 17 free kills for me... Working as intended devs? I literally never use any of the heroes. They are unimaginative and sucky. ew. gross.

Hope this helps.

This game is simply too random.
Real moba games at a professional, esports level such as LoL or Dota have almost no randomness at all. This game was supposed to be a simulator of such games from the coaching side, i.e. strategic and management, meanwhile there is almost no actual management, it is limited to 5 clicks every match and possibly another five if you want to hire another player.

The actual game is 90% a card game, very random. The deck has 5x3+5x3 cards +3x5 passive effects for each team, it is hard to plan anything here.

The behavior of the players is completely senseless, nothing is simulated here, these are the most ordinary scripts in the world of following simple paths and random ticks counting whether and how much damage someone will receive, and with low health, return to base and loss of pace.

So for example, you can split push one lane all the way to the nexus and the enemy team won't retreat to defend it, they will stay in their lane and you can end the game like that.

And if the game goes on for too long, a deathmatch is forced. Even if none of your towers are destroyed, you will lose the game if you lose that one teamfight. So neither objectives nor towers matter.

This also means that only one strategy pays off: 5 characters for late game and teamfights.

Back to randomness: even teamfights are random, characters don't focus their attacks on the most important target, or even on the tank protecting those targets, they just attack randomly.

I've lost too many fights with 5 opponents with 1% hp to be able to say anything positive about this game.

Jungler? He won't gank anything himself, he can stand next to an opponent with 1% hp pushing a tower and he will ignore it. You have to take all actions yourself by playing cards.

[b] I do not recommend it, it has nothing to do with coaching, it's just a random Chinese card game, the English translation is poor, the mechanics are too random, the game runs terribly slow. [/b]

I'm putting it down after ~12 hours (plus some afk time) because it's gotten a bit too repetitive and easy, and I don't feel any desire to start again from the beginning on a higher difficulty. Ultimately, I'm putting myself as a No because I think this game should be a lot better than it is. However, if it seems exactly up your alley and you've got money and time to burn then don't let this review discourage you from checking it out. 

Pros: 
- Simulates the MOBA formula surprisingly well
- The voxel art is pretty good (it actually delivers on the teaser trailer really well) 
- Has a good depth of tactical gameplay (i.e. in the matches themselves) 
- Champions designs are cool and they feel distinct and nuanced
- Pick/ban and team comp building is challenging and rewarding 
- The minigames are generally pretty satisfying

Cons: 
- AI art is everywhere and ruins the experience a bit
- Translation is pretty bad, like others have said, though the important bits seem to be translated better. The only egregious examples tend to be the small visual novel decisions between matches, which hardly matter. 
- The deckbuilding aspect is pretty nonexistent. Once you have a good deck, there's little incentive to swap out cards. Same for multiple players - you can achieve flexibility with champion cards, there's no need to have substitute players 
- The minigames don't mean much. The small optimizations might be important at higher difficulty, but the game felt trivial on easy just based on the games themselves 
- The systems aren't explained well, and this combined with the last point means I stopped paying attention to basically anything but playing cards in games. I never lost a game this way (on normal)

review:
This game is really fun and addictive until it isn't.

The concept is great and scratches an itch I didn't knew I had. Art is okayish, I don't even mind the AI character art of the players that much, I just wish there was more variety. It's 99% the samey looking edgy oversexualized young adults with hair/clothing. There are some things however which just add way too much to my frustration and made me eventually stop playing. I'll list them here in order from least annoying to most.


[h3] 1) What the hell is happening [/h3]

This game is incredibly good at hiding information. You increase your athletes stats after every match. There's things like, "offense" and "defense", which should be pretty self-explanatory. But then there's stuff like "farming" - that might be the rate at which the athlete gains gold but I'm only guessing. "Mechanics"? I have absolutely no idea what that is. The number also doesn't mean anything to me. The 43 Mechanics stat just increased to 45! Is that good? Does this guy now have an advantage over other players? I don't know. 

In any case do these numbers seem to have absolutely no impact whatsoever in the actual match. I just had a game where...

- Top Laner with 60 offense playing Definitely-Not-Nunu which I have been buffing the whole match hits for 200 in teamfights
- Jungler with 50 offense playing Tiny Splinter Cell Wukong which I ignored the whole match oneshots enemy tanks for 2500 damage

Where does this insane difference in numbers come from? They almost have the same attack rating! Their active buffs have no indication for +% damage! What is going on?

By the way this is only if you're lucky. Most of the time the enemy teams Flying Gatling Brain that is 5k gold behind suddenly oneshots one of your champions every round for no apparent reason. "Wth this is OP", you mumble to yourself. "I gotta make sure to pick that champ from now on." So you lock him in first thing next match and what do you know - he's the worst load of horsesh1t you've ever had in your lineup. Insert [final boss vs. final boss when playable] meme here.


[h3] 2) Unfair match endings [/h3]

I've noticed two different ways for the games to end which feel really awkward. 

One is an extremely farmed toplaner pushing without end, destroying every tower and eventually hacking away at the nexus while none of the other lanes seem to give a single hoot. Now people actually having played games like League of Legends might recognize this as a thing that happens in reality - but not one that goes on for fifteen straight minutes in a professional tournament setting with several team- and dragon fights inbetween. Eventually the nexus falls to one guy with everybody else still farming on other lanes.

The other is a full-hp 5 man team having broken through every tower, standing before the nexus which is at 2 hp while 3 guys of the opposing team are still dead and the 2 alive with 40% hp have no way in hell of defending against this onslaught. The match has gone on for quite a while so with it about to end any second now the game naturally decides that it's time for the FINAL FIGHT™, revives and heals everybody to 100% and then pits them in a completely unrelated 5v5 teamfight until one team is wiped out. More often than not this ends in the team which was 2 auto-attacks away from winning losing the teamfight. And more importantly, the whole match.

Both of these scenarios suck, no matter if they happen in favor of yourself or the enemy team. If you win, it feels really cheap and undeserved. Not very satisfying.

If on the other hand you lose, it's straight up rage inducing because there is nothing you could have done to prevent this.


[h3] 3) Systems upon systems [/h3]

This is not such a big deal in the first few ingame weeks, since the only thing you do between matches is leveling up your heroes, have a google translated chat with your athletes here and there and maybe look at the showcased players of the week. 

As time progresses however, an insane amount of weird systems and mini-games get piled on top, to a point where it gets annoying real fuggin fast. 

I wish there was like a central hub from where you could decide what you would like to do after each match. Maybe you don't care for any of this stuff and just want to proceed to the next match. That would be great. Instead you have to click NEXT through every single system and mini-game like a power-point-presentation, if you want to or not.

Suddenly I have to talk to some a-hole shoeseller sponsor and discuss whether he is a better deal than our fried chicken cook. Yeah I guess, more money = better so I fire fat Colonel Sanders and sign a contract with shoe lady. NEXT.

Some intermission screen informing me that today's a "rainy day". Seems to have no visible impact on the game. Well, okay. That's nice I guess. I like rain. NEXT please.

Some puzzle mini-game to raise my athletes stats. Two even have "critical success". Thank you, very cool. Where's my match. NEXT please.

Now I have to roll a dice for each players mood for the next game. I have the chance to improve the relationship between two single teammates from 😡 to 😠 because apparently everyone hated each other from the very beginning. So I'm sending these two incredibly hot young animu teammates of opposing genders off to a candlelight dinner. No, I'm not making this up. Now they both hate each other slightly less while the rest of the teams content for each other is still the same. Yes. Great. NEXT please.

Then my coach has leveled up or something and now apparently has some stats too or something. Oh god, I don't CARE. NEXT!

Then there's three conversations in a row to click through, one where the coach talks to a literal owl that flew in, something something Harry Potter reference. I don't know, I just click-spammed to get through this sh1te before my ADHD brain forgets about the two new champions I actually wanted to try out. NEXT NEXT NEXT YES NEXT COME ON SHUT UP!

Then there's player spotlight, yes, great, none of my guys are there, whatever. NEXT. Another spotlight that looks the same as the one before just with different people in it. Holy hell, this is getting worse than YouTube ads. GO. AWAY. NEXT!

Then I have to build a venue. A. WHAT. WHY? Dude we are like 6 people in this office and now we have to provide money for an eSports arena for some unwashed teens to sit in and watch us play? Can't someone else do this? Apparently not, so I now have to decide on things like ticket pricing and wether to put in a commentator booth or just some plants which both have the same effect on the overall quality of the venue. Oh god is the NEXT button now finally not grayed-out anymore? Thank god. Now it's surely match time.

Lolno. Do I want to hire some more athletes for whatever reasons? Well no, thank you, I'm quite happy with the ones I raised myself through all of these tiresome minigames. Still I have to click through 4-6 pages of scouting/hiring data to get throug this part. Also contracts from my guys apparently have expired so I have to click a big RENEW button for each one to keep them playing. What was the purpose of this? I don't know. I can't click NEXT yet because apparently I have too many medals. I don't know what that means but who cares at this point.  So I click on things until the NEXT button eventually becomes active again. NEXT.

Finally I'm told  about the upcoming match. Clicking through 5 more laner vs laner comparisons, then 1-2 final VS screens and I could already proceed to the ban-phase. But at this point I lost all drive and interest already.

----------

Don't waste your money. Maybe get it on a 75% sale. Fun for a few hours but there's better optimized games that have way more respect for your time than this one. The way it is now it's just too tedious and from the looks of it they have no plans of changing things because they're already working on a DLC with even more stuff. Lmao. Good for them, I guess.

review:
This is the most mixed of mixed reviews I've ever really tried to write. I honestly don't know if I recommend this game or not, but I'll try and keep this short and coherent to maybe help you understand my thoughts.

The game is both addicting and incredibly frustrating. It's half esport team management sim, with scouting, signing, and training players as well as getting sponsors and building a performance venue. The other half is a moba simulation card game, with like 30 unique heroes, a bunch of player related skills, and a whole host of items to learn and play with. I do sort of feel that these two ideas are at odds, it's hard to trade away a player who isn't doing well when that also means you lose all the investment, strategy, and knowledge you had with their personal cards/heroes.

I want to give this game credit for being unique. It really does play like nothing else I've ever found, and when everything goes well, hours pass by in the blink of an eye. The caveat there is pretty massive though. The game's English translation is bad, and while some games could get away with that, a management sim + complex strategy game really needs to be better about communication, from tutorials, to card descriptions, to even just the difference between "Next" and "Skip". That's a big problem, but it's not the reason I'm on the fence about this game- the reason I'm on the fence is how the game can't decide if you as the player are just watching your team play their matches, or if you're actually using your skill and knowledge to play for them. You spend most of the time in game with the moba sim, playing the game, but the strategic depth wears pretty thin pretty quick and a ton of the game is out of your hands, either with randomness or just there's nothing you can do. Attacks can just plain miss and often do, you don't get to decide what cards your players have in game, and you don't have any control over where they move on the map- laners will always run to their lanes no matter what. This makes a lot of game states where the only solution is "lose the game and hope you get lucky with the randomness of the the management sim this week", which is not a terribly enjoyable feeling.

Overall, while there is a lot of fun to be had with this game, there is a lot of bad to go with that good. You need a ton of time investment to just understand it, and then the game just becomes a very mixed experience. For the time you need to put in and the amount of frustration from this single player game, I think you don't get enough back and you should put your resources elsewhere. If you like the unique style of this game though, I can understand wanting to push through.

review:
[h1] Buy For The Story and Dev Support. Play Demo For Game [/h1]
[b]TLDR: Its the demo with a completed story. Very little is added mechanic wise, its extremely short, making the 8 dollar price very steep and almost unjustifiable. If you want to experience the story and support the developer, go ahead.[/b]
[h3] Good [/h3]
A unique take onto the genre! The initial start is extremely fun, in typical incremental fashion you stop doing manual work to focus on upgrading instead over time.
Great soundtrack.
Visual fidelity is fantastic. 
[b]Story is written well. Personally it didn't affect me, but I can see how others might think about the game for months after playing it.[/b]

[h3]However...[/h3]

[b]The demo is the entire game, baring the continuation of the story.[/b] If you want to spend 8 dollars on a "You destroy the planet due to your carelessness and greed" type story, go for it. 
[b]There is also no power scaling of upgrades.[/b] Another generator, another cpu upgrade... these have no context. Adding numbers feels inconsequential, but evolving feels good. More cameras? How about a drone. More generators? How about a whole powerplant. Things like these make the game much more impactful and fun.
[b]The diagrams are just diagrams[/b]I really thought that the diagrams might have a gameplay impact but they are just visuals. 
[b]You cannot interact with the emails in any regard at all. Some emails dont make sense ingame either.[/b] "Click click click..." mate you click for the first 10 minutes then its over. "I keep seeing faces" No you keep seeing your resource bars go up or down, the program is doing the job for you. These are admittedly creepy but also jarring because gameplay is so much more different than what these people imply.

[b] Overall, I just find it extremely hard to justify the price point of this game. It is a very, very good incremental game, but the pricing is not good and its why I have to give it a thumbs down.

review:
FACEMINER is the video game equivalent to one of those fancy restaurants where everything looks and feels perfect, but the actual dish sizes wouldn't even satiate a rat. In other words: it's too short for the asking price.

(Audio)visually, the devs made something that I wouldn't roll my eyes at if called a masterpiece. The soundtrack is a banger and the UI of your 1999-based computer OS was done perfectly. I'm also going to credit the story for being a poignant reminder of what happens when you let a group of 1000 obscenely rich folks build datacenters that use more electricity than a small country so they can sell every single detail about us to each other to get even more obscenely rich, but I'll spare you my leftist analysis.

The gameplay, however, is where the game(!) falls flat on its face. I can really appreciate good soundtracks, killer visuals and a tight story/message, but above all else, I want my video games to have good gameplay to separate them from the movies and music out there. Don't expect the exponential growth factor of Cookie Clicker or the mechanical richness of Universal Paperclips. Trust me, we'll get back to that second one.

90% of the upgrades are the equivalent to "take less damage" and 9% are "watch abstract numbers go up". There are very few upgrades that add new mechanics that keep the player hooked. This is because the game's story has an average runtime of 2-3 hours if you pick the standard game length option. There just isn't enough game for me to solidly recommend this title.

Again, I really appreciate what the devs did here and I'm not going to unjustly call this game a cash grab, but it's just too expensive for what it offers. I'd say this is a $3 experience at most.

If you don't care for the audiovisual aspect (which again, this game nailed), I'd suggest giving Universal Paperclips a spin. It's a free to play web game with a surfeit of mechanics with more or less the same message as FACEMINER, although it's about physical resources rather than data. If Universal Paperclips is a bit too much for you to chew, I can also recommend the web-based game Crank, where you, well, turn a crankshaft until you get robots to do it for you, among many more things.

TLDR - Game lacks any log term engagement for what I can best call an "Idle-like" with failure states and an ending, has a major lack of feedback of failure states and end game progression, and a very short run time for a single run with nothing more to do than to read in game emails while waiting to buy upgrades. 
Overall feels like an unfinished in the mid game, a demo, or at the very least not up to standards for games in the same price bracket or cheaper. 

I went into the game thinking it was a idle/incremental game with a fun 90's retro theme, but found out it's built like an idle game with long wait times to get to the next mechanic like most, but stalls out at the 1 hour mark with no new content afterwords short of more money sinks to prevent failure states, and the build up to the ending (15 minutes at most), which itself lacked any feedback on progress. 
I had issues with temps and power randomly spiking and giving me an instant game over with little feedback causing me to be reset back about 30 minutes total over the period of 2.5 hours of play time. the only reason i manage to beat the game was due to this bug.

Great presentation, but there's not much backing it up.

The gameplay is simplistic even by idle game standards. You upgrade your software to mine faces faster, upgrade your hardware to support better software, and upgrade your infrastructure to support better hardware. That's pretty much the entire game, just playing whack-a-mole by dumping money into whatever upgrade is currently holding you back from buying more mining speed. You unlock some more features later in the game, but they're also just things you upgrade in tandem with your mining speed.
Faceminer isn't just simple, it's also static. The game doesn't change in any significant way as it progresses, you will keep buying levels in auto mining speed and its supporting upgrades for the entire game. I was originally going to complain about the game being short for a real game, let alone an idle game, (taking me two and a half hours to finish even on the slowest difficulty) but frankly there's not enough substance to the game to justify making it any longer than it is.

There's a story, but it's not worth playing the game for. While I do agree with every point it makes, it plays out exactly how you'ld expect in the most heavy-handed way possible to the point where it veers dangerously close to being [i]moral art[/i].

While it may look nice, there's not much substance to Faceminer. Take away the slick presentation, and it's a thoroughly mediocre idle game that I wouldn't even recommend playing for free. And I don't know about you, but I wouldn't pay eight bucks just for a fake Windows 98 interface.

Nice soundtrack though.

Visually, the game feels like it's trying to cash in on the Y2K aesthetic that's been popular for a while now with games like Nubby's Number Factory and Hypnospace Outlaw. There's no real [i]need[/i] for those aesthetics here though - Hypnospace Outlaw was about a very specific point in the Internet's history, for example, so the game recreated those Internet aesthetics. Faceminer could have just as easily been a Windows 11 desktop, and it would functionally change nothing about the story or the gameplay.  In fact, it might have even made the message hit harder? Ultimately, this game is a well-meaning but ineffective piece of satire on a hot-button issue.

review:
I almost want to recommend *Faceminer*, but the question isn’t “can you play it” so much as “should you?” Up front, it has an interesting premise and a bit of charm. The retro interface feels authentic and gives the impression the game might develop into something deeper. But the gameplay automates almost immediately and never evolves, creating an incremental idler that plateaus within an hour. The story tries to build mystery around who wants these faces mined and why, but it never really pays off that curiosity in either answers or impulse.

*Universal Paperclips* is the closest comparison: both games are about destroying the world through automating a single mindless task. Beyond that, the difference is obvious. *Paperclips* begins with a single button and keeps evolving—each new stage shifts the goalposts until you sit atop your throne of paperclips and realize how far you’ve gone in destroying everything to achieve it. *Faceminer* wants to tell a similar story about obsession and exploitation, but it gives away the moral upfront and never lets the mechanics mirror that descent. You’re told mining faces is bad from the start, so there’s no arc—just repetition. And mining faces isn’t fun to begin with, so why is anyone doing it?

The result is a game that looks clever but feels hollow. Its metaphor for crypto and AI collapses under its own contradictions, asking you to balance progress with environmental guilt in a system that insists you stop. Once you understand the point—and you will, because it’s endlessly repeated—there’s nothing left to play for. It’s a neat idea trapped in a loop that proves its own message: not playing really is the winning move.  And so, can I really recommend a game that actively insists you don't play it?
