Decent incremental, but not really worth it.

It's got the cute Win95 aesthetic going and it's got some mechanical depth that's initially interesting, but the depth disappears by the mid-game. There's three paces you can choose from when you start which decide what kind of idle game you want this to be, and I chose the 'normal' one. I had unlocked everything just about an hour or so in, and the remaining hour was spent just watching YouTube and mindlessly buying upgrades while I waited for the game to give me the ending it kept teasing me with.

On that note, actually: the game's plot and ultimate message.

Going in, it seems pretty on-the-nose: a warning about the dangers of modern technology - specifically AI - and the impacts that it has on the world, which could ultimately kill us.
Except then you actually get past mid-game and the company you're working for is actually essentially just a cult that's running its business to willingly heat the Earth up because it'll apparently mutate humans into some ascended form or something. Also, none of this is actually happening and it's just a training simulation for the real thing.

It's just so weird, and that in combination with how the gameplay suddenly tapers off makes me feel like one of those things where someone has a great concept, but they're only able to build out half of it before they ran out of idea.

For what it's worth, I did mostly enjoy the few hours I spent on it. But not enough that I'd say I really got $8 out of it, and I think that's my real sticking point here, especially because I can't see myself going for another run.
If this was ~$2, I'd probably recommend picking it up.
As it stands, though, I just can't.

review:
This game doesn't know what it wants to be. I would put this in the automation genre, but it doesn't let you design layouts for anything, so it's kind of barebones in that genre. You just click upgrades and balance stats. I would put it in the mystery thriller genre, but there's really not much narrative to this game. You get some emails to read, but that's about it. I would put this in the clicker genre, but you barely have to worry about the clicking of faces at all after a few minutes in the beginning of the game, and no other clicking mechanism is ever introduced. It is most closely related to the clicker genre, but I wouldn't recommend it for that.

Some aspects of the game are basically missing. You may see some footage of video where it's spotting faces. That's not gameplay. There's no video footage of faces other than a little video clip in the documents that serves no gameplay purpose. I also found the emergency transmission windows annoying and not at all realistic... to the point where they were the same videos over and over with no rhyme or reason to when they show up.

That said, the Win95 theming is done extremely well, and I hope it gets expanded on. I want to see  improvements to the music player. Maybe add a Winamp upgrade? Also, it'd be nice if early days GPUs were introduced to help with mining the video feeds. I could also see part of the narrative being that you have to upgrade the OS to support newer video codecs but you'd give up your anonymity in the process and have to waste more power on a newer OS. None of that is done here. Everything takes place on a semi-convincing Windows-like OS that doesn't have Paint and doesn't let you edit documents. It also doesn't have a command line interface, something I expected to see considering the focus on energy consumption.

What's unclear to me is whether or not the hardware is on your premises or networked into as an agent. I think that's the weak point I noticed before anything else. It appears to be a situation where the hardware is in a solar farm location nowhere near your real home, but when it overheats, your own computer overheats, so that breaks that illusion. Which is it?

Overall, I like the game, but it feels shallow. It could be a ton better. It doesn't feel particularly special. It is, however, a little bit relevant to today's AI-related problems. It's an interesting base for a game that could evolve into something special later, but right now, it's just not enough to do to keep things engaging. I suffered through the first playthrough just hoping it got more interesting, and it never did.

review:
ive got a lot of feelings about FACEMINER. its a game that makes you think on several very prevalent issues in our modern society. but the game itself can feel like a bit of a drag to actually play.

FACEMINER is a very blatant criticism of ai usage and the effects of ai usage, like the environmental and economic factors. theres also themes of cyber security, specifically once you unlock the ability to purchase facefinder cameras to harvest your own data. the game itself is an interesting form of criticism.

the story is heavily told through the various emails you receive. most of the emails are incredibly short. some are messages from the FACEMINER administration on things like work efficiency or claiming the negative effects are just fearmongering. other emails are from other FACEMINER employees discussing the ethics and effects of their work. a lot of emails provide nothing to the story, just standard emails about mundane stuff. its both an interesting and incredibly boring method of story telling. 

its interesting in the way that it allows you to see into the lives of your fellow coworkers. some seem to be hysterical and outraged at anyone who opposes their work, others fearful of the world theyre creating others are jaded and dont seem to care. these are all very real responses to the usage of ai in modern society, so i definitely think it was important to be included. however, your inbox very quickly gets full of messages. notices about efficiency or expenses, rank up emails, babbling between employees, messages from people opposing the work of FACEMINER, etc. it all just gets jumbled up. and since the inbox is the method of storytelling, all this nonsensical data makes it hard to keep track of the story. 

the gameplay loop is also a bit boring. you can select how fast you want your game to go or if you want to play an endless game. even on the quicker speed, the game still takes ages to actually reach the ending. and endless isn’t even all that fun– it’s the same exact game, just without an ending. there’s no new infrastructure or offsets to switch things up. which, gets frustrating even in a standard run. things get more expensive exponentially. it’s really easy to dig yourself into a financial pit or to basically keep your game at a standstill. 

one major bone to pick is that you have to pay to save your game. you get a free autosave after ranking up, but in order to save, you need to pay. and like all other upgrades in the game, saving becomes exponentially more expensive the more saves you make. it’s honestly just a nuisance.

the game does use ai for image generation. specifically, all datasets are made up of ai-generated faces. it uses nvidia’s ffhq dataset to generate these faces. while the devs claim it’s for thematic purposes (as well as it would obviously be tough and expensive to legally gather enough faces to create the datasets). but how many of the people whose faces were used in nvidia’s dataset consented to their faces being used? and since the ai is trained on real people who may or may not have consented to their images being used for ai training, it undermines the criticisms the game it trying to make. at least, in my opinion. the game’s whole point is to criticise ai usage through the unethical gathering of data and the effects it has on the world. if the game’s face data was gathered unethically, then FACEMINER has become what it set out to criticise. it ‘s a slippery slope.

all in all, a summary of the story is just “ai bad”. do i think it’s got a good story? yes, if you’re willing to do some digging to read the important emails. do i think it’s fun? no, not really. once you’ve made it to mid-/late-game, you’ve done basically everything but get the story’s finale. most late-game features, such as the emissions/offsets have barely any upgrades. if you’re interested in the criticisms this game has on ai and a cynical worldview, then maybe you’d enjoy the game. but it’s definitely a type of game you dont actively play, you just check in every now and then to upgrade it and let it run on its own.

review:
Ever wanted the strange lovechild of Tarkov and Grounded on a Far Cry-ish island? On paper, that’s Lost Rift.  Ocean ambience as far as the eye can see, with a weird sci-fi Bermuda Triangle multiverse... thing, happening in the background.

Crafting is pretty decent, with some nice QOL touches for making sure your buildings are exactly the way you want them, minus some very picky utility items that simply REFUSE to build if you don't have proper flooring.  Base building being removed from the PvP feature is also a huge win, no worrying about chronically online children raiding your base while you sleep.  (Looking at you, RUST.)

However, the charm, especially for Solo players, wears after the first hour as the island turns insanely hostile: mobs respawn before you reach your corpse, TTK is 1–2 gunshots or hyena bites, and those hyenas beeline past raiders straight to you. I did five corpse runs in a row and felt the fun evaporate as I was spending more time trying to recover lost loot than making any meaningful progress in the game loop.  

Verdict:  

Pros: 
-Decent Building system
-Nice QOL touches in some areas
-Base building separate from PvP

Cons: 
-Punishing solo balance (Especially with the chance of being matched against larger groups in PvP)
-Overtuned Damage
-Fiddly placement rules
-Weak VO/Dialogue for the Lore
-Always online even in Single Player Mode
-PvE Island is incredibly small, content being stretched in EA by PvP mode

Score: 6/10  Not worth it yet.  Maybe after some more tuning and content drops.

(In response to the developer post, it's highly unlikely I'll repurchase this game unless a member of my crew buys it.  It's just not in a place where a solo player could enjoy it, but I'll keep an eye out for updates, especially if there's a mode where I can fully enjoy a complete PvE experience.)

review:
I'm giving the game a negative review for PvPvE.

But first, I want to highlight the game's good points:
- An aesthetic approach and a setting that immediately draws you in.
- Truly breathtaking weather changes, some of the most beautiful I've ever seen.
- A pretty good taste of the depth of field, which draws you in and makes you want to discover the mysteries that the universe has to offer ahead.
- The art direction highlights different eras, but also shows a desire to stand out.

In terms of survival mechanics, it's fairly classic for the genre in terms of crafting and building. Nothing breathtaking, but it does the job very well.

Next comes the PvPvE part. I should point out that I am a solo player and will only be talking about my own experience, so as a newbie, I progress through the universe with the help of an NPC who acts as a tutorial and helps you understand the basics and get started. You follow along until this same NPC sends you to the western island. You are told to get ready, and off you go to this island to collect the components you need to progress in this tutorial quest (at least that's what the NPC tells you). Well, I shouldn't have. I find myself alone on an island teeming with creatures and hordes of bandits, but also two teams of five people armed to the teeth. I looked pretty pathetic with my old bow and arrow. I realised straight away that this adventure wasn't for a lone character, so I exercised the utmost discretion, avoiding hot spots as best I could. I gathered what I could, which wasn't much. Once at the extraction point, I got a rude awakening when an opposing team was there to greet me. I fled and died in a riverbed due to lack of energy. (Sad ending) Worse still, I lost everything I had crafted for my character. I felt like I had been literally punished by the game for wanting to explore and follow the tutorial.

In my opinion, this is a major point that needs to be reviewed and changed: the approach to this PvPvE world. It should be clearly defined as optional and, in any case, should not impact your solo play. Or at least it should be a completely different quest and narrative line. I stopped playing immediately after this humiliation and preferred to ask for a refund. I'm waiting to see significant changes and to be sure that I can enjoy the entire game solo, and why not PvPvE, but against a match-up that corresponds to your numerical strength. 1 vs. 10+ an NPC army is not fair.

Still the game seems promising and deserve to be tried. It's just not my type of gaming I seek for now.

review:
I went into Lost Rift hoping for a solid mix of survival, base building, and PvPvE expeditions. 
The concept is there, but in its current state it feels more like “Early Mess” than Early Access.

The good:

*The core idea is interesting: build a base on your island, then venture out on expeditions that mix PvE and PvP tension.

*When it works, the base building system is satisfying.

*Atmosphere and weather effects can look great on good hardware.

*There are occasional chaotic moments (storms, raids, surprise encounters) that feel genuinely exciting.

The bad:

*Performance is rough. FPS drops, stuttering, crashes, and even graphics settings resetting themselves are common.

*Bugs everywhere: falling through floors, ziplines not working, infinite expedition loops, textures breaking, loading screens that never end.

*The colour palette was made by an autistic genius - mostly it works, but when you look closer, it's like a play-doh mash-up of ugly brown in many places.

*Multiplayer is unstable, with frequent disconnects and issues joining friends.

*The map punishes you if you don’t build your base on the “everyone builds here” private island. Any other spot puts you at a serious disadvantage for resources and safety.

*Progression and balance are inconsistent: sometimes you’re far too weak, sometimes enemies are trivial, often it just feels uneven.

*Memory leak - the more you play, the worse it gets, until it's unplayable.

*Core systems feel unpolished — crafting, loot, hazards, and building collision logic all need serious work.

*Swimming is bugged - when you swim, you lose stamina, when you have 0 stamina, you start drowning and losing HP. You cannot dive and loot is on the sea floor.

Verdict:
At its best, Lost Rift shows flashes of the game it wants to be. But right now, it’s hard to enjoy when the experience is dominated by crashes, bugs, and design choices that punish experimentation. It might get there someday, but at this point it feels like you’re paying to beta test an idea that’s still too unstable to be fun.

Not recommended in its current state.

P.S.
Bots positively reviewing the game are not helping. ('nice game, buy' , 'nice!!!!' , 'buy now' etc.)

review:
Yeah...don't get this game if you expect to play it solo. The game is heavily stacked against you.

The game requires you to jump in to a PvPvE instance in order to progress. That could be very fun, but it's ruined by the fact that there's no solo queue.
The game is extremely grindy, and it takes forever to get anything done in an incredibly lethal game world where everything 2 shots you unless you're in the highest tier gear. You dump an entire rifle mag in to an NPC that basically has no armor on and a bow, and yet they'll still two shot you through foliage you can't see through while you're reloading. You'll spend hours and hours of that interaction on repeat until you get to the point where you figure out how to cheese the AI and actually start making progress, but then all of that time will be wasted when you run in to a squad of fully geared players that heard your gunfire and b-lined it to your location. Map is small so they get there fast.

I don't know how or why the oversight of not having a solo queue made it to release, but what a ridiculous mistake it was. The fact that this was also one of the main complaints in the playtest and then you went ahead with a release without solo queue anyway makes that mixed review status well earned. Listen to the players next time.

review:
Not a bad game, but instead of hotfixes for solo players they need to take the game in a different direction. Forced PVP should not be mandatory to progress in the game. Players should be able to have the choice to only play against AI on the expedition island. There needs to be a keep inventory on death setting when playing solo. Any game that relies on forced PVP is bound to die out if solo players are at such a disadvantage that the game progression becomes softlocked two hours in. Let solo players join games of other Solo players without providing a game code. review:
Nice game, good concept of PvPvE, so people who are not professional players/youtubers can actually enjoy PvP. That said, game has couple of caviats:
 - quests are a bit lackluster, and could use a bit better narration
 - gunplay is a bit stiff, especially in close-quarters, very often gun/bow misses in point blank where enemy is in your face, like hiena
 - level design is good but it needs polish in multiple places (e.g. rocks with 90 degrees edges)
 - match-making is often stuck on retrieving server information
 - enemies have night-vision and can see through foliage, they very often also hide behind bushes to shoots you (AI would need to be seriously improved in general)
 - balancing is lacking, e.g. hiena can eat your 50 DR metal armour in 2-3 bites
 - many other bugs

And as a side note, if devs want to avoid for their game to end like Marauders, they need to work on option to start match when there are no other players around.

In general, promising title, but not yet there to be playable longterm.

Edit (02.01.2026):
I have changed my opinion to negative. After the last changes, it is obvious the game is not going in good direction. Couple of reasons for this are:
 - one of survivors vanished
 - trade recipes changed for worse (e.g. you could exchange bottle of water for 35 ammo, now it is ripe coconuts)

review:
This game is advertised as an open world survival game with with base-building that has PVP elements. Once you play it long enough to see the core of this game (meaning the part that has replay value) it is 100% PVP. You can't advance at all in this game without doing PVP missions which consist of repeatedly visiting the same 5 buildings to loot the same boxes 100+ times to collect the items you need to build basic benches or complete the storyline quests on the "PVE" island. The pve island is equally limited with a few locations to visit but once you've been there and looted materials there is literally no benefit to ever going back...unless you enjoy wasting ammo. In addition the base-building in this game is EXTREMELY limited. You can only build with thatch and unless you want to spend 150 hours going on the same extration mission over and over you won't be able to build any benches to put in your grass house. You end up living in a grass hut full of storage boxes, unless you want to build several grass huts full of storage boxes. Overall it gets old pretty fast. 
I feel like for people who are looking for a straight up PVP game with some interesting side-quests on a home island it would be good. It should be advertised as such. For players looking for base-building, crafting, or open world exploration this is a huge dissappointment.

review:
On paper this should be a great game, a tycoon version of House Flipper? Sign me up. Unfortunately this game fails to live up to it's promise in pretty much every way.  The game is nothing but a grind. Don't get me wrong that can be fun, I've sunk hundreds of hours into grindy games like Destiny, Diablo, the Division, etc. The difference? Those are fun. REAL ESTATE Simulator isn't.

The first hour of the game is just an awful loop where you buy the same tent, shipping container or abandoned school bus and can only "improve" it by adding a sleeping bag. Then you sell it to one of the same 5 or 6 people who all use the exact same male or female voice.  All with the promise of unlocking the suburb and city levels where you can actually buy furniture and change the floors and walls and actually improve the listings.

Guess what? It doesn't get better. Yes, there's a painfully small amount of items you can now buy, but it makes very little difference to the value. And it's clunky. Oh, and you can only buy stuff at your office. Short one piece of flooring to finish your upgrade? You have to go back to the bus stop, sit through a loading screen, buy the missing item, leave your office, sit through another loading screen, catch a cab to the suburbs, sit through another loading screen, walk into the house, sit through another loading screen and then put that last piece of flooring into place.  Are we having fun yet? Welcome to Loading Screen Simulator.

The game has some potential, but in it's present state I'd barely consider it a functional demo.

review:
Can't recommend this game for a few reasons.

First, there's basically nothing to do. It starts off with a grind, you purchase your "properties" in the slums, add a sleeping bag and sell them until you unlock the suburbs. After which it starts to snowball pretty quickly. The "negotiations" consist of figuring out what the max an npc is willing to pay (usually about 150/100/80% profit for low/medium/high priced properties) and set all the properties in that specific range to that price, and just offer to npc's until they agree. You can go through dozens of people before you get a person to pay the price you want, regardless of the price you set it to.

Second, there is absolutely no end game. You have nothing to aim for, other than afford the most expensive property. You by the most expensive house, you sell it, repeat. There's no type of skill upgrade system or competition that would make you keep wanting to play. You get a small boost to some stats as you upgrade through the offices (3 total, your starting one and 2 better ones). But these stats are pretty ambiguous and you really can't tell what they do or if they even work.

Finally, six days before I purchased the game (7 before writing this review), they added a "quirky office intruder" (devs words). This intruder does nothing but walk into your office in his underwear, play some random music on a stereo and no customers will come in until you shoo him away. He adds absolutely nothing to the game. No reward. Not fun. Only annoyance. I got so frustrated dealing with this guy because of the random, yet frequent visits he made, causing the customer that I was about to show the house to walks out right before clicking the offer button.

review:
Well, there are some serious QoL issues here that make you question what was the idea behind the implementation.  They didn't change it after player feedback during the demo, so not sure if feedback during EA will have an impact or not.  With that said, there's somewhat of a game here, [i]IF[/i] you can get past the jank.

---Cons---
- Doesn't seem to have a map, but haven't played long enough to see how much that matters
- The controller implementation sucks, as you use the controller stick to move an on-screen cursor, this doesn't impact character movement, but menus are a PITA
- Some in-game hints/prompts show keyboard commands when playing with a controller
- Blocking works for like 1.5 seconds, so you have to time it JUST right
- Have to use the item wheel to switch or use everything - no hot-keys, except for skills you gain later into the game
- No pause in a singleplayer game - yes, I know, this one is ridiculous
- Random issues where I get stuck on nothing and can't move or I can't interact with interactable things in the environment - the issues usually resolve themselves eventually
- Inventory mgmt. is bad - no right-click to move, no shift-right-click, no drag-and-drop - you select an item, then push a button...to move ONE item at a time (not a stack)

With all of the above, plus a timer, you can begin to see where they intended this to go, but was that the right decision.  It feels like they either were planning to make a multiplayer game or add multiplayer later (still might) - the ONLY reasons I can see for not having a pause in the game, other than to simply be a dick and keep that serum timer running.  FYI, even in the puzzle sections that timer is counting down, so don't look at the puzzle too long.

+++Pros+++
+ Interesting premise
+ A new game to play (yay)

I'm going to say that for most people, meaning the average consumer, this will be a pass at this time.  The QoL issues are just a tad too distracting - using the controller for inventory mgmt. is just horrible, better to switch to mouse & keyboard, but similarly, combat with the controller feels janky and your 5 seconds of stamina don't help that out at all.

review:
This game has an interesting concept that I like, but I honestly can't recommend it at this time. I do understand that its early access so I'm gonna talk about the good, the bad, and the ugly that this game has.

TLDR: Game has a cool setting, gameplay mechanics are frustrating, game is buggy, and QoL is extremely lacking in this game. Wait until its more developed and check reviews before purchase.

The bad (Why you shouldn't buy this game): I encountered a game crippling bug about 3 hours into the game playing casually. This was encountered while doing the stepping into darkness quest when I died to a dullard sneaking up behind me. I was halfway through the quest when I was no longer able to turn on the electrical boxes needed to unlock the door holding the blueprint. I tried restarting the game and that didn't work so I decided to just return to base and ready up for the next quest. Turns out I was unable to even do that as I was no longer able to interact with any of the crafting benches and was effectively soft locked due to a relatively minor mistake of allowing an enemy smack me from behind. In addition to this bug, there are bugs where reloading a checkpoint allows for ranged enemies to hit you through the walls before they are able to load in, and there is at least one wall in the shipping container town you can just walk through.

The Ugly: The story has an interesting premise, the execution of it seems a bit janky though, immediately calling an unknown character over the radio by name is a little jarring after a slightly odd animation of inspecting your hands for some reason when you pick up the radio. The player character does in fact have a reason to know the name of the radio contact and its frequency, but this is tucked away in the journal that I would have never encountered if I hadn't been looking around in the journal fragments for hints on how to get to the floral research facility. Only other oddity that sticks out to me is that Natasha (I think that's the name of the creature you encounter in the floral research facility) is mentioned to potentially have boobs for some reason? Maybe I missed similar quips in other enemy entries but this almost felt out of pocket with a lack of establishing the character as someone to make such quips. Either you should establish that they make these comments regularly about the things that try to kill them, or just remove the comment that basically destroys what I'd imagine is supposed to be a tense moment of you hiding from a mutant you are clearly not ready to fight when you look back at it.
Since it'd be easier to just list the QoL issues I had, here's a list
-Inventory management sucks, moving things from your inventory to storage is tedious as you have to re-select an item once the previous stack has been moved over one item at a time. Collecting plants from the hydroponics tables is annoying as you need to select the individual plant and harvest individually to the point I just stopped bothering during my short play through.
-Ladders are extremely annoying, seriously, having to put an input E to interact to get on makes sense, but having to climb up slowly with the sprint making it only barely faster, only to hit the top and stop to have to hit E again to start a slow animation to get off the ladder is frustrating and basically resulted in me finding any other way to get up or down from things if I could to save time. Thankfully ladders are generally avoidable, or rarely required.
-Combat, basically I did my best to run by everything I reasonably could, or if I needed to fight, did so boringly cheaply or by trapping enemies on geometry or in one case, the ground itself. The player fights slowly, enemies are kinda stupid, dodging isn't taught to the player and was discovered by accident. Dullards are way too tanky and hit way to hard. This is likely to encourage players to use Serums that give blunt resistance, but its honestly easier to just run in circles around them to lock them into a spinning around attack thats easy to avoid (while other attacks seemingly home in on the player) and just click until bad guy horizontal. Actual placement of the enemies is alright up until you reach the container town's greenhouse, where you get spammed with ranged enemies to just run past or do what I did, and kill them individually in the dark. The floral research facility however is a much different story, locking doors behind generators that activate the plant enemies. This is a great way to force the player into combat, except the execution is god awful as they also have Dullards which require your attention to safely fight while you get peppered from several angles by plant enemies waiting for you to turn on generators. Once you suffer your way through that you get more generators with more dullards, plants, and now tentarats for even more ranged damage. Get too far away from a Dullard while you're dealing with this and they will run back to their spawn point and instantly full heal once they reach it, prompting you to continue to retreat for net zero progress, or risk further damage chasing them down if theyre low enough to kill. This full heal happens regardless of how close the player is or how much health they have, once you proc their return to spawnpoint behavior they are going to blindly run back to heal. If youre lucky youll get them stuck on something they can't reach you behind and just kill them for free. Enemies do respawn but very slowly thankfully.
-Healing items such as bandages and painkillers should tell you that they are usable, not just 'don't use them' resulting in me scrapping a lot of supplies that would have made my life easier.
-Respawning is basically worthless in most situations. You can just quit to menu for free and then reload the last checkpoint which the game gives you plenty of. Its better than death being overly punishing, but losing your items because you died is easily bypassed by just jumping back in time and not having to deal with making serums to get your old stuff and continue on. I do appreciate though that respawning lets you keep weapons and serums though, this makes death a bad thing without being punishing with how bad combat is. I discovered this by accident when I overshot with my mouse and returned to menu when attempting to respawn, and then kept doing that afterwards.
-As mentioned by other reviewers, the games optimization needs some work. The gates work as good loading zones and hide this loading decently well, the biggest thing is just performance while actually playing. For clarity this game was being run on a hard drive and not an SSD.
-Pausing the game does not pause the timer. In game menus make sense, but if I'm hitting escape I've grown accustomed to being able to get up and take care of something.

The Good: I don't want to leave the review off with nothing but frustration and talking about the games failings. Its an early access title that appears to be shooting for triple A status/quality and is priced accordingly. I thought briefly about refunding but was getting enough fun out of it to keep playing up until my softlock encounter. The story premise is really strong, the enemy designs are interesting and fitting for the mutation theming, learning how to craft items by scrapping them is a great fallback incase you scrap an item you need later or cant find it. Resources respawn at I feel appropriate timings and the hydroponics farm has the potential to be massively useful if it weren't for how time consuming it was. The timer mechanic feels well done, giving players an incentive to return home eventually as well as making time a manageable resource. Pausing the timer at the home base as well is a massively good move. The visible changes to the players hands and arms as you distort more with each serum use is a good touch. I hope to see this game do well in the future.

Howdy Howdy guys. I hope everyone is doing well. Unfortunately, this is the first review I'm ever writing and at the time of this review I would heavily suggest holding off here. I had a chance to play this before release and was excited that things would be better at the EA release. There are definitely some interesting concepts here regarding to the Serum mechanic and gaining abilities through experimentation and having to balance your toxicity.

That being said, there are a whole bunch of QoL that prevent this from being in a state of playability. First and foremost, the tutorials are not handled well at all and do give enough context with certain mechanics. It explains that you can gain abilities through Serum but never goes in depth on what the abilities do or how to utilize them. They are attached to hotkeys when you do get them but it is buggy at best if they will work. I tried breaking a wall with the wallbreaker ability, for instance, and it took me 4 times before it actually worked. And each time I used the ability led to a 20 sec cool down.

Performace is still not great and no matter the settings there was always some level of stuttering. Inventory space is limited but what is more egregious is that when putting stuff in a storage box you can only put in one item at a time and cannot send stacks of items to your box. Furthermore, at the time of writing, there are not hotkeys to send stuff to the box. You have to click on the item you want to send to your box and then mouse click the button to send to box. review:
Let me start by saying, "Serum" has potential. The devs are super receptive to feedback, which is always a good sign. But this game needs a bit more time in the oven. I'm running a 4070 Super with an i7, and I can't get a steady 50 FPS no matter how many settings I lower. I can run Hellblade 2 at 90 fps so it's not my hardware.

One big issue: the inventory tooltips, or rather, the lack thereof. When crafting, there are these mysterious symbols representing materials. It's like trying to decipher hieroglyphs without the Rosetta Stone. Devs, please, some labels would be nice!

Now, about the gameplay. This game loves its timers. Timers for growing, timers for needing more "Serum"". But it's not fun when you're far from home base, desperately trying to complete an objective, and you hear that dreaded "Beep... Beep." If you've used more than 3-4 serums, just accept your fate. You won't make it back to base, you can't re-inject yourself, and you drop all your loot. It's like a cruel game of "Groundhog Day,"but with green serum and bad optimization.

And the controls. Oh boy, the controls. Having an item wheel with no option to pause or slow down time is like trying to juggle flaming swords while riding a unicycle. Tedious and frustrating doesn't even begin to cover it.

I see what they're trying to do, and honestly, I think in about 6 months to a year, "Serum" could be a banger. But for now, it's a diamond in the rough. I'll be keeping an eye on this one, hoping it evolves into the game I know it can be. I'll update this review if there are worthwhile changes but as of now, I'd hold off. But maybe I'm just an entitled gamer and need to "Git gud" and also shell out for a 4090. Just the opinion of a random Steam dude. Grain of .02 cents and all.

review:
It's early access, I get it. But some of the core mechanics are so flawed that I just cannot recommend a buy at this time. I wanted to like this game so badly, I have been looking forward to it for months. Argh.

Gameplay loop is good, the pressure of the timer introduces a fair bit of urgency/stress and really propels the game forward. Voice acting is passable, which is an achievement in these times all by itself. Game doesn't stink of DEI yet either, but I only played it for an hour. On it's face just seems like a straightforward survival game with a cool loop. I thought it was visually impressive as well.

The bad part of this is the timer runs while you are reading docs that explain the story, and running while in the settings menu, and these particular details aren't urgency so much as terrible design, in my opinion. At least for a singleplayer game. That just isn't fun. Gotta run to the bathroom or grab a drink? Better exit the game first. For a game whose story is partially told through documents you find laying around, you better think twice before actually reading one unless you are close to an absorber. Half your time with be spent figuring out the interface at this time anyway, at least early on in the game.

Devs, for God's sake, fix the buggy absorber. For such a critical component of the early game phase, it is just baffling to me that a timer would be running during unskippable dialogue that lasts way too long for the timer, while standing in front of an absorber and being unable to use it because of the unskippable dialogue. All the while timer is ticking down. This alone made me refund the game. Sure, you can still use serum during moments like these, but it's just a bad mechanic to force me to do so while standing 6 inches away from an absorber.

The gate puzzles need a tutorial. It seems obvious to get the green line from one side of the screen to the other, using flowgates that you can rotate, but both times I solved the puzzles I was confused at how completing the flow one way would fail, but completing a flow the other way would succeed, when both times the flow reached one side of the screen to the other. Not to mention the W/S (presumably Y axis) component of the puzzles, which made no sense at all, and as far as I can tell had no impact on the puzzles whatsoever. You really should throw together a tutorial for the puzzles. And pause the timer while reading it.

Most importantly, the combat is flat out *terrible*. I felt completely disconnected from my targets. There was no impact to any of it, I mean at least sync the blows of the machete with the sound of hitting a target. It just felt so soft and underwhelming. IMO there needs to be more impact, better sounds, and at least some feeling of connection with the target I am attacking. The combat in this game is almost as bad as the 'combat' in Icarus, and that alone is so impressively bad it deserves some kind of award itself.

Lastly, the encumbrance mechanic was when I tapped out for good. The interface was bad enough as it is, but I could not figure out how to divest myself of extra weight in the time I had left on the timer. Largely due to how unintuitive the interface is. Cutting my move speed down 95% so I couldn't get to a chest to unload what had made me encumbered to begin with, coupled with no idea how to do it from inventory, and no meaningful tutorial explaining the mechanic is just chef's kiss level of annoyance. 

As a side note, I am convinced whoever designed the interface hates both me and the entire human species. Maybe Ultron designed it to confuse and demoralize us. Maybe the design plan was found in Hitler's bunker and was specifically created to baffle people into a zombielike state so as to easily conquer them while they stared slackjawed at the monitors in front of them. Or maybe it just needs a seriously fresh perspective applied to it.

To be clear, I really liked the framework of this game. There are just so many poor design issues, my God. But for the reasons above, no way I can recommend the game in this state. I will seriously consider giving this another shot later, principally when the combat is more refined. Good luck, devs.

review: Solid 5/10. I don't regret playing through the game but asking anything more than 20 dollars is too much. Game is held back very hard by inconsistent mechanics, annoying audio, and poor optimization. I did not know what the bad reviews were talking about until the second half of the game. Once I got there my frames never climbed above 25. It feels like they just forgot to optimize the last zone of the game and combined with some weird bugs, the whole game felt like it was being held together by duct tape. First half of the game is also wildly different in terms of game play compared to the second. In the first half you are pressured heavily by the timer and healing is not super easy to access so you don't have room to bring serums that give you extra abilities or resistances without constantly having to retreat back to base and spend resources on more serums. This makes combat quite scary, yet more meaningful. Group fights are deadly and most enemies resist the damage type of the starter weapon. Then you get upgrades for your serum making the timer pretty much irrelevant and you get the spear pretty early on which is the correct answer to almost every enemy in the game. Healing becomes easy and cheap and the weapon upgrades and serums exponentially increase your power. By the halfway point you'll have access to movement speed boost and health regeneration which makes you an immortal speed demon. Not even the final boss out damages the health regeneration if you try to avoid his attacks even just a little bit. Your weapon upgrades allow you to kill everything in 3 hits or less and you even get the bow which enemies are too stupid to react to when they get hit by it. After a while it feels like you are just dealing with the games shenanigans with 25 fps to boot while going mach 1 around the map. I would be lying though if I said it was not satisfying to completely obliterate everything in my path for a while and I loved the more desperate survival feel of the first half of the game. The beginning felt like metro last light juggling my time to be on the surface and looting things, as well as just using melee weapons instead of guns to take enemies out. The different serums are really cool but many seem to just bug out and don't work. Halfway through the game I maxed out the double jump serum and then it never worked again for the rest of the play through regardless of resets and save loading. The UI seems to just lie to you about effects all the time and there is super annoying ambiance that plays like every minute and you cant turn it off without turning off all sound effects. This game would definitely be a lot more satisfying to complete if the combat actually made you think and the optimization wasn't ass. This game makes me wish more video games came out prioritizing playability first and content second

UPDATE: Unfortunately I have had to update this review to not recommended. Not because the game is bad as it stands, but because it has been abandoned by the dev and publisher. I cannot, in all good conscious, recommend a game that will likely never be completed and released from early access. A lot of wasted potential here. My actual review below has been left intact in case anybody is still interested.

At this time of writing this review I have just received an in game message to let me know that I have completed all of the current content the game has to offer (early access).

So far I'd say I'm pretty impressed by what's on offer here. While this is 'yet another' survival game in what might be considered by some to be a tired genre these days, I feel Serum offers a good twist on the usual formula. Early on you find a basic recipe for Serum which is used to keep you alive against a widespread infection called the Blight. The protection this gives you is measured in time and can be viewed on your arm counting down as you go (but not counting down when at base camp). As you advance through the world you can see the effect it is having on nature and wildlife, as well as humans who have succumbed to it. As you progress, you learn additional affects for this Serum and can have up to three equipped at once. Some of these affects can have a profound impact on your survivability in combat as well as allowing you to break certain walls, or double jump or see in the dark. I really like this system and the core gameplay loop of venturing out, gathering materials for base and weapon upgrades and dragging them back to camp while also advancing your story quest while out and about works really well. There's also an experience system tied to crafting the Serum so you unlock additional effects as you go.

As for the base, don't be expecting anything too crazy here - you won't be freely designing and placing things where you want, or building in game versions of the Taj Mahal or anything like that. The layout stays the same, you simply upgrade what's there. 

For me the weakest part was probably the combat. It's not that it's bad per se, you have light and heavy attacks, block and perfect block, dodges etc plus different damage types which work better against certain enemies than others. The problem for me is that it feels a bit floaty at times. I've definitely played worse but feel the combat would benefit a lot from more impactful feedback, visually and in terms of audio. Another criticism I would levy is that the game is pretty buggy in places but certainly not unplayable, no worse than most other early access games to be honest.

I've completed the current early access content in approximately 13 hours and thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game. If you like survival games and are looking for something a bit different then this is well worth a look in my opinion. I look forward to returning at a later date to see what kind of content they can add to flesh this out, and see how the story line wraps up.

review:
I was seeing this game on Steam for a long while before I decided to finally get it. I was mostly hesitant from the reviews, but loved the idea of it. The concept itself is awesome and unique and I just wish it was implemented better.

I tried to like this game, but it truly fell short in my opinion. Yes, I understand that it's Early Access, but keep in mind that I've got nearly 1300 hours baked into 7 Days to Die, the king of Early Access games. Better yet, I'm probably at 3000 hours in Escape From Tarkov, the runner-up for the title.

This felt like Desolate, but worse. However, it is substantially better than Subsistence.

The melee combat is so static and boring and it doesn't feel like you're actually hitting the enemies. The base "management" is slim to none, with everything that you need already being available from the start. The only things to really do with it are plant seeds that take 5 minutes to grow, refill your generator, and upgrade your workstations. Issues with framerates was also a major problem for me. *(btw turn on FSR and turn off Frame Generation. you're welcome.)* Chests in the world taking 2 minutes of your available immunity time just for looking at them is a wack mechanic, although the puzzles to unlock them are a breath of fresh air.

The storyline and writing isn't bad, in my opinion, and I love the idea of mixing different blueprints together to make the Serum that you want/need for certain situations. The world looks fantastic, and I like how the items look.

Look, Serum has great potential, but in it's current state, and with the devs stating that they're currently "facing issues with development", I cannot recommend it. It's giving off the feeling of the first few stages of abandonware.

review:
The gameplay is quite fun and challenging that turns into nice satisfaction found in completing all the orders you receive throughout the game alongside buying each upgrade. Despite a few upgrades at first feeling more like setbacks, often the later automation upgrades feel much better and make those early days struggling worth the grind. Personally, the only set back in gameplay is found once you complete your upgrades, as the order complexity and numbers have just hit the point where it is more frustrating to play than it is satisfying, despite there being little challenge.

My only true gripe with the game is the use of AI images in both the title and pre-day hub area, alongside the AI music. It's a simple thing, but it both takes soul out of the game and makes it seem lazy. The character sprites, items and area during the gameplay in your restaurant are clearly hand drawn, and I believe that the style has charm, which just adds salt to the wound as that effort could have been extended to the rest of the games visuals and only would have aided in it's presentation. The AI imagery and even the music don't necessarily take away from the gameplay, but it just leaves a poor taste in your mouth. The transition from gameplay area back to the pre-day hub is also jarring.

I just believe that if the dev continues to make games or continues to work on this game, working on removing AI would greatly help the image of him, his brand and the presentation of his games. In the visual art department, it adds a level of cohesiveness to your game if it all feels the same, and to top it off it could all be in a style thats uniquely yours; 
I believe the AI route was only chosen because he didn't want to spend money nor time on the art, and whilst I understand that point of view, It removes from the game. At the very least he could have commissioned an artist (which, would also, further any good image he has)
The same applies for AI music

Despite this, I do believe that the developer has potential as he has clearly made an interesting and enjoyable game and I wish him luck on his developer journey.

Rating: ★★☆☆☆ (2/5)

Shawarma Legend starts off with a decent hook — managing your own shawarma restaurant sounds fun and quirky on paper. And to be fair, the first 30 minutes or so are pretty enjoyable. There’s a certain charm to the simplicity, and watching your little eatery grow feels rewarding… at first.

However, that charm fades quickly. The gameplay becomes monotonous and highly repetitive, making it feel less like a game and more like a chore. Before long, it starts to resemble a second job — and not the kind you enjoy. Tasks pile up, and the fun turns into a grind.

That said, the game does get easier the more you progress. As you unlock upgrades and automation tools, your restaurant starts running a bit more smoothly. Automation is definitely a game-saver here, and things become a lot more manageable once you’ve invested in it.

A word of advice: don’t unlock the custom order feature too early. It might seem like a cool upgrade, but without enough automation in place, it quickly ramps up the difficulty and becomes overwhelming. Wait until your restaurant is more self-sufficient before diving into that part.

The music is a bit on the childish side, but it’s also somewhat soothing — nothing too memorable, but it fits the light-hearted theme of the game.

All in all, Shawarma Legend just doesn’t offer enough substance to keep you coming back. It might be worth trying if you enjoy casual simulation games and have time to kill, but there are plenty of better, more meaningful games out there. Unless you're a die-hard fan of restaurant sims, I’d suggest giving this one a pass

review:
It feels like the ghost of Tribes, not a successor. You boot the game, finish the tutorial, and then look at what could easily be a mobile game. Details are sparse, quality sparser, and you're immediately greeted by your "Daily" panel that instructs you to buy a 40$ dlc. There is nothing to unlock, no skins to gain, and no weapons to earn. There is nothing but the gameplay unless you pay MORE money. This game is, without a doubt, modeled after F2P games. It looks empty and soulless. 

Then you play it, and remember exactly why you even hazarded the 20$ to try it. It's fun, it's fast, and man it feels great when you snipe people mid air with the spinfusor. But then you play another match, then another, and the luster wears thin. This is not the Tribes you once loved and adored; poured thousands of hours into and woke up early to play just one more match before leaving the house. It's all bitesized and shallow. Everything is there where it should be, yet the spark is lacking to ignite what should have been an inferno of nostalgic joy. 

There's something so viscerally disgusting about charging 20$ for a game that has 80$ of DLC day 1 into Early Access. It makes my skin crawl. The cherry on top is that you don't even actually get your rewards after purchase, but instead must win day after day to slowly unlock things. You are rationed your 40$ treats. I could almost see it if it were setup to where all the DLC + game would be 60$. I wouldn't like it, but I could see it, right? But that's not the case. If you want EVERYTHING in this game, it's 100$. A game modeled after a F2P game. If there were at least SOME skins to unlock for free, sure. You paid for the game, after all. But no. 

There's nothing. 

This is, in a word, soulless. Empty. A shell of what it should, could, or would have been given a different guiding hand. What a shame.

review:
It's 2024 and I get to play a new Tribes game, is this real life? It is real life, and unfortunately it's more of a nightmare than a dream. 

Tribes 3: Rivals scratches that nostalgic itch I've missed since the 2001 hit Tribes 2. After the initial honeymoon phase ends, you will soon realize that while it's still fun skiing around shooting spinfusors at everything, the game is a shell of it's former sell. 

There's a 16v16 CTF mode,  and a 7v7 competitive CTF mode. That's it. There's no vehicles, the maps are small to medium sized, and the game is missing many core features you may remember for previous titles. No text chat. Voice chat is disabled by default and in 20 hours I've heard 1 other person talking in game. 

That's the entire game. There's nothing to earn in-game, no skins or guns or skills or anything, which is fine; this is how Tribes used to be, but it's 2024 and games have changed. There's a 1 year chest you can buy which gives 1 gun and 1 skin with your first victory every day. But you can't even see what skins are available and there's no way to customize your character beyond these (title/banner aside).

Overall this is a huge disappointment, and I question why release it in this state knowing it could be the early death of this game.

review:
I have been a Tribes fan since the 90's.  Tribes 1 was my introduction to competitive multiplayer gaming, and it was amazing.  Tribes 2 changed the flow, slowed things down, but also added some extra depth, in adding extra weapons and vehicles and game modes.  I was an avid "Arena" fan, which was like a deathmatch/battle royale hybrid, long before the BR genre even existed!  This was such a high-skill game, so much learning required to come close to perfecting and no two games were the same!  I didn't get a lot of time in with the following Tribes games, so I'll not comment on them.  It has been so long since a new Tribes release: now I'm ready to dive back in AAAANNNNND:

I played this for a good few hours in its early access week, and it seemed OK for a play-test, but I expected much more for the release.  Wishful thinking.  

Tribes 3 takes the movement from the other Tribes games and does an OK job of it, whilst simultaneously making the maps tiny, so travelling skilfully and learning landscapes frankly unimportant now.  It removes all games modes except for CTF, removes all vehicles, simplifies base infrastructure to the point of utter boredom and stops you from being able to fully customise your loadout.  The game is alright at best, but Tribes 1 & 2 were amazing games, and they've almost totally missed what made them special.  Skiing was only a part of the jigsaw puzzle, and reducing map size so thoroughly has crippled even that.

This is a cash-grab.  They give you jet packs and spinfusers so they can call it Tribes, but it's not Tribes.  Avoid.

review:
There is a core feeling of Tribes preserved in this updated version, but the rest of the previous features that made Tribes are either missing or vacuous. Bases feel empty, defenses and deployables are extremely limited and game devolves into which team has the best light player who can fly from flag stand to flag stand without ever having to touch the ground again or face pressure or threats from the other players. 
Tribe was never about this ridiculousness of an unstoppable flag capping. So the games are empty and meaningless for all the other classes.
Additionally they have made the maps smaller and cut the maximum players to 12v12. They want to push the game as a 'Competitive' game of 8v8 or 4v4, which Tribes never was and cannot conform. The decisions so far by the developers to push the competitive aspect will fail as they have shown no interest in making a Tribes successor title, and the competitive team aspect will never materialize. 
Save your money for another title and let this cook for a few months, though I fear the game will collapse by then.
**Update**
This title was never intended to progress beyond Early Access. The Developer team of 1 has now started other 'Early Access' titles that they also will never release. its time Steam stops continuing fraud.
name: TRIBES 3: Rivals

review:
Basically imagine they took the archaic Tribes 2 mechanics and slapped some of the Tribes ascend mechanics on top of it, creating the worst of both worlds. This is coming from someone with 2000+ hours in Ascend, mostly as a capper. Here's what I immediately didn't like.

* Thrust pack barely does anything and just wastes energy, and is on a 15 second cooldown instead of just using whatever energy you have whenever you want.

* Extremely little air control, you basically can't redirect yourself at all in the air, but can with ease by faceplanting whatever hillside you need to, weird design.

* Can't use your pack while you're holding the flag

* no melee :(

* Grenade is no longer ammo based and is also on a 15 second timer.

* When you enable skiiing you automatically thrust forward slightly

* If you land poorly it doesn't matter at all, you still gain speed and don't take any damage

* Clunky movement, basically makes dueling entirely down to who can aim better, movement, prediction, and dodging skill doesn't matter at all. In Ascend you could win a duel from predicting and dodging well. You could use the air and ground in combination to make it harder for your opponent to hit you. In rivals you're basically always a sitting duck vs a sitting duck. Hitting Midairs is a joke because everyones movement is 100% predictable.

* No health regen. Not that this matter much to me, but I prefer having regen, less downtime and more action. No regen just forces you to go back all the time.

* Phase rifle is weird. You have to lead your shot, not hitscan, but also it feels like autoaim when you do land a hit. I never once landed a hit and thought to myself Nice Shot, everytime it was like, did that bullet just bend towards them, how did that hit??

* Bunch of weird "cinematic" video options you will have to immediately turn off. To be honest I think this is the most obvious sign that the developers do not know their audience or game. Motion blur, Adaptive FoV based on speed, camera tilting, etc.

* half the players seem to be bots, but aren't actually distinguished as bots.

* no text chat

Overall just super unimpressed with this game, felt like I was playing an alpha version of Tribes Ascend. I'd rather just have Ascend back than whatever this amalgamation is.

review:
EDIT: Nevermind, don't buy this shit show because apparently the devs abandoned it. 

[h1]Feedback for the Devs[/h1]

Here's a list of everything I think could help improve the game.


[h3]Offline Skirmishes[/h3]
I'd like to experiment with builds and practice against bots, but if the servers are acting funny, it's a bit difficult to engage in it, so please, above all else, add offline support or a LAN option so it doesn't require an internet connection for experimenting/practicing. This is by far my biggest complaint about the game. Everything else, one can give or take, but I think an offline mode is essential.

[h3]Text Chat[/h3]
I don't enjoy being forced to use VGS or voice chat only. Text chat would be greatly appreciated and very helpful.

[h3]Inventory Stations[/h3]
Tribes 2 did it best with inventory stations. Opened up a menu, set the preferred loadouts, customized it and stepped on the inventory pad to receive their changed gear. That was fantastic.

[h3]Free Loadouts[/h3]
In Tribes 1 & 2, you could have a range of weapons you could select, yet only have so many at a time, but you could easily mix and match in between. I liked being able to do that. Tribes 2 also did it best here and I highly recommend bringing that old system back.

[h3]More Deployables[/h3]
As someone who enjoyed playing the building engineer dude who set up turrets, and sneakily deployed inventory stations near enemy bases, that was a lot of fun. I also loved being able to place down different gadgets that would hinder enemy teams abilities such as stealthing/sensor jamming.

Please consider these points, devs. You'll go a long way to making it feel like Tribes even more.

review:
It feels like each of the components of this game may have been play tested, but not the game as a whole. Open world games depend on meaningful reasons to explore, which is where Brew Barons is the most lacking. One would assume that collecting new recipes and materials to grow your brewing empire would be the reason to venture out into the world, but you will run out of reasons to brew almost immediately. You can fully stock your bar very quickly and contracts from other bars come in extremely slowly, and often require ingredients which I was unable to find even after exploring most of the map. The game is beautiful and it's clear that a huge amount of effort went into developing the game mechanics, so it's all the more glaring that so little attention was put towards the gameplay itself. 

Biggest suggestions:
- Have the bars send you many more contracts with a wide variety of required ingredients, add other main objectives such as multistage quests that are not dependant on your characters
- Add more world minigames like the sunken wrecks, things for the player to do while moving between main objectives
- Make the range to identify world items and events much larger and keep them on your HUD much longer
- Incorporate combat with the pirates into the tutorial, or provide some sense of what the player can take of for combat
- There is no reason to be able to discover recipes with a single ingredient

Hopefully the devs flesh out the game parts of this game, but the amount of work that needs doing makes me feel that it will be a year or more before Brew Barons is actually in a state where it ticks the minimum requirements for an open world game.

review:
First off, I gotta say that I appreciate the devs sticking with the tried-and-tested War Thunder control scheme. On top of that, it really has a lovely concept and art style.

AND NOW WE COME TO THE PROBLEMS. I think I'll just address things in the order I noticed them in-game. The plane has insane weight to it. I don't mean it's going to fall out of the sky at any moment, but rather the time it takes after a maneuver for the plane to stop drifting towards the direction it was going towards prior is insanely long. It makes harvesting fields, during which you will do many loops to turn around, extremely tedious, as over the length of three fields, your plane will still be pulling to the side. On top of that, this game features the biplane with the worst roll rate in the history of mankind. It genuinely makes it terrifying when at the end of an Immelmann, the assistant tries to correct your orientation; you will pull to the side massively, and it takes just way too long while you constantly lose altitude. (I speak of manually flying an Immelmann, not using that upgrade for it).

Now to the upgrades. A whole lot of the parts seem situational at best, maybe even just gimmicky. I would have preferred being able to fine-tune the performance of my plane more while being able to balance my cargo capacity more. Instead, I can get pontoons that will economically ruin me or wings that will cause harvesting wheat to damage my plane.

Decorating bottles. God, it really is an adorable detail. You create your own badge for the bottle, select a nice shape and everything. And I thought, great! This will define my products, and then I can produce them, and the bottle will always look like this - it'll be great! Well, sadly, after that editor, you will never see your bottle again. So it's just another gimmick at best to finish the production chain with that. And remaking your recipes from the Products list? That's currently broken. Speaking of broken, let's talk about the UI. From being able to softlock your game from changing the place you want to go to in your building while the fade-out after pressing exit plays, to the alcohol mixing process ending up in some weird unstable states that disable the use of the brewery. Polishing is badly needed.

The core gameplay loop, in my perception, is just way crappier with all these issues. If I wasn't wrestling with my plane while harvesting, and the brewery didn't softlock me about ten times in five hours, I am sure it could be a LOT MORE ENJOYABLE.

But in its current state? Damn. I want to love this game. I want to enjoy my time in it. But the flight model just needs some real tweaks, and the UI needs some polishing (and please fix the producing from the products list). Would I like more upgrades? Definitely. But I think there are way bigger issues than just a lack of content here and there. I wish I could recommend it, but I can't. I hope the devs read this and fix this game up ASAP - because I think this genuinely could be an absolute gem.
name: The Brew Barons

review:
Mixed thoughts, i love it, but needs balance <3

I think the game is well-made, especially since only two people worked on it. It's really admirable, but I have mixed feelings about the current game balance.

In short: if you're up for flying and sweet graphics, risk a little money. Maybe the game will get much better if just a few things are changed. But for everyone else, don't be disappointed if the game is too demotivating at the beginning. It just needs a bit of fine-tuning! 

I have to rate it negatively for now because, at the moment, it's mostly not fun for beginners.

My toughts about The Brew Barons in long form, I would like to love it, but at the moment, there are too many little things that cloud the big picture.

Starting difficulties:
When you start the game, you already have some starting budget, but that can quickly disappear due to stupid mistakes:

The one-click shop: If you buy something in the upgrade store or just want to look, every click can bankrupt you because there is no query whether you really want to buy the certain upgrade; it is bought immediately. This is not very well implemented.

The Crash of your cash: 
If you crash, you have the relatively slow flight behavior, and then you have a problem if you already have little money because repair costs are too high at the beginning, and you are virtually stuck and can do nothing more except skip 12 hours and hope someone buys something in your bar to get money. Anyway, I haven't found a real solution without restarting the game to solve this.

Flying: 
The flight behavior is a mixture of realistic and arcade; unfortunately, it's not much fun. Visually, it's great, but you can change a lot with a few things in the controls or basic start setting, but unfortunately, not everyone who buys the game at the beginning will want to waste some time on the controls.

Crafting: 
The problem with the crafting, how should I describe it? I thought at first maybe the magic develops more in the crafting than in the flying, which couldn't really convince in the long run, but unfortunately, the bar and the brewing of alcohol are the weakest points in the game at the moment.

The problem is that you might think you've done everything right and maybe farmed all the components for 30 minutes (yes, in this game, everything is collected and harvested by plane, which can sometimes be a bit annoying due to the clunky and sluggish mouse controls, leading to crashes). You mix everything together, and in the end, you get rum or vodka, but the buyer doesn't want it. Maybe you've collected everything with your last money and have no money left for fuel, and you're totally broke. You simply don't feel like investing time in the game anymore because it doesn't reward you.

Even going back to check what's missing while brewing interrupts the brewing process and is seen as bad and annoying from the user's perspective. If I throw something into the pot and then quickly need to check something because I forgot how something was required or similar, I don't want to start over from the beginning. Also, the brewing process should not start automatically at 100 units; that's not so great for the user and is very annoying, at least at the beginning.
I mean the game is called "The Brew Barons," but what's not really fun at the moment is brewing things!

Work or fun:
It doesn't feel good; the game feels more like work than fun. Unfortunately, in a simulation, the game or loot should at least be basic or satisfying, or so many incentives should be created that I can still somehow try it. But right from the start, there are limits placed in the environment (Exploration).

Exploration: 
For example, I want to explore something, but on the next island, I'm already told that I need to upgrade my propeller to harvest. So, you fly for fun and to make new deals, explore aimlessly and want to take something with you right away, but you can't. Money, time, and nerves are wasted because flying takes time. It's just not a good game start.
I think many will be attracted by the great graphics and the many small and loving details, similar to the Porco Rosso anime or perhaps to a target group of people who like to play the Truck Simulator and chill out but with airplanes. Unfortunately, both are disappointed in the current gaming experience.

Controls: 
As mentioned, everything feels very sluggish and realistic, but maybe the default settings can be set up in such a way that you don't have to change the keys and thrust settings forever: Set the thrust to maximum sensitivity, swap CTRL and SHIFT with W and S, and it's a bit clearer and easier because at the beginning, you or quite a few who don't start directly with a gamepad use the mouse and keyboard.

The Positive:
Great graphics, many loving details such as the change of pilots when they get tired or the design of the bar (although there could be more), or the design of your own bottles (it would be nice to be able to view the bottles later, unfortunately, that wasn't possible anywhere). Great approach, as it could attract logisticians, crafters, and airplane and anime enthusiasts, or even explorers.

Conclusion:
But at the moment, it has big problems convincing players from the start because the grind is too demotivating, and at least at the beginning, the effort is too high, and the sense of achievement is too little to sustain in the long run. Perhaps the developers should work on this again to find better balancing that is more motivating and create such details as instant purchases in the shop or better clarity in brewing or better reference points so that recipes succeed and are also bought by customers in the game to simply improve the entry and not demotivate too much.

I hope the developers take action and receive support from you because it's a great idea to fly around, craft, discover, and even face some challenges in combat. Thank you for the great idea.

review:
First of all let's get the elephant out of the room, this game use AI voices, so if you're not into that then stay away. I did not know this, so I was taken off-guard.

Now, this game is one of those 'Amazing idea and concept' but 'Meh executions'. What I mean by this? The whole game idea's amazing, and the fact you're allowed to fight in an old type plane is great--but the gameplay, its performance,  its scope, and the AMMOUNT OF GRIND just doesn't make it a worthwhile purchase. Heck, its two main selling point, the brewing and air fight, are a bunch of let down that just isn't fun. The game felt too slow for a plane game, map too big to traverse that it became boring, and the brewing while fun the first few times it became an annoying and boring drag. It also did not help that running the pub is so basic and not enjoyable that it almost made me wonder why adding it in the first place. 

I have mixed feeling with the plane editor but mostly disappointment. In hindsight it's pretty good, you can change colors of your plane, add banners, etc. etc. But then you have to PAY for for every little things, and it's not cheap either. Why do painting my plane cost so much? Why not just make it free? I HAD TO BUY IT FROM A CATALOGUE, FIND MY OWN PARTS AND PAY AGAIN TO INSTAL IT. It's one thing if it's cheap, it's not. 

The writing, AI Voice, and other nitpicks aren't that great either. Though I do enjoy when one of the pilot parent kept pestering her by calling while she's co-piloting.

It's a frustating and disappointing experience, which is sad because I WANT this game to be good--I love planes, and to be able to be a pilot with a partner while running a booze business sound awesome. The game just can't live up to its concept. So I cannot in good faith recommend this game.

review:
Brew Barons

AI voice acting. And bad writing. It really, really hurts.

It's a cool-ass concept for a game, don't get me wrong. Very pretty, too. In that sort of 'Valkyria Chronicles' way where everything looks pastoral and idyllic and the machines look very... Punk? Hard to describe, really.

That being said, the main core of the game is fairly decent, if a bit lacking at times. You fly around collecting ingredients for your alcohol, then you turn those ingredients into alcohol, then you either stock your own bar, or sell it to the other bars. I do kind of wish each system was more in-depth.

For example, harvesting apples off a tree is just... Shooting the tree, then flying kinda-close to it which vaccuums up the apples. Collecting potatoes involves bombing a potato field, then just flying kinda-close and vaccuuming it up again. Part of me wishes there was a bit more... Danger? Mechanical depth involved? War Thunder plane controls mean flying and controlling your plane is dirt-easy, meaning the core loop is basically impossible to fuck up in any way and is pretty repetitive.

The combat is... Something? I tried it a few times and it felt very... Slow and dull? Maybe I haven't unlocked extra weapons down the line, but the dogfighting wasn't particularly exciting.

The actual map is... A bit too large for how slow your plane is, too. There isn't enough interesting scenery and obstacles to justify how big the map is given just how empty it is and how slow your plane is, and how little there is to do WHILE you're going from island-to-island.

My biggest gripe, though?

The written dialogue and the voice acting is downright atrocious. I could get over a kinda-okay-ish gameplay loop if the game had interesting characters, chatter, dialogue, and potentially voice-acting. Maybe I'm just an old Ace Combat player who thinks every plane game that isn't Ace Combat is shit, but man. If you're going to give me all this downtime and repetitive gameplay where I'm not really doing anything as my plane slowly trundles along to my destination, the least you could do is toss in plenty of chatter between your pilot and copilot, or radio chatter from your plane back to your bar.

What voice-acting that IS in-game has the most stilted dialogue known to man. None of the speech feels natural. Everyone is overly verbose and bland in a way that doesn't make sense. It's like the most boring and uninteresting dialogue known to man, compounded with an AI voiceover that's just completely flat and dull, with the game taking way too many lines to explain something incredibly simple more often than not.

And the tutorial. Man. It's rough. It's opening is good- I like the idea of getting to know your seaplane by taxi-ing it around a canal for a bit, but that's literally the only good part of the tutorial. Everything else is just... Frustratingly slow and has way too much explaining going on for mechanics that are relatively simple.

I'll likely play the game to completion and maybe re-review then, since apparently this game only takes around 20-odd hours to finish in its current state (This estimation from the fact that a player asking for help on the final boss of the game in the Steam forums had 18 hours in it). But man, these first few hours really aren't... Enticing.
